1.overview:
Jacob's family, seventy people, has settled in Egypt. Joseph and his generation die, and their descendants multiply until the land is full of them. A new king who does not know Joseph sees a threat, so Egypt sets taskmasters over Israel and puts them to work building the store cities Pithom and Raamses. When forced labor fails to slow their growth, the king orders the Hebrew midwives, Shiphrah and Puah, to kill every newborn boy. They fear God and refuse. Finally Pharaoh commands all his people to throw every Hebrew son into the river.

Notice that every plan backfires. The harder Egypt presses, the more Israel grows (vv. 12, 20). Pharaoh ends up fighting the blessing of increase God gave at creation, and he cannot stop it.

1.hermeneutics:
Raamses is Pi-Ramesse, “House of Ramesses,” the Delta capital that Ramesses II (reigned c. 1279–1213 BC) built at modern Qantir. Pithom is Per-Atum, “House of Atum,” a temple town in the Wadi Tumilat, placed at Tell el-Retaba or Tell el-Maskhuta. Both sat on Egypt's eastern frontier, where armies left for Canaan and invaders came in. Next to Qantir lies Avaris, the old capital of the Hyksos, Semitic-speaking rulers who held the north of Egypt until they were driven out about 1550 BC. A king who fears that a growing eastern people will “join also unto our enemies” (v. 10) speaks like a court that remembered the Hyksos.

Forced labor by foreigners was routine state policy. The tomb of the vizier Rekhmire at Thebes (c. 1450 BC) paints Syrians and Nubians beside Egyptians, drawing water, mixing clay, and molding bricks for workshops at the temple of Amun, while Egyptian overseers with batons watch. A label calls them captives brought by the king for the work of the temple. The “taskmasters” of v. 11 are *sare missim*, “chiefs of forced labor,” the vocabulary of a state work gang, and v. 14's “mortar, and brick” describes exactly what the painting shows.

The “stools” of v. 16 are literally “the two stones.” Egyptian women gave birth kneeling or squatting on bricks, and the goddess Meskhenet was pictured as a birth brick with a woman's head. A painted birth brick found at South Abydos in 2001 (c. 1750 BC) shows a mother holding her newborn. Pharaoh's order puts the killing at the moment of delivery, at the very spot Egyptians surrounded with protective magic.

structure.summary: No strong pattern; the chapter moves in sequence, through three plans that each fail.

rows.text: Israel grows and fills the land

notes: **Creation language:** Verse 7 stacks the verbs of Genesis 1:28 and 9:7: be fruitful, swarm, multiply, fill. The verb “multiply” (*rabah*) then recurs after each Egyptian move (vv. 7, 10, 12, 20).
**Service:** In vv. 13–14 the root for serving and labor (*avad*, *avodah*) appears five times in two verses. The same root later names what God wants Israel to do for him (3:12).
**Names:** The two midwives are named; the king never is. He is only “Pharaoh” or “the king of Egypt.”

Verse 1 repeats the opening words of Genesis 46:8, “these are the names of the children of Israel,” so Exodus begins by picking up Genesis where the family went down. The Hebrew title of the book, *Shemot* (“Names”), comes from this line. The unit runs through 2:25, from Israel's oppression to the moment God hears their cry.

**Echoes:** Genesis 15:13 foretold a people afflicted in a land not theirs. Matthew's account of Herod killing the children of Bethlehem (Matthew 2:16) retells a king's slaughter of infants with the new deliverer escaping.

traditions.text: Lehi quotes a prophecy of Joseph of Egypt that the Lord would raise up Moses “to deliver thy people out of the land of Egypt.” The same prophecy pairs Moses with a latter-day seer who will be as great as Moses. In Genesis 50:24 Joseph says only that God will visit his brothers; here he names the deliverer before the bondage begins. Read alongside Exodus 1, which opens with Joseph's death (v. 6), the rescue was promised before the new king ever rose.

Jubilees fills the gap between Joseph's death and the new king with a war. Makamaron, king of Canaan, kills a king of Egypt, and the gates of Egypt are closed. Meanwhile the Israelites carry the bones of Jacob's sons, all but Joseph, to burial in Canaan, and some, Amram among them, stay in the hills of Hebron. Egypt then sets taskmasters over Israel for fear they will side with its enemies, which supplies the war Pharaoh worries about in v. 10.

Josephus widens the labor: digging channels for the river, building walls and ramparts, and “they set them also to build pyramids.” He says the affliction lasted four hundred years. He also gives the river decree a motive: a sacred scribe foretold that a Hebrew child would bring Egypt low, so the order aims at Moses before he is born, much like Herod's search in Matthew 2.

Philo describes the work gangs in detail: overseers set over the Hebrews, some shaping clay into bricks, others gathering straw, which he calls “the bond which binds bricks together.” Exodus itself does not mention straw until 5:7, when it is taken away. Philo's description shows how a Jew in Egypt pictured the brickyards.

Rav and Shmuel debate the “new king” of v. 8: one says he really was new, the other that he was the same king with new decrees, acting as though he did not know Joseph. Another teaching explains why the final decree uses the river. Pharaoh's counselors chose water because God had sworn never again to send a flood, not realizing the oath covered the whole world and not a single nation. The Talmud sees the answer at the sea, where the Egyptians drown (14:27).

A teaching handed down in Rabbi Simai's name says Pharaoh consulted three advisers before the decrees. Balaam proposed the plan and later died by the sword; Job kept silent and was punished with suffering; Jethro fled in protest, and his descendants were rewarded with seats in the high court. Exodus never names Pharaoh's counselors, but Jethro reappears in 2:16–22 and 3:1 as the priest who shelters Moses.

One view makes the midwives Moses' own family: Shiphrah is Jochebed, named for tending the newborn, and Puah is Miriam, named for the soothing sounds she made to the baby. The “houses” God made for them (v. 21) are read as the priestly line through Aaron and Moses, or the royal line through David. Rav Avira adds that Israel was redeemed from Egypt for the sake of the righteous women of that generation.

Stephen ties Israel's growth to timing: the people multiplied “when the time of the promise drew nigh” that God had sworn to Abraham. He also says the king treated their fathers so harshly that they cast out their own infants. In his telling, Moses is born at that very moment, which makes the deliverer arrive at the worst point of the crisis.

Augustine asks whether God rewarded the midwives for lying to Pharaoh (v. 19). He answers no: their reward came “not because they lied, but because they were merciful to God's people.” He grants that God bore with their lie, but he holds that women fully taught the truth would have refused both to lie and to kill.

An Egyptian priest who wrote his country's history in Greek. Josephus quotes his account of eastern invaders who seized Egypt, fortified Avaris, and were called “Hycsos,” or shepherd-kings, until they were driven out and built Jerusalem. Josephus, arguing for the great age of the Jewish people, claims these shepherds were “no other than our forefathers.” It is the oldest surviving attempt to fit Israel's time in Egypt into Egyptian history.

2.overview:
A Levite couple has a son. His mother hides him for three months, then seals him in a basket of papyrus and sets it among the reeds of the Nile while his sister watches. Pharaoh's daughter finds the crying baby, takes pity on him, and pays his own mother to nurse him. Later she adopts him and names him Moses. Grown, Moses kills an Egyptian he sees beating a Hebrew, is challenged by a Hebrew the next day, and flees to Midian. There he defends seven sisters at a well, marries Zipporah, and names his son Gershom, “a stranger here.”

God is not mentioned in vv. 1–22. Every rescue comes through people: a mother, a sister, a princess, a fugitive. Then in the last three verses God becomes the subject of every verb: he hears, remembers, looks, and knows. The silence ends just before the burning bush.

2.hermeneutics:
A legend of Sargon of Akkad, the Mesopotamian king of about 2300 BC, survives in Assyrian copies from the 7th century BC. In it Sargon says his mother, a priestess, bore him in secret, set him in a basket of rushes sealed with bitumen, and put him in the river. Akki, a water-drawer, lifted him out and raised him, and the goddess Ishtar later made him king. Ancient hearers knew this shape: a great leader begins as an abandoned infant on the water. Exodus uses the same pieces (rushes, pitch, river, a rescuer) but turns them around. The mother hides her son to save him, and the rescuer is the daughter of the king who ordered his death.

The name Moses fits Egypt. The Egyptian verb *msi*, “to be born,” forms royal names such as Ahmose, Thutmose, and Ramesses (“Ra is the one who bore him”). A princess would naturally give her foundling an Egyptian name. Verse 10 then adds a Hebrew sound-play: Moses sounds like the Hebrew verb for “draw out,” and the boy drawn out of the water will draw his people out through the sea.

The Egyptian *Story of Sinuhe* (c. 1900 BC) was a classic read by scribes for centuries. Sinuhe, a court official, panics when the king dies and flees east across the frontier. Near death from thirst, he is taken in by a Canaanite chieftain, marries the chief's eldest daughter, and prospers as a herdsman among foreigners. Moses' flight runs the same course: fear of Pharaoh, escape east, welcome at a well, marriage to a chief's daughter. An Egyptian reader would recognize the exile story, now told of a Hebrew.

structure.summary: No strong pattern; the chapter moves in sequence through three scenes and a closing turn.
notes: **Seeing:** The verb “see” occurs 7 times: the mother sees the child is good (v. 2), the princess sees the basket and the baby (vv. 5–6), Moses sees the burdens and the beating and looks for witnesses (vv. 11–12), and God sees Israel (v. 25).
**Rescue at the water:** Women rescue Moses at the river (vv. 5–10); then Moses rescues women at a well, where “drew water” occurs 3 times (vv. 16, 19).

**The basket:** Its Hebrew name, *tevah*, appears in Genesis and Exodus only here (vv. 3, 5) and for Noah's ark (Genesis 6–9). Both are sealed with pitch, and both carry one life through deadly water.

The chapter closes the opening unit (1:1–2:25). The bondage that began in 1:8–14 reaches its lowest point when Israel's cry goes up and God responds (2:23–25). Moses' years in Midian set up the next scene, which takes place while he keeps his father-in-law's flock (3:1).

**Links:** God's words at the bush, “I have surely seen … and have heard their cry” (3:7), pick up 2:24–25. The New Testament retells this chapter twice, as Stephen's history (Acts 7:20–29) and as a roll call of faith (Hebrews 11:23–27).

traditions.text: Exodus 2 introduces “the priest of Midian” (v. 16) without saying whose priest he is. In D&C 84 Moses receives the Holy Priesthood under the hand of his father-in-law, Jethro, and the revelation traces Jethro's authority back through Caleb, Elihu, Jeremy, Gad, and Esaias to the days of Abraham. The household that shelters the fugitive in v. 20 thus holds the authority Moses will carry back to Egypt.

In Josephus, Amram learns in a dream that his son will deliver Israel. Pharaoh's daughter is named Thermuthis; the baby refuses every Egyptian nurse until Miriam brings his own mother. Josephus explains the name from Egyptian: “the Egyptians call water by the name of Mo,” and those saved out of it *Uses*. When the king playfully sets his crown on the child, Moses throws it down and tramples it, and only Thermuthis keeps the alarmed scribe from having him killed.

Jubilees names the princess Tharmuth and adds that the baby lay in the basket seven days. His mother came at night to nurse him, and by day Miriam guarded him from the birds. His father Amram taught him to write, and he spent three weeks of years, twenty-one years, at court before he killed the Egyptian.

Philo also derives the name from Egyptian, “for the Egyptians call water ‘mos.’” He says the childless princess had long feigned pregnancy so the boy would pass as her own son. Teachers from Egypt and Greece trained him, with others who taught him Assyrian letters and astronomy. Philo calls the killing of the Egyptian, who had worked Hebrews to death, a pious act.

After the river decree, Amram divorces his wife so as not to father sons for slaughter. Miriam tells him his decree is harsher than Pharaoh's, since it denies life to daughters as well, and he remarries Jochebed. The rabbis read “she saw him that he was a goodly child” (v. 2) through Genesis 1:4, where God saw the light was good: at Moses' birth the whole house filled with light.

Rabbi Yohanan reads the princess's bathing (v. 5) as immersion to cleanse herself of her father's idols. The baby refuses Egyptian nurses because the mouth that would speak with God should not take impure milk. Rabbi Elazar adds that Pharaoh's astrologers foresaw the deliverer's downfall through water, so once Moses was set in the river they canceled the decree; they had misread the sign, which pointed to the waters of Meribah (Numbers 20:13).

A Jewish writer in Egypt, known through quotations in Eusebius. The princess Merris adopts the child and names him Mouses, whom the Greeks call Musaeus, teacher of Orpheus. King Chenephres, jealous, sends Moses against the Ethiopians and then plots his murder. Moses kills the would-be assassin, Chanethothes, flees to Arabia, and marries Raguel's daughter, so the killing becomes self-defense.

A Jewish playwright who staged the Exodus as a Greek tragedy. In Midian, Moses tells his father-in-law a dream: on the summit of Sinai he saw a great throne reaching to heaven, and a noble figure seated him on it. The father-in-law reads it as a good sign from God, a forecast of the mountain where Moses will lead his people (3:12).

Stephen adds that Moses “was learned in all the wisdom of the Egyptians” and was forty when he went out to his brethren. He gives Moses a motive the chapter leaves unstated: he supposed his people would understand that God meant to deliver them by his hand, but they did not. Stephen uses the rejected deliverer of v. 14 as a pattern for Israel's rejection of Jesus.

Hebrews credits the parents' hiding of the child to faith: they were not afraid of the king's command. Moses' choice to side with the Hebrews becomes a refusal to be called the son of Pharaoh's daughter. Exodus says Moses fled because he “feared” (v. 14), while Hebrews says he left Egypt not fearing the king's wrath, so the two can be read of different moments.

Clement gives Moses three names: Joachim from his parents at his circumcision, Moses from Pharaoh's daughter, and Melchi, received in heaven after his ascension. Egyptian masters taught him arithmetic, geometry, music, medicine, and the symbolic writing of the hieroglyphs. He reports that some said Moses killed the Egyptian by a word alone.

A Greek geographer who describes Moses as one of the Egyptian priests, holding part of Lower Egypt, who left because he rejected Egypt's way of picturing the divine as animals. Strabo knows nothing of the basket or the Hebrew birth, but he shares with Exodus 2, Philo, and Clement the picture of a Moses formed inside Egyptian learning.

3.overview:
Moses is keeping his father-in-law's flock when he comes to Horeb, the mountain of God, and sees a bush on fire that does not burn up. When he turns aside to look, God calls his name, tells him to take off his shoes on holy ground, and names himself the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. God has seen Israel's affliction and heard their cry, and he sends Moses to Pharaoh. Moses objects twice: who is he to go, and what name should he give? God promises to be with him and gives his name, “I AM THAT I AM,” then lays out the plan: the elders, Pharaoh's refusal, wonders, and a departure with Egypt's silver and gold.

Listen to God's first answer. To “Who am I?” he does not answer with Moses' qualifications. He says “I will be with thee” (v. 12), and the Hebrew verb there, *ehyeh*, is the same word that becomes his name two verses later.

3.hermeneutics:
In Egypt a god's hidden name held his power. A Ramesside papyrus (Turin 1993, c. 1200 BC) tells how the goddess Isis formed a serpent from the aging sun god Ra's spittle and set it on his path. Bitten and in agony, Ra listed his many public names, but Isis would not heal him until he gave up the secret one, and with it a share of his power. Moses' question “What is his name?” (v. 13) comes from that world, where knowing a name meant having a hold on its owner. God answers with a name built on the verb “to be,” *ehyeh asher ehyeh*, which can also be read “I will be what I will be.” It describes him without giving anyone a handle on him. Only then does he add the name the KJV prints as “the LORD,” his “memorial unto all generations” (v. 15).

The promise of “a land flowing with milk and honey” (v. 8) matches how Egyptians themselves described Canaan. In the *Story of Sinuhe* (c. 1900 BC), the exile praises a district called Yaa in the north of Canaan: figs and grapes, more wine than water, plentiful honey, abundant olives, grain without limit, and cattle of every kind. Israelites laboring in the brickfields of the Delta are promised a land that even Egyptian storytellers pictured as rich pasture and orchard.

structure.summary: No chiasm. The chapter follows the pattern of a prophetic call, also seen with Gideon and Jeremiah.

rows.text: Encounter: the bush and the voice
Introduction: God has seen and heard
Reassurance and sign: “I will be with thee”
Second objection; the name and the plan

notes: **Call pattern:** Norman Habel identified the sequence encounter, commission, objection, reassurance, sign in several prophetic calls. Gideon also protests his weakness and hears “Surely I will be with thee” (Judges 6:15–17); Jeremiah objects “I cannot speak” (Jeremiah 1:6–8).
**Seeing:** The Hebrew verb “see” (including “appeared”) occurs 9 times. Five fall in vv. 2–4, as Moses turns aside to look; then God says “I have surely seen” (v. 7) and “I have also seen” (v. 9).
**Counts:** “Bush” (*seneh*) appears 5 times, all in vv. 2–4. The form *ehyeh* appears 4 times: once in v. 12 and three times in v. 14.

Chapters 3–4 form the call of Moses, from the bush at Horeb to the elders' belief in Egypt (4:31). The scene answers 2:23–25 directly: the cry that went up to God is the cry he says he has heard (v. 7).
**Looking ahead:** The sign of v. 12 comes true when Israel camps “before the mount” (19:1–2) and serves God there. Elijah later flees to the same “Horeb the mount of God” (1 Kings 19:8).

traditions.text: Moses later recalls that God gave him commandments “when he called unto me out of the burning bush,” telling him to call upon God in the name of the Only Begotten. The vision recorded there answers both questions of Exodus 3. To Moses' doubt about who he is, God answers that he is a son in the similitude of the Only Begotten, and God names himself Endless. The same vision promises that Moses will deliver Israel from bondage.

Two revelations open with the voice of “Jesus Christ, your Redeemer, the Great I AM.” They identify the speaker of Exodus 3:14 with Christ, the same reading Latter-day Saints find in John 8:58. Justin Martyr reached a similar conclusion in the 2nd century (see below).

Given at Winter Quarters as the Saints prepared to cross the plains. The Lord introduces himself in the words of the bush, as the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, and adds, “I am he who led the children of Israel out.” The formula of Exodus 3:6 and 15 is applied to a modern exodus.

Philo reads the bush as a symbol of the oppressed people and the fire as their oppressors: the bush burns but is not consumed, so Israel will not be destroyed. The figure in the flame he calls the most godlike of images, an angel. When God gives his name, Philo has him explain that no name can properly be assigned to the only being to whom existence belongs.

Josephus says the shepherds of the region did not dare to climb the mountain, believing God lived there, so Moses found rich pasture no one else used. In his telling the fire fed on a thorn bush while its green leaves and flowers stayed untouched. When God reveals his name, Josephus stops short: it is a name “concerning which it is not lawful for me to say any more.” Philo, writing a generation earlier, also treats the name as beyond proper naming.

Asks why God spoke from a lowly thornbush. Rabbi Yannai compares God and Israel to twins who feel each other's pain, citing “I will be with him in trouble” (Psalm 91:15). Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korha tells a gentile questioner that no place is empty of God's presence, not even a bush. Others read the unburned bush as Israel surviving Egypt.

Rabbi Abba bar Mammel has God say he is named for what he is doing. When he judges he is *Elohim*; when he wars against the wicked, the LORD of hosts; when he bears with sins, El Shaddai; when he shows mercy, the LORD (citing Exodus 34:6). “I will be what I will be” means he is known by his acts.

Explains why *ehyeh* comes twice in v. 14. God tells Moses he was with Israel in this bondage and will be with them in later bondage under other kingdoms. Moses answers that the present trouble is enough, so God tells him to say only “I will be” sent him, the single *ehyeh* at the end of the verse.

Jesus answers the Sadducees, who denied the resurrection, from this chapter, asking whether they had not read what God said to Moses “in the bush.” God called himself the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob long after they had died, so “he is not the God of the dead.” Luke repeats the argument, and both treat the self-introduction of v. 6 as a promise that the patriarchs live.

Stephen places the bush “in the wilderness of mount Sina,” forty years after Moses fled Egypt. Like Exodus, he calls the figure in the flame an angel of the Lord, then has the voice of the Lord speak from the same fire. He adds that Moses trembled and did not dare to look, and he calls Moses the rejected ruler whom God sent back as deliverer by the hand of that angel.

Justin says the one who spoke from the bush was the Son of God, the Word, whom he calls “Angel and Apostle,” because he appeared at times in fire and at times as an angel. He charges that Jews who say the nameless Father spoke to Moses know neither Father nor Son. He also claims pagan priests copied the removal of shoes from this scene.

4.overview:
When Moses says the people will not believe him, God gives him three signs: his rod becomes a serpent, his hand turns leprous and is healed, and Nile water poured out will turn to blood. When he pleads that he is slow of speech, God asks who made man's mouth. When he asks God to send someone else, God grows angry and appoints Aaron as his spokesman. Moses sets out for Egypt with his family. On the way the LORD seeks to kill him until Zipporah circumcises their son. Aaron meets Moses at the mountain of God, and the elders of Israel see the signs, believe, and worship.

Watch the word “firstborn.” God's message to Pharaoh is “Israel is my son, even my firstborn” (v. 22), with a warning against Pharaoh's own firstborn. The very next scene turns on Moses' own son and the blood of circumcision, an early hint of the Passover night (12:29).

4.hermeneutics:
A rod that becomes a serpent was a sign aimed at Pharaoh's world. The rearing cobra, the uraeus, sat on the brow of every royal crown as the king's protector and the emblem of his power. Egypt's lector priests also claimed control over animals. The Westcar Papyrus (copied c. 1650 BC) tells of a priest who made a wax crocodile that came alive in the water and seized a man, then picked the beast up and it was wax again in his hand. Moses' sign (vv. 3–4) is a wonder of the kind Egypt's experts claimed for themselves, which is why Pharaoh's magicians will copy it (7:11–12) and why Aaron's rod swallowing theirs matters.

Egyptians practiced circumcision. A relief in the tomb of Ankhmahor at Saqqara (c. 2340 BC) shows youths being circumcised, the oldest known picture of the rite. Circumcision alone would not have marked an Israelite in Egypt as different. What set Israel apart was the covenant timing, the eighth day (Genesis 17:12), and the covenant meaning. Zipporah, a Midianite, performs the rite on her son with a flint (v. 25), and the text treats it as the missing covenant sign without which Moses cannot go on to Egypt.

One of Pharaoh's standard titles was “Son of Ra”: the king ruled as the son of the sun god. God's message in vv. 22–23 meets that claim head on. Israel, a nation of brickmakers, is “my son, even my firstborn,” and Pharaoh's refusal to free God's son will cost him his own. The contest that follows is framed as a dispute between two fathers over their sons.

structure.summary: An inclusio: the chapter opens with “they will not believe” and closes with “the people believed.”

notes: **Believe:** The verb *aman* occurs 6 times (vv. 1, 5, 8 twice, 9, 31). Five are doubts or conditions; the last is the outcome.
**Mouth:** “Mouth” occurs 7 times in vv. 10–16. Twice God promises “I will be with thy mouth” (vv. 12, 15), using the same *ehyeh* he used of himself at the bush (3:12, 14).
**Hand:** “Hand” occurs 12 times, from “What is that in thine hand?” (v. 2) to the rod of God in Moses' hand (v. 20) and the wonders “I have put in thine hand” (v. 21).

This chapter completes the call that began at the bush (3:1–4:31). Moses' objections run out at v. 17, and the unit closes when the elders believe and worship. Verse 31 echoes 3:16: God has “visited” Israel and “looked upon their affliction.”

**Looking ahead:** The belief of v. 31 proves shaky in ch. 5, when the officers blame Moses, and is secured only at the sea, where Israel “believed the LORD, and his servant Moses” (14:31). The rod first put in Moses' hand here (v. 17) is the one he lifts over the sea (14:16).

traditions.text: Where the KJV has God harden Pharaoh's heart, the JST reads “I will prosper thee; but Pharaoh will harden his heart.” A note in the Church's edition explains that the Lord is not responsible for Pharaoh's hardness, and the JST makes the same change at many points through the plague chapters. Origen worked at the same problem from another direction (see below).

The JST explains the attack at the lodging. The Lord was angry with Moses “for he had not circumcised his son.” After Zipporah circumcises the child, Moses is ashamed, hides his face from the Lord, and confesses that he has sinned. The cause the JST names is the one the rabbis also assumed (see Talmud below).

Lehi quotes Joseph of Egypt foreseeing this chapter: the Lord will give Moses “power unto him in a rod,” will not loose his tongue to speak much, and will make a spokesman for him. Moses' slow speech and Aaron's role (vv. 10–16) are here part of the plan from the start. The prophecy then applies the same pairing of writer and spokesman to Joseph's latter-day descendants.

Jubilees removes the LORD from the attack at the lodging. Prince Mastema, chief of the hostile spirits, sought with all his power to kill Moses on the road, to save the Egyptians from the judgment Moses was bringing, and the angel of the presence delivered him. Jubilees uses the same device in Genesis 22, where Mastema proposes the test of Abraham, so a hostile spirit takes on the troubling act the text assigns to God.

The Aramaic translation read in synagogues has “an angel of the LORD” meet Moses, not the LORD himself. It turns Zipporah's puzzling words into an explanation: by the blood of this circumcision the bridegroom has been given back to us. In v. 26, were it not for this blood, the bridegroom would have deserved death.

Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korha teaches that all of Moses' merits did not shield him when he neglected circumcision. Rabbi Judah the Prince defends him: circumcising before the journey would have endangered the child. He was punished, the Talmud concludes, because at the lodging he saw to the inn before the rite. Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel holds that the one in danger was the uncircumcised baby, not Moses.

Explains Moses' “slow tongue” (v. 10) with a story from his childhood. The boy kept taking Pharaoh's crown, and Jethro, then a royal adviser, proposed a test: set gold and a burning coal before him. Moses reached for the gold, but the angel Gabriel pushed his hand to the coal, which he put in his mouth and burned his tongue.

Philo has Moses say his voice was weak and his speech slow, and had grown worse since he heard God speak, one way to read the end of v. 10. God answers that he made the mouth, tongue, and voice, and that if an interpreter is needed, Aaron will be “a subordinate mouthpiece for thee.” Philo also notes that the third sign, water into blood, was not shown to Moses in advance but promised.

Josephus retells the signs plainly: the rod becomes a serpent, and Moses' hand comes out of his bosom white as chalk, then is restored. He has Moses protest that he is a private man of no ability, unable to persuade either his own people or Pharaoh. Aaron meets him at the border, and Israel's leaders take courage when they see the signs.

Origen takes up God's hardening of Pharaoh's heart as a test case for free will. The same heat of the sun “melts wax indeed, but dries up and hardens mud,” and the same rain makes tilled ground fruitful and neglected ground grow thorns. God's single action meets two kinds of will, so Pharaoh's hardening came from what Pharaoh already was. His answer and the JST's arrive at the same place: the fault lies in Pharaoh.

Hosea 11:1 recalls the Exodus as God calling his son out of Egypt, the language of Exodus 4:22. Matthew applies that verse to the child Jesus returning from Egypt: “Out of Egypt have I called my son.” Israel, God's firstborn, becomes a pattern for Jesus, the Son.

5.overview:
Moses and Aaron go to Pharaoh with the LORD's demand: let my people go to hold a feast in the wilderness. Pharaoh answers, “Who is the LORD?” and says he does not know him. Calling the request an excuse for idleness, he orders that the Israelites no longer be given straw but still make the same number of bricks. The people scatter across Egypt to gather stubble, and the Israelite officers set over them are beaten when the quota falls short. The officers appeal to Pharaoh and are told again that they are lazy. Leaving the palace, they turn on Moses and Aaron, and Moses turns to the LORD: why did you send me?

The first meeting with Pharaoh makes everything worse. The people who believed in 4:31 now curse their deliverers, and the chapter ends on Moses' unanswered question. God's answer opens the next chapter (6:1).

5.hermeneutics:
Egyptian officials counted bricks closely. A leather roll in the Louvre, from year 5 of Ramesses II (c. 1274 BC), lists forty men in charge of brickmaking, each with a target of 2,000 bricks, and records deliveries against it. One entry shows three deliveries totaling 1,630 bricks, with a deficit of 370. A papyrus from about 1220 BC (Anastasi III) notes that workmen were “making their quota of bricks daily.” The “tale of the bricks” in vv. 8 and 18 is this kind of quota, and the beating of the Israelite officers when it falls short (v. 14) fits a system that held foremen answerable for every gang's numbers.

Straw mattered. Chopped straw mixed into Nile mud binds the clay and keeps bricks from cracking as they dry, and it is still used in Egypt today. A satirical letter in Papyrus Anastasi IV (c. 1210 BC) lists the miseries of a remote posting, among them “no men to mould bricks and no straw in the district.” Without a supply, workers had to scour the harvested fields for stubble (v. 12), cutting their output while the quota stayed fixed.

Time off for worship was a known request. Work registers from Deir el-Medina, the royal tomb-builders' village at Thebes, mark days when men were absent, including some who went to make offerings to their god. The Louvre roll shows no brick deliveries on certain days of the month, possibly festivals. Moses asks for three days to sacrifice (v. 3), the kind of request Egyptian foremen heard. Pharaoh's answer that the people are “idle” (vv. 8, 17) comes from a king counting lost workdays for a god he does not recognize.

notes: **Two messengers:** Moses opens with “Thus saith the LORD” (v. 1); the taskmasters answer with “Thus saith Pharaoh” (v. 10). The chapter asks which master Israel serves.
**Counts:** “Straw” (*teven*) occurs 8 times and “bricks” 5 times. The Israelite officers call themselves Pharaoh's “servants” three times (vv. 15–16).
**Heavy:** Pharaoh orders the work made heavier (v. 9, *kavad*). The same root later describes Pharaoh's own heart as heavy, the KJV's “hardened” (7:14; 8:15).

Chapter 5 opens the unit of the first audience (5:1–7:13): a failed appeal, Moses' complaint, the renewed promise of 6:1–8, the genealogy of Moses and Aaron, and the contest of rods before the plagues begin at 7:14.
**Links:** Pharaoh's “I know not the LORD” (v. 2) uses the verb of 1:8, where a king “knew not Joseph.” The plagues answer him: “the Egyptians shall know that I am the LORD” (7:5).

traditions.text: When his brothers mock his shipbuilding, Nephi reminds them that the Israelites in Egypt were “laden with tasks, which were grievous to be borne.” Would they have left bondage, he asks, if they had not listened to Moses? His brothers' complaints echo those of the Israelite officers who turn on Moses in v. 21, and Nephi uses the Exodus to answer them.

Given after the Saints were driven from Jackson County, Missouri. The Lord says Zion's redemption “must needs come by power,” promises a man who will lead them as Moses led Israel, and adds that as their fathers were led at the first, so Zion will be redeemed. Unlike ancient Israel, they are promised that both his angels and his presence will go before them. Like Exodus 5, the revelation speaks to a people whose first attempt at deliverance has failed.

Josephus has Moses open by reminding the king of his own past service to Egypt and of what God did for him at Sinai. He then puts the straw order after the contest of rods, not before it. The king stopped supplying chaff and made the Hebrews gather it at night while still making bricks by day, so their labor was “thus doubled upon them,” and the people blamed Moses for their worsened misery, as in v. 21.

Expands Pharaoh's question in v. 2 into a scene. Pharaoh tells Moses and Aaron to wait, goes in to search his archive, reads through the gods of Moab, Ammon, and Sidon, and returns to say the name is not there. Rabbi Levi compares him to a priest's foolish servant who looks for his master in a graveyard, and Moses and Aaron answer that the gods on Pharaoh's list are dead while their God lives.

Explains the “vain words” Pharaoh forbids in v. 9. The Israelites had scrolls they read on the Sabbath, promising that God would redeem them, and Pharaoh's order was meant to stop them from taking comfort in them and from resting. Rabbi Shimon ben Yohai objects to Pharaoh's charge that they were idle (vv. 8, 17), reading the Hebrew word as an insult and cursing the Egyptians for it.

On v. 4, citing Exodus Rabbah, Rashi says the tribe of Levi was never put to forced labor, which is why Moses and Aaron could come and go before Pharaoh. On v. 14, he says the Israelite officers took beatings rather than drive their fellow Israelites. For that mercy they were later chosen among the seventy elders who shared Moses' spirit (Numbers 11:16).

God answers Moses' complaint (vv. 22–23) by mourning the patriarchs, who received promises, met hardship, and never questioned him: Abraham had to buy a grave for Sarah and Jacob a field for his tent. Moses, by contrast, asked God's name at once and now asks why. The words that follow, “Now shalt thou see what I will do to Pharaoh” (6:1), are read as a limit: Moses will see Pharaoh's fall but not the conquest of Canaan.

A Jewish writer in Egypt, quoted by Eusebius, who gives a vivid answer to Pharaoh's question in v. 2. In his account the king has Moses imprisoned, the prison doors open by miracle, and Moses comes before the king again. Scoffing, the king demands the name of the God who sent him; Moses “bent down and whispered in his ear,” and the king fell speechless.

Psalm 81 recalls the Exodus as God removing Israel's shoulder from the burden and freeing their hands from the basket of earth. Augustine reads the basket as servile work, the earth-carrying of brickmaking in Egypt, and the burdens as sins, since everyone who sins is the slave of sin (John 8:34). The one who removes the burden is Christ, who calls all that labor and are heavy laden (Matthew 11:28).

An Egyptian counter-story. King Amenophis sends diseased people to work in the quarries east of the Nile; they seize Avaris under Osarsiph, a priest of Heliopolis, who “was called Moses.” Josephus rejects the story at length, arguing that Moses lived centuries earlier and that his name means one preserved out of the water. In Manetho's version the forced labor and the Moses figure belong to an Egyptian revolt.

6.overview:
God answers the complaint Moses made at the end of ch. 5. He has heard Israel's groaning and remembered his covenant with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, and he sends Moses back with a string of promises: I will bring you out, rescue you, redeem you, take you as my people, be your God, bring you into the land, and give it to you. The people, worn down by their labor, will not listen. Sent to Pharaoh again, Moses objects that he has “uncircumcised lips.” The story then stops for a genealogy of Reuben, Simeon, and Levi that runs through Moses and Aaron to Aaron's grandson Phinehas.

Watch where the genealogy is placed. It interrupts the scene at the moment Moses doubts himself, and when the story resumes in v. 30 his objection is repeated almost word for word. The two brothers are entered in Israel's family record before they ever stand before Pharaoh.

6.hermeneutics:
“A strong hand” and “a stretched out arm” (vv. 1, 6) were Pharaoh's own language. Egyptian kings were praised as strong of arm, and Ramesses III took the title *nb-khepesh*, “lord of strength.” Canaanite rulers used the idiom when writing to Pharaoh: in an Amarna letter (14th century BC), Abdi-Heba of Jerusalem says the strong arm of the king put him in his father's house (EA 286). James Hoffmeier argues that Exodus turns this royal boast against its owner. The arm that holds Israel meets a stronger one, and the phrase becomes Israel's set way of recalling the Exodus (Deuteronomy 4:34; 26:8).

“I will redeem you” (v. 6) uses *ga'al*, the duty of a near relative. In Israel's law, a man who sold himself into service could be bought back by a brother, uncle, or cousin (Leviticus 25:47–49). Hammurabi's laws (c. 1750 BC) likewise made a captured soldier's own household pay his ransom first, before the temple or the palace (§32). The verb casts God as next of kin to a family in bondage.

God's promise to take Israel “to me for a people” and be “to you a God” (v. 7) has the shape of a legal declaration. Aramaic marriage contracts from the Jewish colony at Elephantine in Egypt (5th century BC) have the groom declare that she is his wife and he her husband, “from this day for ever.” A spoken formula made the bond. Here both halves of the covenant formula stand together, and later texts reuse it (Leviticus 26:12; Jeremiah 31:33) or reverse it (Hosea 1:9).

notes: **Picking up the thread:** Verses 28–30 restate the setting and repeat Moses' objection from v. 12, a device ancient writers used to return to a story after a digression.
**“I am the LORD”** occurs five times (vv. 2, 6, 7, 8, 29; v. 7 adds “your God”). In vv. 6–8 seven first-person verbs carry the promise: bring out, rid, redeem, take, be, bring in, give.
**Three tribes only:** The list opens like a roll of all Jacob's sons but stops at Levi, the third. Reuben and Simeon get a verse each; Levi gets ten, with the lifespans of Levi, Kohath, and Amram.

The subsection runs from Moses' first audience with Pharaoh (5:1) to the sign of the rod (7:13). Exodus 6:2–7:7 retells the call of chs. 3–4 in a second form, with the divine name, the promise to the fathers, Moses' objection about his speech, and Aaron as his mouthpiece. The plagues begin at 7:14.

**Looking ahead:** The genealogy names men who matter later: Nadab and Abihu, who die offering strange fire (Leviticus 10:1–2); Korah, who rebels (Numbers 16:1); and Phinehas, whose zeal turns away the Lord's wrath (Numbers 25:11).

traditions.text: Joseph Smith's revision has the Lord name himself the Lord God Almighty and the Lord Jehovah, then turn the end of the verse into a question: “And was not my name known unto them?” The Book of Abraham agrees, since the Lord tells Abraham his name is Jehovah (Abraham 1:16; 2:8). Where the KJV says the patriarchs did not know the name, these texts say they did.

The names in vv. 20–25 matter in Restoration teaching because the lesser priesthood came down through them. The Lord “confirmed a priesthood also upon Aaron and his seed,” and it continued with the house of Aaron until John the Baptist. D&C 107 names it the Priesthood of Aaron and reserves the legal right to preside over it to literal descendants of Aaron.

Where the KJV has Moses call himself a man of uncircumcised lips, the Joseph Smith Translation reads “stammering lips, and slow of speech,” the complaint he made at the bush (4:10). Enoch makes the same objection in the Book of Moses: he is but a lad and slow of speech. The Lord answers him that if he opens his mouth it will be filled.

Rabbi Yohanan, in the name of Rabbi Benaiah, explains the four cups of wine at the Passover meal by four verbs of deliverance in vv. 6–7: I will bring you out, rescue you, redeem you, and take you. Other rabbis in the same passage offer different reasons for the number four. The cups are still drunk at the seder.

Reads vv. 1–9 as God's rebuke of Moses' complaint, “wherefore hast thou so evil entreated this people?” (5:22). God laments the patriarchs who are gone and cannot be replaced. Rashi spells out the contrast: Abraham paid dearly for a grave, Isaac's wells were seized, and Jacob had to buy a field in the promised land, yet none of them questioned God.

Notes that v. 3 says God was not known by his name, not that he did not make it known. The patriarchs heard promises from God Almighty but never saw them kept, so they did not know him by the trait the name stands for, faithfulness to his word. Rashi rejects the reading that they never heard the name, since God gives it to Abram in Genesis 15:7. The JST reaches the same conclusion by a different route.

Asks why the genealogy stops at three tribes. Jacob had rebuked Reuben, Simeon, and Levi on his deathbed (Genesis 49:3–7), so Scripture lists them apart to show they were still worthy men. Rashi, who passes this on, adds that Aaron comes first in v. 26 and Moses first in v. 27 to show the brothers were equal.

traditions.text: Asks who Putiel was, whose daughter bore Phinehas (v. 25). One answer is Jethro, who was said to have fattened calves for idols; the other is Joseph, who mastered his desire. The Talmud says the tribes later mocked Phinehas with the first, after he killed Zimri (Numbers 25).

A Jewish writer in Egypt who worked out biblical chronology, known from quotations in Eusebius. He uses the ages in vv. 16–20 to fix the generations: Levi dies at 137, Kohath fathers Amram at 40, and Amram fathers Aaron and Moses at 75. He makes Jochebed the daughter of Amram's uncle, a cousin, where the Hebrew makes her Amram's aunt, the kind of marriage later forbidden (Leviticus 18:12).

Quotes vv. 2–4 to argue that the one who appeared to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob was God and also the Angel sent by the Father, whom he goes on to call the Son born of the Virgin. Restoration scripture likewise identifies the God who covenanted with Israel as Jesus Christ (3 Nephi 15:5; D&C 110:3–4).

Writing on the tabernacle, he says the four-letter name was borne only by those allowed into the inner sanctuary. He gives its sound as “Jave” and its meaning as “Who is and shall be,” a form close to the modern reconstruction Yahweh.

A Greek historian listing lawgivers who credited their laws to gods: Minos to Zeus, Lycurgus to Apollo. Among the Jews, he says, Moses referred his laws to the god invoked as Iao. It is an early outside witness to the name of v. 3, in a Greek spelling.

7.overview:
The Lord answers Moses' objection: Moses will be “a god to Pharaoh,” and Aaron will speak for him. Moses is eighty and Aaron eighty-three when they go in. Aaron throws down his rod and it becomes a serpent. Pharaoh's magicians do the same, but Aaron's rod swallows theirs, and Pharaoh will not listen. Then the first plague. Moses meets Pharaoh at the river in the morning, Aaron stretches the rod over Egypt's waters, and the Nile turns to blood. The fish die, the river stinks, and Egyptians dig beside it for water to drink. The magicians copy the sign, and Pharaoh goes home unmoved. Seven days pass.

The chapter holds a seam. Verses 1–13 finish the commission and the first audience; v. 14 opens the plague cycle. The rod ties the halves together: the rod that swallowed the magicians' rods is the one that strikes the river.

7.hermeneutics:
In Egyptian belief Pharaoh was a god, the son of Re and the living Horus on earth. To this king the Lord sends Moses as “a god to Pharaoh” (v. 1), with Aaron as his prophet. Moses stands to Pharaoh as a god stands to a king, speaking through a spokesman, and the god-king's own servants are about to be outmatched.

The “magicians” (*hartummim*) bear a title taken from Egyptian *hery-tep*, part of the title of the chief lector priest, the temple scholar who read the sacred books and recited the spells. The Westcar Papyrus (copied c. 1650 BC) tells stories about such men: the lector priest Webaoner makes a wax crocodile that comes alive, and Djadjaemankh folds back the water of a lake to recover a lost pendant. Egyptians expected their court experts to command animals and water. The cobra, too, rose on Pharaoh's brow as the sign of his power, so a serpent contest in his throne room was played with his own emblem.

Egypt lived on the Nile. Rain almost never fell, and the yearly flood, praised in hymns as the god Hapy, watered and renewed the fields. To turn the river to blood was to strike the source of the land's life, at the very place Pharaoh went each morning (v. 15). An Egyptian lament, the Admonitions of Ipuwer, says “the river is blood.” Most Egyptologists read that line as a stock picture of a land in chaos, not a memory of the plague, but it shows the image was at home in Egypt.

notes: **Three sets of three:** Scholars such as Moshe Greenberg and Nahum Sarna note that the first nine plagues fall into three groups. The first of each group is announced to Pharaoh in the morning, as he goes out to the water (7:15; 8:20; 9:13). The second is announced at the palace, and the third comes without warning.
**The river:** The Hebrew word for the Nile (*ye'or*) appears 14 times in vv. 14–25, and the rod (*matteh*) 9 times in the chapter.
**Refrain:** “As the LORD had said” closes the sign (v. 13) and the first plague (v. 22). It returns at 8:15, 8:19, 9:12, and 9:35.

Verses 1–13 close the subsection that began with Moses' first audience (5:1). The rod and serpent repeat the signs given at the bush (4:2–5), now performed before Pharaoh. Verse 14 opens the plague cycle, which runs to 11:10.
**Looking ahead:** Revelation's two witnesses have power “over waters to turn them to blood” (Revelation 11:6), and the second and third bowls turn the sea and rivers to blood (16:3–4).

traditions.text: The Joseph Smith Translation calls Aaron Moses' “spokesman,” where the KJV has prophet, the word used at the bush (4:16). In Moses 1 the Lord had already told Moses he would be made stronger than many waters, for they would obey his command as if he were God. The first plague is a command to the waters.

Where the KJV has the Lord say he will harden Pharaoh's heart, the JST reads, “Pharaoh will harden his heart, as I said unto thee.” In v. 13 it makes Pharaoh the one who hardens his own heart. The Hebrew of v. 13 names no agent at all; it says only that Pharaoh's heart was strong. The KJV supplied the “he.”

This Greek Jewish book reads the plagues as measure for measure. Egypt's river was troubled with blood “for a manifest reproof of that commandment, whereby the infants were slain,” the order to drown Israel's sons in that river (1:22). Israel, meanwhile, was given water in the desert.

The angel telling Moses the story explains how the magicians could match his signs: the prince of Mastema, a satanic figure, helped the Egyptian sorcerers. The angels let them do harm but did not let them undo it. Exodus shows the same limit, since the magicians make more blood but cannot cure the river.

A rule book of the Qumran community recalls that Moses and Aaron arose by the hand of the Prince of Lights, while Belial raised up “Jannes and his brother” against them when Israel was first saved. It is the earliest known text to name one of Pharaoh's magicians.

This Aramaic paraphrase supplies names for the wise men and magicians of v. 11: Janis and Jamberes. It brings them back later in its retelling of the Torah, so the pair became fixed figures in Jewish tradition as Moses' chief opponents.

Gives the magicians as Yohana and Mamre and has them mock Moses: was he bringing straw to Afarayim, a town full of straw, by bringing magic to Egypt? Moses answers with a proverb, that to a city of herbs you bring herbs, since there the goods are understood.

A Jewish writer in Egypt, quoted by Eusebius. In his version Moses strikes the Nile and it floods all Egypt, and from that time, he says, the yearly inundation began. The priests answer with a serpent and by changing the river's color, and Egyptians dedicate a rod in every temple in memory of Moses' rod.

Asks why water was struck first, and answers that the Egyptians honored water above all, believing it the first principle of creation. Rashi, a thousand years later, gives a similar reason: Egypt has no rain and the Nile waters the land, so the Egyptians worshiped the river, and God struck their god before he struck them.
traditions.cite: Life of Moses 1.98; Rashi on Exodus 7:17

traditions.text: Has Moses tell Pharaoh that his works come from the providence and power of God, and that divine power exceeds human. In the first plague the river turns to blood for the Egyptians, but for the Hebrews the same water stays sweet and fit for drinking.

Rashi explains why Pharaoh went to the water in the morning: claiming to be a god who had no need to relieve himself, he went secretly to the Nile at dawn. On “seven days” (v. 25) he says each plague lasted about a week and the other three weeks of the month were for warning, so the Mishnah can say the judgment of Egypt lasted twelve months.

Paul warns Timothy of teachers in the last days who resist the truth “as Jannes and Jambres withstood Moses.” Exodus never names the magicians, so the letter draws on the Jewish tradition seen in the Damascus Document and the Targum. The comparison fits the chapter: like the magicians, these teachers have the outward form of godliness but deny its power (3:5).

A Greek philosopher, quoted by Eusebius, who says Jannes and Jambres were Egyptian sacred scribes judged second to none in magic. The Egyptians chose them to stand against Musaeus, his name for Moses, and they were able to undo even the worst of the disasters he brought on Egypt.

In his history of magic Pliny names a school of magicians descended from Moses, Jannes, and Lotapes, Jews by origin. Where Exodus and Paul set Jannes against Moses, the Roman writer lumps the two together as founders of one craft.

8.overview:
Three plagues. Frogs come up out of the river into Pharaoh's house, his bed, the ovens, and the kneading troughs. The magicians can bring up frogs too, but only Moses can take them away; Pharaoh asks for relief “to morrow,” and when the frogs die and lie in stinking heaps, he hardens his heart. Aaron strikes the dust and it becomes lice on man and beast. This time the magicians fail and tell Pharaoh, “This is the finger of God.” Then swarms of flies fill the houses of Egypt. Pharaoh offers to let Israel sacrifice inside Egypt, then a short way into the wilderness, and once the flies are gone he goes back on his word.

Watch vv. 22–23. For the first time the Lord sets the land of Goshen apart: “I will put a division between my people and thy people.” From the flies onward the plagues fall on Egypt and leave Israel untouched.

8.hermeneutics:
Frogs were welcome in Egypt in their season. They multiplied as the Nile flood went down, and the frog was the sign of Heqet, a goddess of birth and fertility whose amulets women wore in childbirth. The plague takes a token of the river's blessing and multiplies it past bearing, into bedrooms, ovens, and kneading troughs (v. 3), then leaves it rotting in heaps (v. 14). The text names no goddess, but the Lord's stated aim is judgment “against all the gods of Egypt” (12:12).

Moses refuses to sacrifice inside Egypt because Israel would offer “the abomination of the Egyptians” (v. 26). Some animals were sacred there. Herodotus (5th century BC) reports that Egyptians would not sacrifice cows, which belonged to Isis, and that no Egyptian would kiss a Greek or use a Greek's knife, since Greeks ate them. Genesis already notes that Egyptians would not eat with Hebrews and despised shepherds (43:32; 46:34). Israel slaughtering cattle and sheep in plain view could start a riot, and Moses says so: “will they not stone us?”

Leave to go and worship was a request Egyptian overseers knew. A register of absences from Deir el-Medina, the village of the royal tomb-builders (British Museum EA 5634, year 40 of Ramesses II), records workmen off duty for a festival or for rites with their god, beside days lost to illness and family deaths. Pharaoh's counteroffers, sacrifice “in the land” (v. 25) and then “not very far away” (v. 28), are the moves of an employer who wants his workers back on the job.

notes: **The cycle:** Each set of three opens with a warning at the water in the morning (A: 7:15; 8:20; 9:13), continues with a warning at the palace (B: 8:1; 9:1; 10:1), and ends with a plague sent unannounced (C: 8:16; 9:8; 10:21).
**The magicians fade:** They copy the frogs (v. 7), fail at the lice (vv. 18–19), and are absent at the flies. At the boils they cannot even stand (9:11).

**Counts:** Frogs (*tsefarde'a*) 11 times in vv. 2–13; lice (*kinnim*) 5 times in vv. 16–18; flies (*'arov*) 7 times in vv. 21–31. The verb “sever” (*palah*, v. 22) appears here first and returns at 9:4 and 11:7.

The plague cycle (7:14–11:10) runs from the river turned to blood to the warning of the firstborn's death. This chapter holds plagues two through four. With the flies the Lord begins to set Goshen apart, a line that leads to the Passover night, when the destroyer passes over Israel's houses (12:23).
**Looking ahead:** The magicians' phrase “the finger of God” returns at Sinai, where the tablets are “written with the finger of God” (31:18).

traditions.text: The brother of Jared sees “the finger of the Lord” touch the stones he has prepared, and falls in fear, not knowing the Lord had flesh and blood. The magicians in v. 19 recognize God's finger only by what it does; the brother of Jared, by his faith, sees it.

Alma teaches that whoever hardens his heart receives “the lesser portion of the word” until he knows nothing of God's mysteries. Pharaoh follows that course here: twice he hardens his own heart as soon as relief comes (vv. 15, 32), and each time the next plague is harder than the last.

Among the signs before the Second Coming the Lord names a great hailstorm and flies sent over the earth to take hold of the wicked. The plagues of Egypt become a pattern for latter-day judgments, as they do in Revelation.

Explains the swarming creatures as fitting punishment. Because the Egyptians worshiped serpents and beasts without reason, God sent a multitude of senseless beasts on them, so that they would learn that what a man sins by, “by the same also shall he be punished.” It adds that the bites of locusts and flies killed them, and no remedy was found.

Divides the ten plagues by agent. Aaron brought the three from earth and water (blood, frogs, lice), Moses the three from air and heaven, the two together the boils, and God kept three for himself, beginning with the flies. Following the Greek Bible, he calls the fourth plague the dog-fly, the boldest of creatures. He asks why God used anything as small as lice and answers that he uses slight things to humble the proud.

Has the lice break out of the Egyptians' own bodies, beyond any remedy, and has Pharaoh offer to let the Hebrews go but keep their wives and children. For the fourth plague Josephus does not mention flies; God fills the country with various sorts of pestilential creatures that killed people and spoiled the farms.

Reads the *'arov* of v. 21 as a mixture of wild beasts, serpents, and scorpions, close to Josephus. He passes on a midrash that the plagues follow the tactics of a king besieging a city: first he cuts off the water, then he sounds trumpets to terrify the people, and the croaking frogs were the trumpets.
traditions.cite: Rashi on Exodus 8:17 (KJV 8:21), citing Exodus Rabbah 11:3 and Tanchuma

traditions.text: Notes that v. 6 says “the frog” in the singular. Rabbi Akiva says one frog came up and bred until it filled Egypt; Rabbi Elazar ben Azariah tells him to leave legends alone and says the one frog whistled and the rest followed. Rabbi Eliezer draws a rule from v. 19: the magicians failed because a demon cannot make anything smaller than a grain of barley.

Theodosius of Rome taught that Hananiah, Mishael, and Azariah learned from the frogs. The frogs, under no command to honor God's name, still went into the hot ovens (v. 3); how much more should men who are commanded give themselves to the fiery furnace.

traditions.date: rabbinic, compiled by the early Middle Ages
traditions.text: Rabbi Judah groups the plagues by their initials into three words, the first two holding three plagues each. Rabbi Yose the Galilean argues from v. 19: if God's finger brought ten plagues in Egypt, then the great hand seen at the sea (14:31) must have brought fifty.

Asks how the magicians could make serpents and frogs but not lice, short-lived little flies. He answers that their power was real but granted from above, and when it reached the lice a greater power, which he ties to the Holy Spirit, stopped them; so they confessed the finger of God. The Talmud's barley-grain rule asks the same question.

Jesus uses the magicians' phrase when he answers the charge that he casts out devils by Beelzebub: “if I with the finger of God cast out devils” (Luke 11:20). Matthew's version of the saying names the Spirit of God instead (12:28). Ambrose sets the two side by side to show that the finger of God is the Holy Spirit.

In the bowl judgments, which echo Egypt's plagues, John sees three unclean spirits “like frogs” come out of the mouths of the dragon, the beast, and the false prophet. They are spirits of devils working miracles to gather the kings of the earth to battle. The frog that Pharaoh's magicians could multiply but not remove becomes an image of deceiving wonders.

9.overview:
Three more plagues. A disease strikes Egypt's livestock in the field, and on the day the Lord sets, Egypt's cattle die while not one animal of Israel's does. Pharaoh sends to check and still refuses. Moses throws ashes from a furnace toward the sky, and boils break out on people and animals, so that the magicians cannot even stand before him. Then Moses warns of a hail worse than any Egypt has known and tells Pharaoh to bring servants and herds indoors. Some of Pharaoh's officials heed him; others leave theirs in the field. Hail and fire strike everywhere but Goshen, and Pharaoh admits, “I have sinned this time.” When the storm stops, he hardens his heart again.

Watch v. 12. Until now Pharaoh hardened his own heart, or his heart “was hardened.” Here for the first time the narrator says “the LORD hardened the heart of Pharaoh,” as foretold at the bush (4:21).

9.hermeneutics:
Cattle carried religious weight in Egypt. The Apis bull of Memphis was kept and worshiped as a living god, and Herodotus describes how the priests knew the calf by its markings: black, with a white triangle on the forehead. Hathor took the form of a cow, and Herodotus says cows were sacred to Isis. The murrain (vv. 3–7) names none of these, but a disease that kills Egypt's herds and spares Israel's strikes animals Egyptians honored as well as their wealth.

Hail in Egypt was a portent. Upper Egypt has almost no rain; Herodotus reports that when rain fell at Thebes under Psammenitus (6th century BC), the Thebans said it had never happened before. A storm of thunder, hail, and fire running along the ground (v. 23), “such as hath not been in Egypt since the foundation thereof” (v. 18), would terrify a land watered from below by the Nile. Moses spreads his hands to the Lord so that Pharaoh may know “that the earth is the LORD's” (v. 29). After the river, the sky.

Verses 31–32 read like a farmer's note. Flax and barley ripen early; wheat and spelt (KJV “rie”) come later. The Gezer Calendar, a 10th-century BC Hebrew tablet, lists the farming year in the same order: a month for flax, then the barley harvest, then the harvest of the other grain. In Egypt barley ripens in late winter, so the hail falls shortly before the spring Passover, and the wheat left standing is what the locusts will eat (10:5, 15).

notes: **Escalation:** The murrain kills animals only. The boils fall on “man, and upon beast” and on the magicians themselves (v. 11). The hail kills anyone left in the field (vv. 19, 25), and it gets the longest warning speech of any plague so far (vv. 13–19).
**Hail:** The Hebrew word for hail (*barad*) appears 14 times in vv. 18–34.

**Pestilence:** Moses had feared God would fall on Israel “with pestilence” (5:3). The same word (*deber*) now strikes Egypt's cattle (“murrain,” v. 3) and is threatened against Pharaoh (v. 15). These are its only three uses in Exodus.

The plague cycle runs from 7:14 to 11:10. This chapter holds plagues five through seven. With the hail the third set of three begins, and Pharaoh for the first time admits wrong (v. 27), though only “this time.”

**Looking ahead:** Verse 16 states the purpose of the whole cycle: Pharaoh is raised up so that God's name may be declared throughout the earth. Revelation's seventh bowl ends in great hail out of heaven (Revelation 16:21), and its first trumpet brings hail and fire mingled with blood (8:7).

traditions.text: At the verse where the KJV and the Hebrew first make the Lord the subject of the hardening, the Joseph Smith Translation reads, “And Pharaoh hardened his heart.” The JST makes the same change at each verse where the KJV has God harden Pharaoh, so that in Restoration scripture the stubbornness is Pharaoh's own.

Hail becomes a standing sign of judgment in Restoration scripture. Abinadi warns King Noah's people that the Lord will send hail among them, with the east wind and insects that devour their grain. The Lord tells the Saints of a great hailstorm sent to destroy the crops of the earth, and the Kirtland Temple prayer asks that the works of the Church's enemies be swept away by the hail.

Gives the boils to Moses and Aaron together, since they came from furnace dust (earth, Aaron's element) thrown into the air (Moses' element). In the hail he marvels that lightning ran through the hailstones without melting them, and says some animals died of the hail and some of the lightning.

Sees the hail and fire as creation itself fighting for the righteous. The ungodly were struck by strange rains and hail, and, most wonderful of all, “the fire had more force in the water,” burning in the midst of the hail to destroy the fruits of an unjust land.

The angel tells Moses that the Lord smote the Egyptian sorcerers with malignant ulcers, so that they were not able to stand. Jubilees reads v. 11 as the end of the contest between Moses and the magicians, whom it says the prince of Mastema had been helping.

Has the Egyptians' bodies break out in terrible boils, and says a great part of them perished, a death toll Exodus does not report. The hail is unlike any Egypt had known and breaks the trees heavy with fruit. Josephus does not treat the cattle disease as a plague of its own.

Notices a problem: if “all the cattle of Egypt died” (v. 6), where did Pharaoh's chariot horses come from (14:7)? Not from Israel, whose herds left with them. They belonged, he says, to the Egyptians who feared the word of the Lord and brought their animals indoors before the hail (v. 20). So the animals saved by heeding Moses later pulled the chariots that chased Israel.

His retelling, preserved by Eusebius, adds earthquakes to the hail. Moses caused hail and earthquakes by night, so that those fleeing the quakes were killed by the hail and those sheltering from the hail died in the quakes. He also has the Egyptians' bodies break out in boils.

Paul quotes v. 16, “for this same purpose have I raised thee up,” and concludes that God has mercy on whom he will and hardens whom he will. He then answers the objection his own reader would raise, why God still finds fault, with the image of the potter and the clay. The chapter became a main text in later Christian debate over predestination and free will.

Answers critics who said a good God could not harden Pharaoh's heart (citing v. 35). God, who foreknows all, gives over to their unbelief those he knows will never believe, so that Pharaoh, seeing the finger of God at work, might still not believe.

Explains the hardening with two images. Rain falls alike on all ground, but tilled soil bears fruit and neglected soil thorns; the sun's one heat melts wax and hardens mud. God's signs were the same for everyone, and Pharaoh's hardness showed the kind of material he was.

The Roman historian gives a hostile Egyptian version: a plague that disfigured the body broke out in Egypt, and King Bocchoris, told by the oracle of Ammon to purge the land, drove out the Jews as hateful to the gods. Moses then led the exiles. Here the skin disease falls on Israel, not on Egypt.

A Roman historian whose work survives in Justin's summary. He says the Egyptians, troubled by scabies and skin disease and warned by an oracle, expelled Moses and the sick from Egypt so the disease would not spread. Like Tacitus, he reverses the boils of v. 9 into a reason for the Exodus.

10.overview:
Moses warns Pharaoh of locusts, and for the first time Pharaoh's own servants press him: “knowest thou not yet that Egypt is destroyed?” Pharaoh offers to let the men go, but not the children, and drives Moses and Aaron out. An east wind brings locusts that eat everything the hail left, until nothing green remains. Pharaoh begs forgiveness, a west wind sweeps the locusts into the Red Sea, and he refuses again. Then, without warning, a darkness that can be felt covers Egypt for three days, while Israel has light in its homes. Pharaoh now offers to let the families go if the flocks stay. Moses refuses, and Pharaoh threatens him with death if he sees his face again.

Follow the bargaining. Pharaoh gives a little more each time: the men only (v. 11), then everyone but the herds (v. 24). Moses does not move: “there shall not an hoof be left behind” (v. 26).

10.hermeneutics:
Pharaoh's offers follow a familiar way of keeping subjects in line: hold their families. The annals of Thutmose III (15th century BC) record that the children and brothers of conquered Canaanite chiefs were brought to Egypt and kept there, so their fathers would stay loyal, and a son was sent home to rule when a chief died. Letting the men go without the children (vv. 10–11), and later everyone without the herds (v. 24), would leave Pharaoh holding what guaranteed their return. Moses' list in v. 9, young and old, sons and daughters, flocks and herds, refuses any pledge.

Locusts ride the wind, and the text names the winds. An east wind blows all day and night off the desert and brings the swarm (v. 13); the Lord turns it into a “sea wind,” from the Mediterranean, which carries them off to the *yam suph* (v. 19). Swarms of this kind could strip a region in hours, which is why Pharaoh calls them “this death” (v. 17).

The darkness strikes at the center of Egyptian religion. The sun god Re crossed the sky by day and passed through the underworld by night, where the serpent Apophis tried each night to swallow his boat. Priests performed rituals and burned wax figures of the serpent to keep him at bay. Three days without sunrise (vv. 22–23) would look like Re defeated and the order of the world undone, while in Israel's homes the light continued.

notes: **Serve:** The verb *'abad* (“serve”) appears 7 times (vv. 3, 7, 8, 11, 24, 26 twice). It is the root of Israel's bondage in Egypt, and the whole dispute is about whom Israel will serve (compare 4:23).

**Locusts and winds:** The locust (*arbeh*) is named 7 times (vv. 4, 12, 13, 14 twice, 19 twice), and the plague is framed by two winds, the east wind that brings it (v. 13) and the sea wind that takes it away (v. 19).
**Closing the cycle:** The darkness ends the third set of three. Moses and Pharaoh part vowing never to see each other's face again (vv. 28–29).

This chapter ends the nine plagues that come in sets of three. Chapter 11 announces the tenth, the death of the firstborn, and closes the plague cycle at 11:10. The bargaining over flocks and herds is settled in 12:32, when Pharaoh tells Israel to take them and go.

**Looking ahead:** The command to tell the story to children (v. 2) is repeated for the Passover (12:26–27; 13:8). The Philistines later recall how Pharaoh and the Egyptians hardened their hearts and still let Israel go (1 Samuel 6:6).

traditions.text: Where the KJV has the Lord say he has hardened Pharaoh's heart and his servants' hearts, the Joseph Smith Translation reads, “for he hath hardened his heart,” and therefore the Lord will show his signs before him. At vv. 20 and 27 it again makes Pharaoh the one who hardens. In this reading the signs answer Pharaoh's stubbornness instead of causing it, and the servants who beg him to yield in v. 7 show that hearts could still turn.

At Christ's death, thick darkness covers the land of the Nephites so that the survivors “could feel the vapor of darkness.” No candle, torch, or fire can be lit, and it lasts three days. The Book of Mormon account echoes the felt darkness and the three days of vv. 21–23, now as a sign of the Savior's death.

Gives the darkness a whole chapter. The Egyptians lay shut in their houses as “the prisoners of darkness,” no fire could give them light, and they were tormented by terrors and visions, while the rest of the world shone with clear light. Wisdom adds that they deserved to be imprisoned in darkness because they had kept shut up the sons through whom the light of the law was to be given to the world.

Describes the locusts devouring everything incessantly, like a stream, until a wind carried them away. The darkness he calls one very long night, equal in length to three days. It ended, he says, when Moses pleaded for the Egyptians and the light returned, so the prophet who brought the plague also lifted it.

Says a thick darkness without the least light spread over the Egyptians for three days and nights; their sight was blocked and the thick air hindered their breathing, so that they died miserably. Pharaoh threatens to cut off Moses' head if he comes again. Moses answers that he will not come, but that the Egyptians themselves will soon urge the Hebrews to leave.

Reads the verb in v. 2, “what I have wrought in Egypt,” as how God made sport of Egypt, the same verb Balaam uses when his ass makes a fool of him (Numbers 22:29). The Philistines use it too when they remember what God did to Egypt (1 Samuel 6:6). On this reading the story told to Israel's children is of a proud king made foolish.

Counts two darknesses: three days when no one could see another (v. 23a), then three days so thick no one could rise or sit (v. 23b). The darkness came, he says, to hide the deaths of wicked Israelites who refused to leave Egypt, so that the Egyptians could not say Israel was struck too. It also let Israel see where the Egyptians kept their valuables, so they could not later deny having them.
traditions.cite: Rashi on Exodus 10:22, citing Tanchuma and Exodus Rabbah

traditions.text: On Pharaoh's warning, “evil is before you” (v. 10), he passes on a midrash: Pharaoh had seen by astrology a star called Ra'ah, “Evil,” rising over Israel's path in the wilderness, a sign of blood. When Moses later prays after the golden calf that the Egyptians not say God brought Israel out “for mischief” (32:12), the midrash hears an answer to Pharaoh's star.

Asks how v. 14 can say there will never again be such locusts, when Joel says the same of the swarm in his own day (Joel 2:2). Joel's plague, he answers, was a mix of several kinds of insect, while Moses' was of the *arbeh* alone, and of that one kind there was never another like it.

In his *Life of Moses* the same sun shone on Egyptians and Hebrews, but the Hebrews delighted in its light while the Egyptians were insensible to its gift. He reads the plague as a picture of the soul: we carry in our own nature and by our own choice the causes of light or darkness. After three days, he notes, the Egyptians too shared in the light again.

John's visions reuse both plagues against a new Egypt. At the fifth trumpet, locusts come out of the smoke of the bottomless pit with the power of scorpions, sent against those without God's seal. At the fifth bowl, darkness fills the beast's kingdom and its people gnaw their tongues for pain, yet still do not repent, as Pharaoh did not.

11.overview:
The LORD tells Moses that one more plague will make Pharaoh drive Israel out, and that the people should ask their Egyptian neighbors for jewels of silver and gold. Moses then announces the last plague to Pharaoh: about midnight every firstborn in Egypt will die, from Pharaoh's heir to the son of the slave woman at the hand mill, and the firstborn of cattle too, while not even a dog will growl at Israel. He leaves Pharaoh “in a great anger.” Two closing verses sum up the whole contest: Moses and Aaron did all these wonders, and Pharaoh still would not let Israel go.

The scene never changes. At the end of chapter 10 Pharaoh tells Moses never to see his face again, and Moses agrees. Verses 4–8 are his parting speech in that same audience, and only in v. 8 does he walk out. Verses 1–3 step aside to report what God had already told him.

11.hermeneutics:
Egypt's king bore the title “Son of Ra,” the sun god, and his eldest son stood to inherit that sacred office. Moses' commission had already set the terms of the contest: “Israel is my son, even my firstborn,” and if Pharaoh would not let God's son go, his own firstborn would die (4:22–23). Verse 5 begins with “the firstborn of Pharaoh that sitteth upon his throne,” so the last plague reaches the god-king's own line of succession, the one thing an Egyptian would have thought beyond reach.

Grinding grain on a stone hand mill was the lowest daily work in an Egyptian household, done by women servants on their knees. Old Kingdom tombs held small limestone statues of servant women bent over grinding stones, put there to keep making bread for the dead owner. Verse 5 runs from the throne to the mill, the top and bottom of Egyptian society, to say that no house will escape.

Israel's own law later required that a Hebrew slave going free not be sent away empty but loaded from flock, threshing floor, and winepress (Deuteronomy 15:13–14). God had promised Abraham that his descendants would leave their oppressors “with great substance” (Genesis 15:14), and told Moses at the bush that Israel would not go out empty (3:21–22). Heard against that background, the silver and gold of v. 2 is a freed slave's due, paid at last.
