notes: **Go out:** the Hebrew verb *yatsa* comes four times in vv. 4–8. God will go out into Egypt at midnight (v. 4); Pharaoh's servants will tell Moses to get out, Moses will then go out, and he went out (v. 8). The departure Pharaoh keeps refusing is already under way in the speech itself.
**Firstborn:** *bekhor* comes four times in v. 5 alone, running from Pharaoh to the slave woman to the cattle.
**Let go:** v. 1 promises twice that Pharaoh will “let you go.” Verse 10 ends with the same verb, negated: he would not let Israel go.

Chapter 11 closes the plague narrative that began at 7:14. Verses 9–10 pick up the words spoken before the first plague, “multiply my signs and my wonders in the land of Egypt” (7:3), and close the contest with them. Chapter 12 opens a new section of instructions, the Passover, before the blow announced here falls (12:29).
**Forward:** the silver and gold come back as Israel's offering for the tabernacle (25:3; 35:22). Psalm 105:36–37 sets the death of the firstborn beside the silver and gold, as this chapter does.

traditions.text: Where the KJV of v. 10 says that the LORD hardened Pharaoh's heart, the JST reads “Pharaoh hardened his heart.” The JST makes the same change at each point in the plague story where God is said to harden Pharaoh, from 4:21 onward, so the stubbornness is Pharaoh's own. Jubilees also moves the hardening away from God, giving it at the sea to the spirit Mastema (48:17).

A Greek-speaking Jewish book, probably from Alexandria, that retells the plagues as the work of divine wisdom. On the last plague it notes that master and servant, king and commoner died alike, as v. 5 announces, and that the Egyptians, who had disbelieved every earlier sign, confessed Israel to be God's son when their firstborn died. At midnight God's “Almighty word leaped down from heaven” like a warrior.

The angel who narrates Jubilees says the accusing spirit Mastema was bound on the fourteenth of the month, so that he could not accuse Israel on the day they asked the Egyptians for garments and vessels of silver, gold, and bronze. The goods were taken “in return for the bondage,” and the angel adds that Israel did not leave Egypt empty-handed, the promise of 3:21.

In Josephus, Pharaoh threatens to cut off Moses' head if he comes again. Moses answers that he will not speak to the king about it any more, but that the king and the leading Egyptians will soon beg the Hebrews to go, the threat of v. 8. On the night itself, he says, the Egyptians gave Israel gifts, some to hurry them away and some out of neighborly friendship.

Notices the small Hebrew word *na* in v. 2 (“speak now”) and reads it as “please.” God pleads with Moses to have Israel ask for the silver and gold, so that Abraham could not say that the slavery promised in Genesis 15:13 came true while the “great substance” did not. The people, the same passage adds, would rather have left at once with nothing, like a prisoner who asks only to be freed today.

Asks why Moses said “about midnight” (v. 4) when he knew the hour exactly. One answer: if Pharaoh's astrologers misjudged the time, they would call Moses a liar, so he left them no opening. Another reads the phrase as “like midnight,” spoken at midnight about the same hour on the following night.

Tells of a lawsuit before Alexander the Great in which the Egyptians sued the Jews for the silver and gold borrowed at the Exodus. Geviha ben Pesisa answered from the Torah: 600,000 men had served 430 years (12:37, 40) without wages, and Egypt owed that debt first. The Egyptians asked for three days, found no reply, and fled. Tertullian knows a similar countersuit (below).

On the law that torn meat is to be thrown to the dogs (22:31), this early commentary on Exodus recalls v. 7: on the night Israel left, no dog moved its tongue against them. God does not withhold the reward of any creature, it says, so the dogs are paid with the carcass.

Answers critics who said God taught Israel to cheat the Egyptians. Israel had built Egypt's fenced cities in brick and mortar for years without pay, so the few vessels they took were a small wage for heavy labor; the Egyptians also owed them their lives, through Joseph. He notes that the tabernacle was later built from these spoils.

Marcion used the borrowed gold to accuse the God of the Old Testament of fraud. Tertullian answers by staging a lawsuit: the Egyptians claim their vessels, and the Hebrews counter-claim the arrears of their slavery, the bricks and the cities they built. He reports that the case was settled on those terms, much as the Talmud tells of Geviha ben Pesisa.

Turns the spoiling of the Egyptians into a rule for Christian learning. Israel left the idols behind but took the gold, silver, and garments for a better use, at God's command; in the same way Christians may claim what is true in pagan philosophy and put it to God's service. Moses himself, he notes, was “learned in all the wisdom of the Egyptians” (Acts 7:22).

12.overview:
The LORD gives Moses and Aaron the first law of Israel's calendar: this month begins the year. On the tenth day each household takes a lamb, kills it on the fourteenth at evening, strikes its blood on the doorposts and lintel, and eats it roasted, with unleavened bread and bitter herbs, dressed to travel. When the LORD passes through Egypt and sees the blood, he will pass over the house. At midnight the firstborn of Egypt die, Pharaoh sends Israel away by night, and about 600,000 men on foot, with a mixed multitude, march from Rameses to Succoth.

The chapter keeps stopping the story to give law. Rules for every later Passover come before the plague falls (vv. 14–20, 24–27) and again after Israel has left (vv. 43–49). The night is told as something Israel will repeat, with children asking what it means.

12.hermeneutics:
“Against all the gods of Egypt I will execute judgment” (v. 12; compare Numbers 33:4). Egypt worshiped gods in animal form. Herodotus reports that in the district of Thebes, the city of the god Amun, sheep were not sacrificed: rams were sacred there, and Amun's images bore a ram's head (Histories 2.42). Moses had already warned Pharaoh that Israel's sacrifices would be “the abomination of the Egyptians” (8:26). An Israelite household that killed a lamb, roasted it whole, and marked its door with the blood did in plain view what parts of Egypt held sacred, on the night Egypt's gods were judged.

Israel's older month names were tied to farming. The month of the Exodus is Abib, the month of green ears of grain (13:4; compare 9:31), and Kings uses other old names, Zif, Bul, and Ethanim (1 Kings 6:1, 38; 8:2). The Gezer calendar, a 10th-century BC inscription from a Canaanite city later held by Israel, likewise lays out the year by farm work: sowing, hoeing flax, barley harvest, pruning vines, summer fruit. After the exile Jews used Babylonian names, so the same month became Nisan (Nehemiah 2:1; Esther 3:7). Verse 2 cuts across the farmer's year: the year now begins from the night of deliverance, and every date on the calendar counts from the Exodus.

notes: **Did as commanded:** “as the LORD had commanded Moses and Aaron, so did they” closes the first instructions (v. 28) and, almost word for word, the last (v. 50). The story of the night sits between the two.
**Night:** the Hebrew word comes seven times (vv. 8, 12, 29, 30, 31, and twice in v. 42), ending with “a night to be much observed.”

**Pass over:** the noun *pesach* names the offering five times (vv. 11, 21, 27, 43, 48), and the verb behind it comes three times (vv. 13, 23, 27). The phrase “the selfsame day” (vv. 17, 41, 51) ties the yearly feast to the day of leaving.

The Passover section runs from 12:1 to 13:16. It opens with God speaking to Moses and Aaron “in the land of Egypt” and closes with the laws of the firstborn and the sign on the hand (13:1–16); the march resumes at 13:17. The tenth plague, announced in ch. 11, is told here (v. 29), inside the instructions for remembering it.

**Links:** Israel's first Passover in the promised land is kept at Gilgal (Joshua 5:10–11), and Josiah's Passover is measured against every one since the judges (2 Kings 23:21–22). Luke sets the Last Supper at the Passover meal (Luke 22:7–15).

traditions.text: The revelation known as the Word of Wisdom closes with a promise drawn from this chapter: those who keep it are told that “the destroying angel shall pass by them,” as it passed by the children of Israel, and not slay them. The destroyer of v. 23 becomes a pattern for the protection promised to Latter-day Saints who obey a commandment.

In the book of Moses, Adam is told to offer the firstlings of his flocks, and an angel explains that the offering is “a similitude of the sacrifice of the Only Begotten.” Abinadi says the law of Moses, with its performances and ordinances, kept Israel mindful of God, and that all these things were types of things to come. Read together, they treat the Passover lamb, a male of the first year without blemish (v. 5), as one of those types.

The angel reminds Moses that on the Passover night the powers of Mastema were let loose to kill the firstborn, while Israel ate the lamb, drank wine, and praised God. Jubilees fixes the slaughter “between the evenings,” from the third part of the day, and forbids breaking any bone. It also promises that no plague will strike Israel in a year when the Passover is kept in its season, a promise close to D&C 89:21.

Philo notes that at Passover the whole people sacrifice, from noon to evening, without waiting for priests, as Israel did in its joy on the night of leaving. Each house, he says, takes on “the character and dignity of a temple.” He also reports the allegorists of his day, who read the pascha as the soul passing over from the body and its passions.

Josephus reports a count taken under the governor Cestius: the high priests numbered the Passover victims, slaughtered from the ninth hour to the eleventh, at 256,500. No fewer than ten people shared each lamb, and often twenty, since no one could eat it alone. The household rule of v. 4 still shaped the feast in the first century.

Josephus dates the departure to the fifteenth of the month, and he reckons the 430 years of v. 40 from Abraham's arrival in Canaan, leaving only 215 years in Egypt itself. Paul also counts 430 years from the promise to Abraham to the law (Galatians 3:17). Josephus adds that the people lived thirty days on the bread they carried out of Egypt.

A damaged Aramaic letter from one Hananiah to the Jewish garrison at Elephantine, on Egypt's southern border, dated to the fifth year of Darius II. It tells the soldiers to keep the feast of unleavened bread from the fifteenth to the twenty-first of Nisan, to stay pure, and to let no leaven be seen; the word Passover itself is restored in a gap. It is the earliest dated text outside the Bible that bears on this chapter's feast.

The Mishnah lays out the Passover meal as a teaching rite: at the second cup the son asks how this night differs from all other nights, the question of v. 26. Rabban Gamaliel says no one has done his duty without explaining the Passover lamb, the unleavened bread, and the bitter herbs (v. 8). In every generation, it adds, each person must see himself as if he had come out of Egypt.

Asks why the lamb was taken on the tenth day but killed on the fourteenth (vv. 3, 6). Israel had no commandments by which to merit redemption, so God gave them two, the blood of the Passover and the blood of circumcision, and had them set the lamb apart four days early, since reward comes only for a deed. The circumcision link rests on vv. 43–48, where no uncircumcised man may eat.

John the Baptist calls Jesus the Lamb of God, and John's Gospel sees v. 46 fulfilled when the soldiers do not break Jesus' legs. Paul applies the feast's leaven to moral life: “Christ our passover is sacrificed for us,” so the old leaven must be purged.

Calls the Passover lamb a type of Christ, whose blood believers apply to their houses, that is, to themselves. The lamb roasted whole (v. 9), he says, was spitted in the form of a cross, one spit running from the lower parts to the head and another across the back for the legs. As the blood saved those in Egypt, Christ's blood will deliver believers from death.

A bishop in Asia Minor whose Easter sermon retells this chapter at length as the model of Christ's suffering. He asks what the Pascha is and answers with a Greek pun, deriving the name from *paschein*, “to suffer,” though the word comes from the Hebrew *pesach*. The sermon was lost for centuries and was recovered from papyri in the 20th century.

The Roman historian gives a hostile account of Jewish origins: most writers, he says, held that King Bocchoris drove the Jews out of Egypt during a plague, on an oracle's advice. He explains Jewish customs from that story: unleavened bread recalls the haste with which they seized grain, and they sacrifice a ram to mock the god Ammon. The ram detail touches the same Egyptian background as v. 12 (see Hermeneutics).

13.overview:
The LORD claims every firstborn in Israel, of people and of animals. Moses then tells the people how to remember the day they left Egypt: seven days of unleavened bread each year in the month Abib, an explanation for their sons, and a sign on the hand and between the eyes. In the land, every firstborn male animal goes to the LORD, while the firstborn of a donkey and every firstborn son are redeemed. Then the march resumes. God steers Israel away from the short road through Philistine country, Moses takes Joseph's bones, and the LORD goes before the camp in a pillar of cloud by day and of fire by night.

Both of Moses' speeches turn on a child. A father explains the feast to his son (v. 8) and answers when the son asks, “What is this?” (v. 14). The rites are built so that the next generation will ask.

13.hermeneutics:
The shortest road from Egypt to Canaan ran along the north coast of Sinai, a route Egyptian texts call the Ways of Horus. In the New Kingdom it was a military highway lined with forts and water stations; a relief of Seti I at Karnak shows the chain of fortresses, starting from the border fort of Tjaru. A column of escaped slaves on that road would have met Egyptian garrisons within days. The reason given in v. 17, “lest peradventure the people repent when they see war,” fits that road, and the wilderness route avoids it.

People across the ancient Near East wore amulets, small objects or written charms carried on the body for protection. Two tiny silver scrolls from a burial cave at Ketef Hinnom in Jerusalem, from about 600 BC, carry a form of the priestly blessing of Numbers 6:24–26, rolled up to be worn. Verses 9 and 16 take that familiar habit and change what is carried: the sign on the hand and the frontlets between the eyes hold the memory of the Exodus, “that the LORD's law may be in thy mouth” (v. 9).

Egyptians wanted to be buried at home. In the Story of Sinuhe, a Middle Kingdom tale, the king coaxes the exile Sinuhe back from Canaan with the promise of an Egyptian burial, so that foreigners will not wrap him in a ram's skin. Joseph, embalmed and coffined in Egypt like an Egyptian official (Genesis 50:26), had asked for the reverse. Carrying his bones out (v. 19) marks a departure with no return in view.

notes: **The hand that brought them out:** “by strength of hand” opens the first speech (v. 3), “with a strong hand” closes it (v. 9), and “by strength of hand” closes the second twice (vv. 14, 16). Each panel ends where the Exodus began, with God's hand.
**Feast and firstborn:** the panels pair two ways of remembering the same night. The bread recalls the haste of leaving; the firstborn recall the deaths in Egypt (v. 15).
**The pillar:** the closing verses name it four times (vv. 21–22), twice by day and twice by night, and stress that it never left the people.

The chapter straddles a seam. Verses 1–16 close the Passover section (12:1–13:16) with laws for remembering the night. Verse 17, “when Pharaoh had let the people go,” opens the account of the sea, which runs to Miriam's song (15:21).

**Back and forward:** Joseph's bones fulfill the oath of Genesis 50:25 and are buried at Shechem in Joshua 24:32. The pillar of cloud and fire settles over the finished tabernacle and leads every later stage of the journey (40:36–38; Numbers 9:15–23).

traditions.text: In the Joseph Smith Translation, the dying Joseph prophesies a seer named Moses who will deliver Israel from Egypt, with a rod in his hand to smite the waters of the Red Sea. The chapter then adds a detail Genesis lacks: Israel kept Joseph from burial so that he might be carried up and laid in his father's sepulchre, and so remembered their oath. Verse 19 is that oath kept.

traditions.date: c. 590 BC; Jaredite era (Book of Mormon)
traditions.text: Rebuking his brothers, Nephi retells the Exodus: the Lord their Redeemer went before Israel, leading them by day and giving light to them by night. He tells it as a warning, since Israel hardened its heart even while being led. The brother of Jared's company is led the same way, with the Lord going before them and speaking from a cloud.

Given through Brigham Young at Winter Quarters, this revelation organizes the “Camp of Israel” for its journey west. It closes with the Lord naming himself as the one “who led the children of Israel out” of Egypt, and promises that his arm is stretched out to save his people in the last days. The pioneers read their own trek through the pattern of this march.

While all Israel was busy with the spoils of Egypt, it says, Moses was busy with Joseph's bones. Serah daughter of Asher, the last of that generation, showed him where the Egyptians had sunk Joseph's metal coffin in the Nile. Moses called on Joseph not to delay the redemption, and the coffin rose to the surface.

The Mekhilta offers several readings of “for that was near” (v. 17), among them that Abraham's oath to Abimelech of Gerar still bound Israel, since a grandson was alive. It also says God did not want Israel to see the bones of their brothers strewn in Philistia. The Talmud names them: men of Ephraim who miscounted the years of bondage, left Egypt early, and were killed by the men of Gath (1 Chronicles 7:21).

Philo describes the pillar as a cloud that gave light like the sun by day and a fiery blaze by night, so the Hebrews would not stray. Perhaps, he suggests, it hid one of the great King's servants, an unseen angel guiding the way. Exodus itself soon calls the guide “the angel of God” and moves him with the pillar (14:19).

Sets the light given Israel against the darkness on Egypt: God gave a burning pillar of fire, “a guide of the unknown journey” and a sun that did no harm. Earlier the book says divine wisdom herself was a cover for Israel by day and a light of stars by night.

An Alexandrian Jewish work in which the high priest Eleazar explains the law to Greek visitors. God, he says, ordered the divine words placed on gates and doors and a symbol fastened upon the hands, so that every act would be done in righteousness and in remembrance of God. It is an early witness that vv. 9 and 16 were kept literally.

Sets out the four passages written in the tefillin, the leather boxes worn on the arm and head: this chapter's two speeches (vv. 1–10, 11–16) and the two Shema passages of Deuteronomy 6:4–9 and 11:13–21. From “a memorial between thine eyes” (v. 9) it argues that the head box, though it has four compartments, must be one piece. Tefillin found at Qumran already carry passages from this chapter.

When Mary and Joseph bring the infant Jesus to the temple, Luke explains it from this chapter: every male that opens the womb shall be called holy to the Lord (vv. 2, 12). They also offer a pair of turtledoves or two young pigeons, the offering the law allows a poor family.

Jesus faults scribes and Pharisees who “make broad their phylacteries” to be seen, the boxes worn under vv. 9 and 16. Hebrews counts Joseph's charge about his bones among the acts of faith: dying in Egypt, he spoke of the departure still to come.

Paul writes that all the fathers were under the cloud and all passed through the sea, and were all baptized unto Moses in the cloud and in the sea. The pillar of vv. 21–22 becomes, with the sea, a figure of Christian baptism, a reading Tertullian and Ambrose develop.

14.overview:
God turns Israel back to camp by the sea, so that Pharaoh will think them trapped and come after them. He does, with six hundred chosen chariots, and the people, seeing the army behind them, accuse Moses of bringing them out to die. Moses tells them to stand still and see the LORD's salvation. At God's word he stretches his hand over the sea. The pillar moves behind the camp, an east wind blows all night, and Israel walks through on dry ground between walls of water. The Egyptians follow, their chariot wheels come off, and at dawn the sea returns over them.

Watch Israel's fear. In v. 10 they fear the Egyptians; in v. 13 Moses tells them, “Fear ye not”; in v. 31 they fear the LORD and believe him and his servant Moses. The chapter ends in seeing and believing.

14.hermeneutics:
The chariot was the elite weapon of New Kingdom Egypt: a light two-wheeled car drawn by two horses, carrying a driver and an archer, built for speed on firm open ground. Egyptian temple reliefs show the king himself charging in one. “Six hundred chosen chariots, and all the chariots of Egypt” (v. 7) is the full strike force of the age. On wet ground the same machine bogs down, and Exodus says the LORD took off their wheels so that they drove heavily (v. 25). Egypt's pride becomes its trap.

Ramesses II's account of the battle of Kadesh (c. 1274 BC), carved on temple walls across Egypt, tells how the king, deserted by his troops and surrounded by Hittite chariots, called on Amun, who gave him strength, so that he routed the enemy single-handed. In Egyptian royal storytelling the god fights through the king. Exodus 14 turns the picture around: Pharaoh's chariots are the enemy destroyed, and Israel does not fight at all. “The LORD shall fight for you, and ye shall hold your peace” (v. 14).

Israel camps “over against Baal-zephon” (v. 2), a place named for Baal of Zaphon, the Canaanite storm god whose mountain stood on the Syrian coast and whose cult reached Egypt's Delta. In the myths from Ugarit, Baal wins his kingship by defeating Yam, the Sea. Here, in front of a site bearing his name, the LORD gives orders to wind and sea alike.

notes: **Three commands:** “And the LORD said unto Moses” opens each scene (vv. 1, 15, 26). The first two promise that the Egyptians shall know “that I am the LORD” (vv. 4, 18); by v. 25 they say it themselves: “the LORD fighteth for them.”

**Fear and seeing:** fear moves from the Egyptians (v. 10) to “fear ye not” (v. 13) to fearing the LORD (v. 31). The verb “see” comes five times, three in Moses' promise (v. 13) and twice at the end (vv. 30, 31).
**Honour and hardening:** God will “get me honour” on Pharaoh three times (vv. 4, 17, 18), and the hardening verb also comes three times (vv. 4, 8, 17).

The sea section runs from 13:17, when Pharaoh lets the people go, to Miriam's song in 15:21. Chapter 14 tells the events in prose; chapter 15 sings them. The last line, that Israel “believed the LORD, and his servant Moses,” answers Moses' worry at the bush that the people would not believe him (4:1).

**Echoes:** Joshua's crossing of the Jordan is told as a second Red Sea, so that Israel might fear the LORD for ever (Joshua 4:23–24). Isaiah 51:10 calls on the God who made the depths of the sea a way for the ransomed.

traditions.text: In Moses' vision, set after the burning bush and before the deliverance, God tells him, “thou shalt be made stronger than many waters,” for they will obey his command as if he were God. The Restoration account places the parting of the sea inside Moses' commission, before he ever returns to Egypt.

Given to Oliver Cowdery, who wanted to translate, this revelation describes revelation as the Lord speaking to mind and heart by the Holy Ghost. It then names that gift as “the spirit by which Moses brought the children of Israel” through the Red Sea on dry ground. The crossing becomes the model for personal revelation.

traditions.date: c. 590 BC; c. 23 BC (Book of Mormon)
traditions.text: Book of Mormon prophets return to this scene more than to any other in Exodus. Before facing Laban, Nephi urges his brothers to “be strong like unto Moses,” who spoke to the waters of the Red Sea, and later reminds them that the waters divided at Moses' word and Pharaoh's armies drowned. Nephi the son of Helaman cites the same power to argue that God can show a prophet the judgments to come.

The JST makes Pharaoh the one who hardens his own heart in vv. 4 and 8, and in v. 17 says only that the Egyptians' hearts shall be hardened. In v. 20 it makes plain that the cloud was darkness to the Egyptians and gave light to the Israelites. JST Genesis 50:34 has Joseph foresee Moses smiting the waters of the Red Sea with his rod.

The angel narrating Jubilees says he stood between the Egyptians and Israel, as the angel of God does in v. 19, and that God cast the pursuers into the abyss as Egypt had cast Israel's children into the river, a thousand Egyptians for each infant. The spirit Mastema, bound during the Passover days, was let loose to urge the chase, and it was he who hardened the Egyptians' hearts, by the Lord's design.

A Jewish writer in Egypt whose work survives in quotations. He reports two Egyptian versions of the crossing: the people of Memphis said Moses knew the country and waited for the ebb tide, while the people of Heliopolis said a divine voice told him to strike the sea with his rod, and it divided. In the second version a fire blazed in the Egyptians' faces, and fire and flood destroyed them together.

A Jewish poet who wrote the Exodus as a Greek tragedy. A surviving Egyptian soldier reports the disaster: the army camped by a city called Baal-zephon, saw the pillar of cloud rise between the camps, and followed Israel into the sea, where their wheels would not turn, “as if fast bound in chains.” One soldier cries out to flee, since Israel's God is fighting for them, the cry of v. 25.

Josephus adds a storm to the returning sea, with rain, thunder, and lightning over the Egyptians, as Psalm 77:17–18 also pictures it. He defends the miracle by noting that the Pamphylian Sea drew back for Alexander the Great's army, though he leaves readers to judge. The next day, he says, the current washed the Egyptians' weapons ashore and Moses armed the people with them, an answer also given in an older writer quoted by Eusebius.
traditions.cite: Antiquities 2.16.3–6; Eusebius, Preparation for the Gospel 9.29

traditions.text: Records a dispute over who entered the sea first. Rabbi Meir says every tribe wanted to go first and Benjamin jumped in; Rabbi Judah says none would go until Nahshon son of Amminadab of Judah leaped into the water. While Moses lingered in prayer, God told him that his beloved were drowning, and the answer was v. 16: lift up thy rod.

Reads “the one came not near the other all the night” (v. 20) as the angels, who wished to sing their nightly song to one another. God stopped them: the work of his hands was drowning in the sea, and they would sing? The rabbis drew from it that God does not rejoice over the fall of the wicked.

Counts the crossing as an act of faith: by faith Israel passed through the Red Sea as by dry land, and the Egyptians, trying the same, drowned. The same water that saves one people destroys the other, a contrast Philo also draws (On the Contemplative Life 86).

Calls the crossing the clearest figure of baptism: the people, set free, escape the Egyptian king by passing through water, and the water destroys the king with all his forces. So the nations are freed from the world by water, and leave the devil, their old tyrant, overwhelmed in it. Paul's “baptized unto Moses” (1 Corinthians 10:2) lies behind the reading.

15.overview:
Moses and Israel sing to the LORD for the victory at the sea. The song praises him as a warrior who threw horse and rider into the sea, mocks the enemy's boast, asks who among the gods is like him, and looks ahead: the nations of Canaan will freeze in fear as Israel passes, until God plants his people on his own mountain and reigns for ever. Miriam the prophetess leads the women with timbrels and dancing, singing the first line back. Then the march goes on into the wilderness of Shur: three days without water, bitter water at Marah made sweet by a tree, and rest at Elim with twelve wells and seventy palm trees.

Within a few verses Israel goes from singing to murmuring. Three days after the sea, the people who believed (14:31) ask, “What shall we drink?” (v. 24). Marah opens the wilderness pattern of need, complaint, and provision.

historicalContext.label: Author
historicalContext.text: Verse 1 gives the song to Moses and the children of Israel, and v. 21 gives its refrain to Miriam. Tradition credits Moses with the book; many scholars see the song as an older poem set into the narrative.

historicalContext.label: Date written
historicalContext.text: Tradition places the song at the event. Many scholars count it among the oldest Hebrew poetry, perhaps 12th–10th century BC, because of its archaic grammar; the surrounding prose may be later.

historicalContext.label: Date of events
historicalContext.text: Days after the Passover: about 1446 BC by 1 Kings 6:1, or the 13th century BC in many scholars' view.

historicalContext.label: Language
historicalContext.text: Archaic Hebrew poetry (vv. 1–18, 21), with prose in vv. 19–20 and 22–27.

historicalContext.label: Setting (events)
historicalContext.text: The shore of the sea, then the wilderness of Shur east of Egypt: Marah, three days on, and the oasis of Elim (vv. 22–27).

historicalContext.label: Parallel accounts
historicalContext.text: Exodus 14 tells the same events in prose; compare Psalms 78:13; 106:9–12. Alma 36:28 and Revelation 15:3 take up the song.

15.hermeneutics:
In the Baal myths from Ugarit (about 1300 BC), the storm god Baal defeats Yam, the Sea; then a palace is built for him on his mountain, Zaphon, and he is proclaimed king. The Song of the Sea moves in the same order: victory at the sea (vv. 1–12), the march to God's mountain and sanctuary (vv. 13–17), and the shout, “The LORD shall reign for ever and ever” (v. 18). The difference is pointed. The sea here is no rival god; it is water that God's breath piles up and lets fall (vv. 8, 10), and the enemy is Pharaoh. The question “Who is like unto thee, O LORD, among the gods?” (v. 11) is asked in a world that told the other story.

When an army came home victorious, Israel's women went out to meet it with hand drums, dancing and singing short refrains back and forth, as they did for Saul and David (1 Samuel 18:6–7) and as Jephthah's daughter did (Judges 11:34). Clay figurines of women holding frame drums are common finds in Iron Age Israel and Phoenicia. Miriam's part (vv. 20–21) is that familiar role: she leads the women out and answers with the song's opening couplet. Here the returning warrior is the LORD himself, and the army never fought.

breakdown.label: I will sing unto the LORD: a man of war
Pharaoh's chariots sink like a stone
Thy right hand; the enemy's boast; they sink like lead
Who is like unto thee among the gods?
Israel guided on; the nations still as a stone
Planted on God's mountain; the LORD shall reign
The deliverance recalled; Miriam and the women with timbrels
Marah: bitter water sweetened; a statute and a promise
Elim: twelve wells, seventy palm trees

structure.summary: An opening hymn, three stanzas that each close on a simile of sinking or stillness, and a closing acclamation (a common scholarly division). Not a chiasm.

rows.text: Opening hymn: “I will sing unto the LORD”
Stanza three ends: “as still as a stone”
Close: the sanctuary; “The LORD shall reign”

notes: **Similes:** the enemy sinks “as a stone” (v. 5) and “as lead” (v. 10); then the nations of Canaan stand “still as a stone” (v. 16) while Israel passes. The same image moves from the drowned to the terrified.
**The name:** the LORD (*YHWH*) is named ten times in vv. 1–18, and v. 3 stops to say “the LORD is his name.” “Thy right hand” comes twice in v. 6 and again in v. 12.
**Frame:** Miriam's couplet (v. 21) repeats the opening line (v. 1), so her refrain brackets the whole song.

Verse 21 ends the deliverance from Egypt (1:1–15:21), closing with Miriam's couplet. Verse 22 begins the journey to Sinai (15:22–18:27). Marah opens a run of wilderness crises: bitter water here, then hunger (ch. 16), thirst at Rephidim (17:1–7), and war with Amalek (17:8–16).

**Forward:** “I am the LORD that healeth thee” (v. 26) names God by a promise. In Revelation the victors stand by a sea of glass and sing “the song of Moses” and the song of the Lamb (Revelation 15:2–3).

traditions.text: Telling his son Helaman of his conversion, Alma ends in the song's terms: he will praise God for ever, for God brought the fathers out of Egypt and “swallowed up the Egyptians in the Red Sea.” Like Moses, he sets his own deliverance beside Israel's.

This revelation on priesthood ends with a new song that the redeemed will sing together in the last days: the Lord has brought again Zion and redeemed his people Israel. Like Moses' song it celebrates a redemption already worked and ends on God's glory “forever and ever.”

Philo pictures two choirs on the shore, the men led by Moses and the women by Miriam, singing hymns of thanks to God the Saviour. He says the Therapeutae, a contemplative Jewish community in Egypt, ended their festal nights by joining their men's and women's choirs into one, “an imitation of that one” at the Red Sea, and sang until sunrise.
traditions.cite: On the Life of Moses 1.180; On the Contemplative Life 85–89

traditions.text: Says the Hebrews spent the whole night after the crossing in hymns and rejoicing, and that Moses composed his song of praise in hexameter verse, the meter of Homer. For his Greek readers the song becomes a classical ode, and Moses something like a Greek poet.

After the crossing, Wisdom says, the righteous praised God with one accord, for wisdom “opened the mouth of the dumb” and made the tongues of infants eloquent. The Talmud tells the same scene in detail: babies on their mothers' laps and infants at the breast saw the divine presence and sang the words of v. 2, This is my God.

Rabbi Akiva reads the extra word “saying” in v. 1 to mean that the people answered Moses after each line with the refrain “I will sing unto the LORD,” as in reciting the Hallel psalms. Rabbi Nehemiah holds that they sang it together with him, as the Shema is recited.
Rabbi Meir notices that the Hebrew verb of v. 1 can be read “then Moses will sing.” He takes the future tense as proof from the Torah that the dead will rise, so that Moses will sing this song again.

Says that a maidservant at the sea saw what Ezekiel and the other prophets never saw, so plainly was God revealed that anyone could point and say, “This is my God” (v. 2). The Mekhilta also counts ten songs in Scripture, from the night in Egypt to the new song of the age to come, and places this one second.

The Hebrew behind the KJV's “prepare him an habitation” (v. 2) is a rare word that most translations render as glorify. One teaching reads it as a call to beautify the commandments: a fine sukkah, a fine Torah scroll. Abba Shaul splits the word into “I and he”: be like God, compassionate as he is compassionate.

The Mekhilta asks what tree healed Marah's water and lists answers from a willow to an olive, the bitterest of trees, to a cedar; Rabban Simeon ben Gamaliel notes that God heals bitter with bitter. It reads the statute and ordinance of v. 25 as the Sabbath and honoring parents. The Talmud counts Marah as the place where Israel received ten commandments before Sinai.

In Ezekiel's Greek drama of the Exodus a scout reports Elim to Moses: a shady meadow by a stream, twelve springs pouring from a single rock, and seventy tall palms laden with fruit. He then describes a bird larger than an eagle, with a purple breast and golden neck, that all other birds follow, a creature often identified as the phoenix.

John sees those who have overcome the beast standing by a sea of glass mingled with fire and singing the song of Moses and of the Lamb. The victory at the Red Sea becomes the pattern for the final victory of God's people.

Justin lists the tree Moses cast into Marah's bitter water among the figures of the cross, alongside the rod that divided the sea and the tree of life in paradise. Ambrose applies it to baptism: water without the preaching of the cross is of no avail, but when the cross is proclaimed over the font, the water is made sweet for grace. Tertullian had already said that the tree of Moses was Christ (On Baptism 9).
traditions.cite: Dialogue with Trypho 86; On the Mysteries 3.14

16.overview:
A month out of Egypt, in the wilderness of Sin, the whole congregation complains that they would rather have died by the flesh pots of Egypt. The LORD promises bread from heaven. Quail cover the camp at evening, and in the morning a small round thing lies on the ground like frost. The people do not know what it is; Moses tells them it is the bread the LORD has given. Each person gathers an omer, what is kept overnight breeds worms, and on the sixth day a double portion keeps fresh. Some go out on the seventh day anyway and find nothing.

The manna is a test, and the LORD says so before any of it falls: “that I may prove them” (v. 4). The first law Israel is tested on is the Sabbath, given here before Sinai and before the Ten Commandments.

historicalContext.label: Author
historicalContext.text: Not named in the text. Jewish and Christian tradition credits Moses; many scholars see Exodus as compiled later from older sources.

historicalContext.label: Date written
historicalContext.text: Unknown. Tradition places it in Moses' lifetime (15th or 13th century BC); scholarly proposals reach the 6th–5th century BC.

historicalContext.label: Date of events
historicalContext.text: The fifteenth day of the second month after leaving Egypt (v. 1). Reckoning from 1 Kings 6:1 puts the Exodus about 1446 BC; many scholars prefer about 1250 BC.

historicalContext.label: Setting (events)
historicalContext.text: The wilderness of Sin, “between Elim and Sinai” (v. 1), usually placed in the western Sinai peninsula.

historicalContext.label: Parallel accounts
historicalContext.text: Numbers 11:4–9, 31–34 (manna and quail again); Psalm 78:24–25; Deuteronomy 8:3. The Book of Mormon recalls the manna in 1 Nephi 17:28 and Mosiah 7:19.

16.hermeneutics:
Bedouin in the Sinai still gather a sweet substance they call *mann*. Scale insects feeding on tamarisk trees give off drops of sugary honeydew that harden in the cool of the night and must be collected early, before the heat and the ants take them; the entomologist F. S. Bodenheimer described the process in 1947. The comparison shows what Exodus claims beyond nature. The natural product comes in small amounts for a few weeks in early summer, while the manna of this chapter feeds a whole people every morning for forty years (v. 35), comes double on the sixth day, and fails on the seventh.

Quail cross the Mediterranean in spring and autumn and come down exhausted on the coasts of Egypt and Sinai. Diodorus Siculus describes settlers at Rhinocolura, on that coast, stretching reed nets along the beach for miles to catch them (1.60.10). A flock settling on a camp at evening (v. 13) was a known sight in the region. Exodus gives the quail a single verse and spends the rest of the chapter on the bread, which is where the test lies.

Babylon had a day called *shapattu*, but it was the fifteenth of the month, the day of the full moon, and Babylonian day-lists marked the 7th, 14th, 19th, 21st and 28th as days of restriction for the king. Israel's seventh day follows a seven-day count that ignores the moon entirely. In v. 23 the Sabbath arrives without explanation, and the manna itself keeps the count: six days of bread, then none.

breakdown.label: Wilderness of Sin: the whole congregation murmurs
Bread from heaven promised; the glory in the cloud
Quail at evening; manna on the ground at morning
An omer apiece; what is kept overnight breeds worms
The double portion and the first Sabbath
The manna described; an omer kept before the Testimony

structure.summary: No strong pattern; the chapter moves in sequence. Once the manna falls, three rules test the people.

rows.text: Gather an omer each: some more, some less, and none lack
Leave none till morning: some do, and it stinks
Gather none on the seventh day: some go out, and find none

notes: **Three rules, two failures:** the omer rule works out for everyone, but the overnight rule and the Sabbath rule are each broken by “some” (vv. 20, 27).
**Murmuring:** the Hebrew verb and noun for “murmur” come 8 times, all in vv. 2–12. Once the bread arrives the complaint vocabulary stops.
**Repetition to watch:** “morning” 10 times; “bread” 8; “omer” 6; “sabbath” 4 (vv. 23, 25, 26, 29), with a related word for “rest” in v. 23.

Between the sea and Sinai, Exodus sets three tests in a row: bitter water at Marah (15:22–27), no food in the wilderness of Sin (ch. 16), no water at Rephidim (17:1–7). One Hebrew verb, “prove” or “tempt,” ties them together (15:25; 16:4; 17:2, 7), and it returns at Sinai when Moses says God has come “to prove you” (20:20). Verse 34 looks ahead: the Testimony the jar is laid before is not given until ch. 25 (25:16).
**Forward:** the manna and quail return in Numbers 11, where the people tire of them, and the manna stops the day after Israel eats the produce of Canaan (Joshua 5:12).

traditions.text: Nephi, mocked by his brothers for building a ship, reminds them that Israel “were fed with manna in the wilderness” and still reviled Moses and hardened their hearts. Centuries later King Limhi, whose people are in bondage, tells them to trust the God who fed Israel with manna so that they would not perish. In both places the manna is an argument: the God who fed Israel in the desert can deliver this family or this people too.

Written in Greek by a Jew of Alexandria, the book calls the manna the food of angels, as Psalm 78:25 does, and says it turned into whatever each eater wanted. It also explains why the manna melted in the sun (v. 21): so that people would learn “that we ought to prevent the sun” to bless God and pray at dawn. The Talmud later develops the same idea of a food that tasted different to each person (below).

Philo takes the people's puzzlement in v. 15 as the question of every soul looking for its food. Moses' answer, that this is the bread the Lord has given, he reads as the word of God, which both lights the soul and sweetens it. Deuteronomy 8:3 draws a similar lesson, that the manna taught Israel to live “by every word that proceedeth out of the mouth of the LORD.”

Josephus says the manna was like honey in sweetness and like bdellium in appearance, and adds that “even now in all that place this manna comes down in rain.” He is describing the natural honeydew of the Sinai (see Hermeneutics) while still treating the forty years of manna as God's provision.

Pirkei Avot lists the manna among ten things created at twilight on the eve of the first Sabbath, together with the well, the mouth of Balaam's donkey, the rainbow, Moses' staff, and the tablets. On this view the manna was not improvised in the desert but set aside at creation, and it belonged with the Sabbath from the start.

The oldest rabbinic commentary on Exodus records Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai's saying that the Torah was given to be expounded only by those who ate the manna, since a man who must find his bread cannot sit and study. Rabbi Eliezer of Modiin read the daily ration of v. 4 as a lesson in trust: whoever has food for today and asks what he will eat tomorrow lacks faith.

As a baby tastes many flavors in its mother's milk, the rabbis say, Israel tasted every kind of food in the manna. They also made the gathering a measure of character. The righteous found the manna at their doors, ordinary people went out and gathered it, and the wicked had to roam about for it.

This apocalypse, written after Jerusalem fell to Rome in AD 70, foresees that when the Messiah is revealed “the treasury of manna shall again descend from on high,” and the righteous will eat it in those years. The jar laid up in vv. 33–34 becomes a sign of a meal still to come, the same hope behind the “hidden manna” of Revelation 2:17.

After the feeding of the five thousand, the crowd reminds Jesus that their fathers ate manna, bread from heaven. He answers that his Father gives the true bread from heaven and that he himself is the bread of life. He then turns v. 35 back on them: their fathers ate manna in the wilderness and died, but whoever eats this bread will live for ever.

Paul calls the manna “spiritual meat” and warns the Corinthians that eating it did not keep many in the wilderness from falling. Raising money for the poor in Jerusalem, he quotes v. 18, “he that had gathered much had nothing over,” as the model for Christians who share so that all have enough.

Hebrews places “the golden pot that had manna” inside the ark, beside Aaron's rod and the tablets, which is how it read the jar laid up before the Testimony. Revelation promises the faithful at Pergamos a share in the hidden manna and a white stone with a new name.

Preaching on John 6, Augustine notes that Moses, Aaron, and Phinehas also ate manna yet are not among the dead Jesus speaks of, because they understood the visible food spiritually. The difference, he says, lay in how it was eaten, and he applies the warning to Christians receiving the Eucharist. He calls the manna a shadow and Christ the truth.

17.overview:
At Rephidim there is no water, and the people quarrel with Moses until he fears they will stone him. The LORD sends him ahead with the elders and the rod that struck the river; God stands on the rock in Horeb, Moses strikes it, and water comes out. Moses names the place Massah and Meribah for the people's chiding and testing. Then Amalek attacks. Joshua leads the fighting while Moses stands on a hilltop with the rod of God, and Israel prevails only while his hands stay raised, so Aaron and Hur hold them up until sunset. Moses writes a memorial and builds an altar, Jehovah-nissi.

Both halves answer the question the people ask in v. 7: “Is the LORD among us, or not?” The water answers it at the rock where God stands, and the battle answers it again from the hill.

historicalContext.label: Author
historicalContext.text: Not named in the text. Jewish and Christian tradition credits Moses; v. 14 has the LORD tell Moses to write the memorial against Amalek in a book.

historicalContext.label: Date written
historicalContext.text: Unknown. Tradition places it in Moses' lifetime (15th or 13th century BC); scholarly proposals reach the 6th–5th century BC.

historicalContext.label: Date of events
historicalContext.text: Between the second month (16:1) and the third, when Israel reaches Sinai (19:1). Reckoning from 1 Kings 6:1 puts the Exodus about 1446 BC; many scholars prefer about 1250 BC.

historicalContext.label: Setting (events)
historicalContext.text: Rephidim, the last camp before Sinai (19:2); the rock is “in Horeb” (v. 6), the mountain of God (3:1). Amalek descends from Esau (Genesis 36:12) and later lives in the Negev (Numbers 13:29).

historicalContext.label: Parallel accounts
historicalContext.text: Numbers 20:2–13 (a second Meribah); Deuteronomy 25:17–19 (Amalek); Psalm 95:8. Nephi recalls the smitten rock in 1 Nephi 17:29.

17.hermeneutics:
Armies in Egypt and Assyria marched behind standards: poles topped with the emblem of a god, carried into battle so the god went with the troops. Assyrian palace reliefs show the emblem of the god Ashur riding in the king's chariot. Moses on the hill with “the rod of God in mine hand” (v. 9) is doing what a standard-bearer did, in full view of the fighting below. The name of the altar, Jehovah-nissi, “the LORD is my banner,” says outright whose standard Israel fought under.

Mesopotamian prayers of the type called *shuilla*, “lifting of the hand,” were named for the gesture that went with them, and raised hands are the common posture of prayer in ancient Near Eastern art. Exodus, though, never says that Moses prays. It records only his hands, rising and falling with the battle, and leaves the reader to decide what they meant (see Traditions).

To erase a name was the harshest punishment the ancient world could give the dead. Egyptian kings chiseled rivals' names off monuments, as Thutmose III did with Hatshepsut's, and Egyptian execration texts wrote enemies' names on bowls and figurines that were then smashed. Verse 14 turns the practice inside out: Moses must write in a book the LORD's vow to blot out Amalek's memory, so the sentence of forgetting is itself kept on record. Deuteronomy 25:19 holds the same tension in one verse: “blot out the remembrance of Amalek,” and “thou shalt not forget it.”

Amalek attacks; Joshua fights, Moses climbs the hill
Raised hands and heavy hands; Aaron and Hur hold them
A memorial written; the altar Jehovah-nissi
