notes: Each panel ends with Moses giving a name. The first records the people's doubt; the second answers it with the LORD as Israel's banner.
**Hand and rod:** “hand” occurs 8 times in Hebrew (vv. 5, 9, 11 twice, 12 three times, 16). The rod that struck the river now strikes a rock and is then held up over a battle.
**Amalek** is named 7 times in vv. 8–16. Joshua appears here for the first time in the Bible, already a commander.

Chapter 17 closes the run of wilderness tests that began after the sea: Marah, the manna, and now Massah, all marked by the Hebrew verb “prove” or “tempt” (15:25; 16:4; 17:2, 7). Here, for the first time, the people test God rather than God testing them. The Amalek battle is Israel's first war, and Rephidim is the last camp before Sinai (19:2).

**Later echoes:** Numbers 20 tells of a second Meribah, where Moses strikes a rock twice and is barred from Canaan. Psalm 95:8 warns against hardening the heart “as in the day of temptation.” Saul's war in 1 Samuel 15 carries out the sentence of v. 14.

traditions.text: Nephi, urging his brothers to help build a ship, reminds them that Moses smote the rock and water came forth “according to the power of God which was in him.” In his telling, Israel's response is the point: though the Lord went before them, leading them by day and giving light by night, they hardened their hearts and reviled Moses. Nephi's text of Isaiah 48:21 from the brass plates recalls the same miracle, that the Lord clave the rock and the waters gushed out.

A Jewish writer in Egypt whose work survives in quotations preserved by Eusebius. He took up a question the text leaves open: how could a people who left Egypt unarmed fight a battle? His answer was that those not drowned in the sea used the weapons of those who were.

Josephus makes Hur the husband of Miriam, “their sister Miriam's husband,” a detail Exodus never gives. He has Aaron and Hur stand on either side of Moses to hold up his hands, ends the fighting at nightfall, and has Israel take rich spoil from the Amalekite camp.

Philo has Moses, inspired, strike the rock and a stream pour out. In the battle Moses' hands grow by turns lighter and heavier, and Philo reads it as a figure: earth was the enemy's portion and heaven Israel's, and the heavenly portion prevailed. He calls the altar the refuge of God, following the Greek Septuagint's rendering of Jehovah-nissi.

The Mishnah asks outright whether Moses' hands won or lost the war. Its answer: when Israel looked upward and turned their hearts to their Father in heaven they prevailed, and when they did not, they fell. It reads the serpent on the pole (Numbers 21:8) the same way, so that the gesture points the people to God.

A teaching in the Talmud asks why Moses sat on a stone (v. 12) instead of a cushion. Because Israel was in distress, he chose to share it. From this the rabbis drew a rule: whoever shares the community's trouble will live to see its comfort.

Two rabbis disagree over the name of the place where Amalek attacked. Rabbi Eliezer said Rephidim was simply its name, while Rabbi Joshua heard in it a hint that Israel's hands had grown slack in the Torah, citing the “feebleness of hands” of Jeremiah 47:3. The image of slack hands sits close to the scene of Moses' own heavy hands in v. 12.

A retelling of biblical history, long misattributed to Philo, says that for forty years God brought forth for Israel “a well of water following them.” Exodus has water from the rock only at Rephidim and later at Meribah (Numbers 20), but this tradition makes the water a companion for the whole journey, the idea Paul draws on (below).

Paul tells the Corinthians that the fathers in the wilderness “drank of that spiritual Rock that followed them,” and that the Rock was Christ. He uses the image as a warning: they all had the same spiritual food and drink, and still most of them were overthrown in the wilderness. These things were written, he goes on, as examples for Christians, who should take heed lest they fall the same way.

Barnabas pictures Moses piling weapons on the hill and standing on them with arms outstretched, so that Israel would see a figure of the cross. It notes that Moses gave Joshua the name Jesus (the same name in Greek, Numbers 13:16) and reads v. 14 as a prophecy that the Son of God would cut off the house of Amalek at the roots in the last days.

Arguing with a Jewish teacher, Justin says the victory did not come from Moses praying, since he was seated on a stone and not kneeling in tears. It came because his outstretched arms made the sign of the cross while one bearing the name Jesus led the fight. Barnabas and Justin read the scene the way the Mishnah refuses to, as power in the gesture itself.

Tertullian asks why Moses, of all times, prayed seated with his hands spread out while Joshua fought Amalek, and answers that the cross was being shown in advance. In the same chapter he reads the serpent Moses set on a pole as the power of the cross over the old serpent. The Mishnah pairs the same two scenes, hands and serpent, but reads both as Israel looking upward to God.

18.overview:
Jethro, priest of Midian and Moses' father-in-law, hears what God has done for Israel and brings Moses' wife Zipporah and their two sons to the camp at the mount of God. Moses tells him the whole story. Jethro blesses the LORD, declares him greater than all gods, and offers sacrifices, and Aaron and the elders eat bread with him before God. The next day Jethro watches Moses judge the people alone from morning to evening and tells him it will wear him out. He advises appointing able men over thousands, hundreds, fifties, and tens, with only the hard cases brought to Moses. Moses does all he says, and Jethro goes home.

Israel's first system of courts comes from a Midianite priest, and Moses takes the advice without argument. Between Amalek's attack and the covenant at Sinai, a foreigner blesses Israel's God and helps order Israel's life.

historicalContext.label: Author
historicalContext.text: Not named in the text. Jewish and Christian tradition credits Moses; many scholars see Exodus as compiled later from older sources.

historicalContext.label: Date written
historicalContext.text: Unknown. Tradition places it in Moses' lifetime (15th or 13th century BC); scholarly proposals reach the 6th–5th century BC.

historicalContext.label: Date of events
historicalContext.text: Uncertain. Verse 5 has Israel already camped at “the mount of God,” and Deuteronomy 1:6–15 sets the choosing of judges at Horeb, just before Israel leaves it.

historicalContext.label: Setting (events)
historicalContext.text: The camp at the mount of God (v. 5), where Moses first met God while keeping Jethro's flock (3:1).

historicalContext.label: Parallel accounts
historicalContext.text: Deuteronomy 1:9–18 (Moses' own retelling, without Jethro); Numbers 11:16–17 (seventy elders share the burden). D&C 84:6 adds that Moses received the priesthood under Jethro's hand.

18.hermeneutics:
Egyptian lists of foreign lands from the temple of Amenhotep III at Soleb in Nubia (14th century BC), copied again under Ramesses II, name “the land of the Shasu of Yhw.” The Shasu were herders of the desert fringe, and this group is usually placed in the region of Edom and Seir, south of the Dead Sea and near Midian. It is the oldest mention outside the Bible of a name like Israel's divine name, and it ties that name to the region Jethro came from. Scholars debate what the link means. For a first hearer, a Midianite priest who blesses the LORD and offers sacrifice with Israel's elders (vv. 10–12) would not have seemed out of place.

Ancient kings called themselves the supreme judges of their lands, but in practice they delegated. The Egyptian text known as the *Duties of the Vizier*, inscribed in the tomb of Rekhmire (15th century BC), has the vizier hear petitions every morning in his hall and send lesser matters to the officials under him. Pharaoh Horemheb's decree appointed judges in the cities and warned them against taking bribes. Jethro's plan follows the same administrative logic, with layered courts and only hard cases sent up, but sets a moral test on the judges: men who “fear God, men of truth, hating covetousness” (v. 21). His units of thousands, hundreds, fifties, and tens are the divisions of an army, fitting a people on the march.

breakdown.label: Jethro hears and brings Zipporah and her sons
Moses greets him and tells all the LORD has done
Jethro blesses the LORD; sacrifice and bread before God
Moses judging alone from morning to evening: “not good”
Jethro's counsel: able men over thousands and tens
Judges appointed; Jethro goes home

structure.summary: No strong pattern; the chapter moves in sequence, in two scenes on two days.

rows.text: Day one: Jethro hears, comes, rejoices, and sacrifices
The morrow: Jethro sees, counsels, and departs

notes: **Father in law:** Jethro is called Moses' “father in law” 13 times. His own name appears 7 times, all in vv. 1–12; in the counsel scene he is only the father-in-law.
**Deliver:** the verb for “deliver” comes 5 times in vv. 4–10, from the meaning of Eliezer's name to Jethro's blessing.

**Good and alone:** Jethro rejoices over “all the goodness” (v. 9) and then tells Moses his way is “not good” (v. 17), with “alone” twice (vv. 14, 18). The same Hebrew pair, “not good” and “alone,” stands in Genesis 2:18.

Chapter 18 closes the journey section (15:22–18:27) and pairs with ch. 17: Amalek, a desert people, attacks Israel, and Jethro, a desert priest, blesses Israel's God. Because v. 5 already has Israel at the mount of God, the chapter may stand here by theme rather than by date (see Traditions).

**Forward:** Moses retells the appointment of judges in Deuteronomy 1:9–18 without naming Jethro, and the sharing of his burden returns in Numbers 11:16–17 with seventy elders. Moses later asks Hobab, son of Raguel the Midianite, to guide Israel through the wilderness (Numbers 10:29–32).

traditions.text: In a revelation on priesthood, the Lord traces Moses' authority back through Jethro: Moses received the Holy Priesthood “under the hand of his father-in-law, Jethro.” Jethro received it from Caleb, and the line runs back through Elihu, Jeremy, and Gad to Esaias, who lived in Abraham's day and received it under the hand of God. Exodus 18 shows Jethro as a priest who offers sacrifice and eats with Israel's elders before God, and D&C 84 gives his priesthood a line of descent.

A Jewish writer in Egypt, quoted by Eusebius, worked out Jethro's family tree. He traces Jothor (Jethro) back to Abraham through Keturah: Jokshan, then Dedan, then Raguel, whose sons were Jothor and Hobab. On this reckoning the priest of Midian was Abraham's descendant, and Zipporah was a daughter of Abraham's house like Moses himself.

Philo, unusually, reads Jethro as a figure of vanity, a mind puffed up with opinion that offers human customs in place of the laws of nature. Even the confession of v. 11 counts against him in Philo's reading: a man who truly knew God would not compare him with other gods. The rabbis took Jethro the opposite way, as a model convert (below).

Josephus calls Jethro Raguel and has him propose rulers over tens, fifties, hundreds, thousands, and even ten thousands, with the hardest cases passed up the chain to Moses. He stresses that Moses did not hide where the plan came from: “he has named Raguel in the Books he wrote” as the one who invented this ordering of the people. Where Philo's Jethro is a figure of pride (above), Josephus's Raguel gets full credit.

The Dead Sea community ranked its members at its yearly covenant ceremony, the priests first, then the Levites, then all the people in their thousands, hundreds, fifties, and tens, so that each Israelite would know his place. Jethro's units became the pattern for a community that modeled itself on Israel's camp in the wilderness.

Two rabbis spell out Jethro's qualifications in v. 21. For Rabbi Joshua, “able men” are men of means and “hating covetousness” means refusing bribes. Rabbi Elazar of Modiin reads it as men willing to lose their own money, since a judge who will give up his own property will guard other people's all the more. The same passage counts a judge who gives a true verdict as a partner of God in the work of creation.

When Moses begs him to stay, Jethro refuses with a figure: Moses is the sun and Aaron the moon, and a candle adds nothing beside them. He goes home (v. 27) to bring his own people to the Torah. The Mekhilta finds the result in Judges 1:16, where the Kenites, the children of Moses' father-in-law, go up and dwell among the people of Judah.

What did Jethro hear (v. 1)? Rabbi Joshua said the war with Amalek, which Exodus has just told. Rabbi Elazar of Modiin said the giving of the Torah, whose voice made the kings of the nations tremble in their palaces, and Rabbi Eliezer said the parting of the sea. The second answer puts Jethro's visit after Sinai.

Rav and Shmuel disagreed over the unusual verb for “rejoiced” in v. 9. One read it as Jethro circumcising himself and becoming a proselyte; the other as a shudder running through his flesh at Egypt's ruin. From the second reading Rav drew a rule of tact: for ten generations, do not speak ill of gentiles in front of a convert's family.

Rashi gives Jethro seven names: Reuel, Jether, Jethro, Hobab, Heber, Keni, and Putiel. A letter was added to Jether to make Jethro when he converted, and the name also recalls that he “added” a section to the Torah, the counsel of v. 21. On v. 11 he says Jethro knew every idol in the world, having served them all, so his verdict that the LORD is greater carried weight.

Rashi takes “on the morrow” (v. 13) to be the day after the Day of Atonement, when Moses came down with the second tablets, so at least the judging scene falls after Sinai. He adds that Jethro objected to Moses sitting like a king while all the people stood. And he reads Hobab of Numbers 10:29 as Jethro himself, pointing to Judges 4:11.

19.overview:
In the third month Israel reaches the wilderness of Sinai and camps before the mountain. Moses goes up, and God offers a covenant: Israel has seen what he did to Egypt and how he bore them on eagles' wings, and if they obey his voice they will be his peculiar treasure, a kingdom of priests, and an holy nation. The people agree. For three days they wash their clothes and keep apart from their wives, while bounds are set around the mountain that no one may cross. On the third morning come thunder, lightning, a thick cloud, a very loud trumpet, fire, and smoke, and the whole mountain quakes.

The chapter is built on that boundary. The people are invited to be a kingdom of priests, yet they may not touch the mountain, and Moses keeps climbing up and down to carry words between them and God.

historicalContext.label: Author
historicalContext.text: Not named in the text. Jewish and Christian tradition credits Moses; many scholars see several sources combined in the Sinai account.

historicalContext.label: Date written
historicalContext.text: Unknown. Tradition places it in Moses' lifetime (15th or 13th century BC); scholarly proposals reach the 6th–5th century BC.

historicalContext.label: Date of events
historicalContext.text: The third month after leaving Egypt (v. 1). Reckoning from 1 Kings 6:1 puts the Exodus about 1446 BC; many scholars prefer about 1250 BC.

historicalContext.label: Setting (events)
historicalContext.text: Mount Sinai, also called Horeb. Its location is unknown: Christian tradition since late antiquity places it at Jebel Musa in the southern Sinai peninsula, and some look to northwest Arabia (Galatians 4:25).

historicalContext.label: Parallel accounts
historicalContext.text: Deuteronomy 4:10–14; 5:2–5. D&C 84:23–24 says Moses sought to sanctify the people so they might behold the face of God.

19.hermeneutics:
Hittite treaties of the 14th and 13th centuries BC, between the great king and a lesser king, follow a set form: the great king's titles, a history of what he had done for the vassal, the vassal's obligations, and blessings and curses. George Mendenhall argued in 1954 that Israel's covenant borrows this form. Verses 4–6 compress it into three moves: a history (“ye have seen what I did unto the Egyptians”), a condition (“if ye will obey my voice indeed”), and a status. The relationship is offered, not imposed, and the people answer it (v. 8).

The status word is *segullah*, “peculiar treasure” (v. 5), a king's private holding. In a letter from the Hittite king to his vassal at Ugarit, the same word in Ugaritic (*sglt*) describes the vassal king as his lord's servant and treasured possession. Read against that background, v. 5 makes Israel the LORD's own vassal people, valued above the rest of a world that is also his (“for all the earth is mine”).

Ancient temples were graded zones of holiness, and the people who served in them had to be pure. Hittite instructions for temple officials require one who has slept with a woman to bathe at sunrise before serving the gods, on pain of death if he defiles their bread. Exodus applies temple rules to a mountain: washing (v. 10), abstinence (v. 15), and a death penalty for crossing the boundary (v. 12), with the people at the foot, priests nearer (v. 22), and Moses at the top.

breakdown.label: Arrival in the wilderness of Sinai in the third month
Eagles' wings: a kingdom of priests offered
The people agree; God will come in a thick cloud
Three days of washing; bounds set around the mountain
The third day: thunder, cloud, trumpet, fire, and smoke
Moses called up, then sent down to warn again

structure.summary: No strong pattern; the chapter moves in sequence, carried by Moses going up and down the mountain.

rows.text: He comes to the elders, then returns the people's answer
He goes down and sanctifies the people
The LORD comes down; Moses goes up to the top
Moses goes down and speaks to the people

notes: **Up and down:** in Hebrew “go up” comes 8 times and “come down” 7. The verbs are used of Moses, of the people forbidden to go up, and of the LORD himself, who comes down (vv. 11, 18, 20).
**Mount** occurs 16 times and “people” 18, the two poles of the chapter.
**Voice:** the Hebrew word for “voice” serves for God's call (“obey my voice,” v. 5), for the “thunders” and the trumpet (vv. 16, 19), and for the voice by which God answers Moses (v. 19).

Chapter 19 opens the third part of Exodus, the covenant at Sinai (19:1–24:18). Israel stays at this mountain through the rest of Exodus, all of Leviticus, and Numbers 1–10, leaving only in Numbers 10:11–12. The storm of vv. 16–19 returns in 20:18–21, so the theophany frames the Ten Commandments.

**Back to the bush:** God told Moses at this mountain that the sign of his call would be Israel serving God “upon this mountain” (3:12). Chapter 19 is that sign fulfilled. Deuteronomy 4:10–12 recalls the day: the people heard a voice but saw no form.

traditions.text: The revelation says Moses “plainly taught” Israel in the wilderness and sought diligently to sanctify his people that they might behold the face of God. They hardened their hearts and could not endure his presence, so the Lord took Moses out of their midst, and the Holy Priesthood also, and the lesser priesthood continued. The washing and the boundary of this chapter are, in that light, a preparation the people did not complete.

Describing the resurrection, the Lord says a trump will sound “both long and loud, even as upon Mount Sinai,” and all the earth will quake. The trumpet that called Israel to the foot of the mountain (vv. 13, 16, 19) becomes the signal that calls the righteous dead to come forth.

Jubilees dates Moses' ascent to the sixteenth day of the third month and makes the Feast of Weeks, which falls in that month, an annual feast “to renew the covenant every year.” Noah kept it first, Abraham and his sons after him, and Israel forgot it until it was celebrated again on the mountain. Later Judaism likewise ties Sinai to the Feast of Weeks, Shavuot, as the festival of the giving of the Torah.

Philo asks why the law was given in a desert and not in a city. Cities, he says, breed pride and false worship; a people had to be purified before receiving laws; laws should be ready before they settled in cities; and food and water in a barren place proved the laws came from God. He ends by admitting that the true causes “God alone knows.”

In Josephus the people keep themselves pure for three days, including abstaining from their wives, and on the third day a cloud spreads over the camp with lightning, thunder, wind, and heavy rain. The frightened people stay in their tents until Moses appears, cheerful, and the air clears.

The Mekhilta gives another reason for the desert: it belonged to no one, so no tribe could claim the Torah as its own and no nation could say it was never offered. It then tells how God offered the Torah to the descendants of Esau, of Ammon and Moab, and of Ishmael, who each refused a command that cut against their ways, before Israel accepted.

Rashi, following the Mekhilta, notes that “there Israel camped” (v. 2) uses a singular verb and reads it as one man with one heart, unlike the quarrelsome camps before. On v. 1, where the Hebrew says “this day” rather than “that day,” he says the Torah's words should feel as new as if they were given today.

Rabbi Avdimi read “at the nether part of the mount” (v. 17) as under the mountain: God held it over Israel like an upturned cask and said, accept the Torah or be buried here. A later sage objected that a covenant made under duress could be challenged, and Rava answered that Israel accepted it again willingly in the days of Esther (Esther 9:27). The same tractate says Moses added a day of preparation on his own, and God agreed.

Hebrews retells the scene from the people's side: a mountain burning with fire, blackness and tempest, a trumpet, and a voice so terrible that the hearers begged to hear no more. It quotes the rule that even a beast touching the mountain must die (v. 13). Christians, it says, have come instead to mount Sion, the heavenly Jerusalem, and to Jesus the mediator of the new covenant.

Peter applies v. 6 to Christian believers: “a chosen generation, a royal priesthood, an holy nation, a peculiar people.” Revelation likewise says Christ has made his people kings and priests unto God. Both take Israel's Sinai calling and extend it to the church.

Augustine counts fifty days from the Passover lamb to the giving of the law at Sinai, and fifty days from Christ's Passover to the coming of the Holy Spirit. The law was written by the finger of God (31:18), and Augustine, setting Luke 11:20 beside Matthew 12:28, identifies that finger with the Spirit, so Sinai and Pentecost answer each other. Jubilees' covenant feast in the third month (above) makes a similar link from the Jewish side.

20.overview:
God speaks the Ten Commandments to all Israel. He names himself as the God who brought them out of Egypt, then forbids other gods, graven images, and taking his name in vain; commands the Sabbath and honor for father and mother; and forbids killing, adultery, stealing, false witness, and coveting. The people, shaken by the thunder, lightning, trumpet, and smoke, stand far off and beg Moses to speak to them instead. Moses goes into the thick darkness where God is. The chapter closes with the first laws Moses is to pass on: no gods of silver or gold, and an altar of earth or unhewn stone, with no steps.

The commandments open with a statement, not a command: “I am the LORD thy God, which have brought thee out” (v. 2). What follows is asked of people God has already rescued.

historicalContext.label: Author
historicalContext.text: Not named in the text. God speaks the commandments (v. 1) and later writes them on tablets (31:18; 34:1). Tradition credits Moses with the book; many scholars see several sources combined.

historicalContext.label: Date written
historicalContext.text: Unknown. Tradition places it in Moses' lifetime (15th or 13th century BC); scholarly proposals reach the 6th–5th century BC.

historicalContext.label: Date of events
historicalContext.text: The third day of preparation at Sinai, in the third month after leaving Egypt (19:1, 16). Reckoning from 1 Kings 6:1 puts the Exodus about 1446 BC; many scholars prefer about 1250 BC.

historicalContext.label: Setting (events)
historicalContext.text: Mount Sinai: the people at the foot of the mountain, Moses entering the thick darkness (v. 21).

historicalContext.label: Parallel accounts
historicalContext.text: Deuteronomy 5:6–21, which grounds the Sabbath in the Exodus rather than creation and puts the wife before the house. Abinadi recites the commandments in Mosiah 12:34–36; 13:12–24.

20.hermeneutics:
Hittite treaties open by naming the great king and recalling what he had done for his vassal, and only then list the vassal's duties. The Decalogue opens the same way: a name and a rescue (v. 2), then the commands. The treaties also required a copy to be laid up in the temple of each party's god and read aloud at set times. Some scholars, following Meredith Kline, suggest the “two tables” (31:18) were two copies of one text, one for each party, both kept in the ark because God's sanctuary and Israel's were the same place.

Every major temple in the ancient Near East centered on a statue of its god. In Mesopotamia a newly made statue went through the “washing of the mouth” (*mis pi*) ritual, after which priests treated it as the god's living presence, feeding and clothing it daily. Verses 4–5 forbid any such image, and v. 23 repeats the ban for gods of silver and gold. Verse 22 gives the reason in a sentence: Israel has heard God talk from heaven and seen no form, as Deuteronomy 4:12 also says.

The laws of the ancient Near East were royal. The relief on Hammurabi's stele shows the king standing before the sun god Shamash, but the laws inscribed below it are Hammurabi's own, given in his name. In Exodus the lawgiver is God himself, speaking to the whole people in the second person singular, “thou.” Each Israelite is addressed directly, with no king in between.

breakdown.label: God speaks: the LORD who brought thee out of Egypt
No other gods; no graven images
The name of the LORD not taken in vain
The Sabbath, grounded in the six days of creation
Honour thy father and thy mother
No killing, adultery, stealing, false witness, or coveting
The people stand afar off; Moses enters the darkness
First laws: no gods of gold; altars of earth or stone

structure.summary: An inclusio: the storm on the mountain frames the Ten Commandments. The altar laws (vv. 22–26) open the next unit.

open.text: Thunders, lightnings, trumpet, smoke; the people tremble

close.text: Thunderings, lightnings, trumpet, smoke; the people stand afar off

rows.label: A
rows.text: I am the LORD thy God, who brought thee out

rows.label: B
rows.text: Toward God: no other gods, no images, the name

rows.label: C
rows.text: Sabbath and parents: the two positive commands

rows.label: D
rows.text: Toward the neighbour: five short prohibitions

notes: **God and neighbour:** “the LORD thy God” occurs 5 times, all in vv. 2–12; “thy neighbour” occurs 4 times, all in vv. 16–17. In Hebrew, vv. 13–15 are two words each.

**Counting to ten:** the chapter never numbers the commandments; “ten” comes from 34:28 and Deuteronomy 4:13. Jewish tradition counts v. 2 as the first and vv. 3–6 as the second; Philo, Josephus, and the Reformed churches count v. 3 first and v. 4 second; Catholics and Lutherans join vv. 3–6 and divide v. 17 in two.
**Verse numbers:** Jewish Bibles print vv. 13–16 as a single verse, so their 20:14 is the KJV's 20:17 and the chapter ends at 20:23.

The theophany that began at 19:1 ends at 20:21, when the people retreat and Moses alone goes into the darkness. At v. 22 the Book of the Covenant begins: laws given to Moses to pass on, running to 23:33, which Moses reads to the people and they accept in 24:7.

**Forward:** the commandments are written on tablets of stone (31:18), broken at the golden calf, and written again on new tablets (34:1, 28). Moses repeats them on the plains of Moab in Deuteronomy 5.

traditions.text: Abinadi, on trial before King Noah's priests, recites the commandments “which the Lord delivered unto Moses in the mount of Sinai.” He is interrupted after the command against images, withstands the guards with his face shining like Moses' on the mount, and then reads them the remainder, because, he says, they are not written in the priests' hearts. He goes on to teach that salvation does not come by the law alone but through the atonement God himself will make.

Early revelations restate the commandments for the Church. D&C 42 gives the commands against killing, stealing, lying, and adultery as the law of the Church, adding that whoever looks on a woman to lust after her shall deny the faith. D&C 59 sets them under love of God and neighbor, adds “nor do anything like unto it,” and applies the Sabbath command to the Lord's day.

Teaching at the temple in Bountiful, the risen Jesus quotes the commands against killing and adultery as words written by them of old time, then extends each one inward, to anger and to lustful looking. The Nephites hear the same deepening of the commandments that Matthew 5 records.

Philo divides the ten into two tables of five: duties toward God, ending with honor to parents, and duties toward people. He puts adultery before murder and calls adultery the greatest violation of the law. On v. 18, where the Hebrew says the people “saw” the voices, he explains that God's words are actions, seen by the eyes before they reach the ears.

Josephus says it is not lawful for Jews to set down the words of the commandments directly, so he gives only their sense. His summary makes the one God the first commandment and the ban on images the second, the same division Philo uses.

A single papyrus sheet from Egypt carries the Ten Commandments in Hebrew followed by the opening of the Shema, the same pairing the Temple service used (below). Its order puts adultery before murder, as Philo does and as Paul does in Romans 13:9. Until the Dead Sea Scrolls were found it was the oldest known manuscript of any part of the Hebrew Bible.

Why do the commandments open with “I am the LORD thy God” and not with a command? The Mekhilta answers with a parable: a king who comes to a province first builds its walls, brings in water, and fights its wars, and only then asks to rule. So God freed Israel, split the sea, sent manna and quail, and fought Amalek before announcing his laws.

The Mekhilta also lays the two tablets side by side, five against five. The opening “I am the LORD” stands opposite the ban on killing, because murder diminishes the image of the King. Other gods stand opposite adultery, and the Sabbath opposite false witness, since one who breaks the Sabbath testifies that God did not create the world in six days.

The Mishnah says the priests in the Temple recited the Ten Commandments each morning before the Shema. The Talmud explains why the practice was not kept elsewhere: it was stopped because of heretics who claimed that only these ten were given by God at Sinai. Rabbi Simlai counted 613 commandments in all and said Israel heard two of them, “I am” and “thou shalt have no other gods,” from God's own mouth.

Asked what good thing brings eternal life, Jesus lists the commands against murder, adultery, theft, and false witness, with honor to parents and love of neighbor. Paul lists adultery, killing, stealing, false witness, and coveting and says all are summed up in “Thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself.”

Irenaeus argues that the patriarchs had the meaning of the Decalogue written in their hearts before Sinai, and that Christ did not cancel it. It remains with Christians, receiving through his coming “extension and increase, but not abrogation.” What Christ ended, in his view, were laws given as a sign, such as circumcision and the Sabbath rules.

Augustine reports that Christians already divided the ten two ways: four toward God and six toward people, or three and seven. He prefers three and seven, joining other gods with images and splitting the last command into coveting a wife and coveting goods, partly because three hints at the Trinity. His Latin text of v. 17, like Deuteronomy 5:21, put the wife before the house.

21.overview:
Moses receives the first of the “judgments” he is to set before Israel. They open with the Hebrew servant, who goes free in the seventh year unless he chooses to stay and has his ear bored at the door, and with the daughter sold as a maidservant, who keeps her rights to food, clothing, and marriage. Then come crimes that carry death: murder, striking or cursing a parent, kidnapping. Cases of injury follow, including a pregnant woman hurt in a fight and the rule of “eye for eye.” The chapter ends with oxen that gore and pits left uncovered.

Most of these laws are written as cases: if a man does this, then that follows. The rule of “eye for eye,” later a byword for revenge, sits inside this case law as a measure for the courts, and the very next verses set free a slave who loses an eye or a tooth.

historicalContext.label: Author
historicalContext.text: Not named in the text. Exodus 24:4 says Moses wrote “all the words of the LORD”; tradition credits Moses. Many scholars count this law collection among the oldest parts of the Pentateuch.

historicalContext.label: Date written
historicalContext.text: Unknown. Tradition places it in Moses' lifetime (15th or 13th century BC); scholarly proposals range from early Israel to the 7th century BC or later.

historicalContext.label: Date of events
historicalContext.text: Israel reaches Sinai in the third month after leaving Egypt (19:1). 1 Kings 6:1 places the Exodus about 1446 BC; many scholars prefer the 13th century BC.

historicalContext.label: Setting (events)
historicalContext.text: Mount Sinai. The people stand far off while Moses draws near “unto the thick darkness where God was” (20:21) and receives these laws for them.

historicalContext.label: Parallel accounts
historicalContext.text: Deuteronomy 15:12–18 (servants); Leviticus 24:17–22 (eye for eye); Numbers 35:9–34 (refuge for the accidental killer, v. 13). 3 Nephi 12:38–39 quotes v. 24, and the Joseph Smith Translation revises vv. 20–21.

21.hermeneutics:
Israel's laws had older relatives in Mesopotamia, above all the Code of Hammurabi (Babylon, c. 1750 BC). Its §§196–201 also demand eye for eye and tooth for tooth, but only between equals. Blind a commoner and you pay a mina; blind a slave and you pay half his price to his owner. Exodus gives one rule for every free person (vv. 23–25), and then sends the injured slave himself out free for his eye or his tooth (vv. 26–27).

The goring ox was a stock case in that legal tradition. In the Laws of Eshnunna and in Hammurabi §§250–252, an owner who had been warned pays silver when his ox kills: half a mina for a free man in Hammurabi, a third of a mina for a slave. Eshnunna §53 also has two owners split the value of the live ox and the dead one, as v. 35 does. Exodus keeps the shape of these cases and changes the stakes. The ox is stoned and its meat may not be eaten, as if it were a murderer (compare Genesis 9:5), the careless owner may be put to death unless a ransom is set (vv. 29–30), and a slave's life is set at thirty shekels.

Hammurabi §117 lets a debtor hand over his wife or children to work off a debt for three years, with release in the fourth. Exodus sets six years of service and release in the seventh (v. 2), the same count of six and seven that governs Israel's Sabbath. What it adds is the servant who chooses to stay. The awl through his ear at the household door marks a lifelong bond he took on himself.

structure.summary: No strong pattern; the chapter moves in sequence, grouping its cases by subject.
notes: **Two kinds of law:** Most cases open with “if” and state a penalty. Verses 12–17 instead use a short, fixed formula, *mot yumat* (“he shall surely be put to death”), four times in six verses.
**Freedom at both ends:** The word for “free” occurs 4 times, all for slaves: at the opening servant law (vv. 2, 5) and again for the slave who loses an eye or a tooth (vv. 26–27).
**Repetition to watch:** “for” (*tachat*) comes 8 times in vv. 23–25, life for life through stripe for stripe. The Hebrew word for “ox” comes 14 times in vv. 28–36.

Chapters 21–23 hold the laws Moses later reads aloud from “the book of the covenant” (24:7), which gives the section its name. It runs from 20:22 to 23:33, opening with the altar law (20:22–26) and closing with the feasts and God's promises for the land (23:14–33). The heading in v. 1 starts the case law proper, and Jewish reading names the weekly portion 21:1–24:18 from it (*Mishpatim*, “judgments”).

**Later echoes:** Deuteronomy 15:12–18 restates the servant law and adds gifts at release. Jeremiah 34:8–17 condemns Jerusalem's nobles, who freed their Hebrew servants by covenant and then took them back.

traditions.text: At the temple in Bountiful the risen Jesus quotes v. 24, “an eye for an eye, and a tooth for a tooth,” and answers it with the command not to resist evil and to turn the other cheek. Just before, he tells the Nephites that the law has all been fulfilled in him. The words run parallel to the Sermon on the Mount (below).

Where the King James text says a master who beats his slave to death “shall be surely punished,” the Joseph Smith Translation speaks of being put to death in vv. 20–21. The change brings the slave's death under the same penalty v. 12 sets for killing any man.

Amulek, teaching the Zoramites, builds on the rule of v. 12. The law, which he calls just, “requireth the life of him who hath murdered,” and no man's blood can atone for another's sins. From there he argues that nothing short of an infinite atonement will suffice, turning life for life into an argument for Christ's sacrifice.

The Greek translation made in Alexandria reads vv. 22–23 its own way. If the child is born “imperfectly formed,” the man who struck the mother pays a fine; if it is “perfectly formed,” he gives life for life. The Hebrew leaves open whose harm is meant, and the Greek decides it for the unborn child. Philo builds on this reading.

Following the Greek text, Philo says a child still unshaped in the womb is not yet a man, so causing its loss brings a fine. A child already formed in every part is a human being, killed while still “in the workshop of nature,” and the striker must die. He moves straight on to condemn the exposure of infants, which he calls common among other nations.

In his summary of the law of Moses, Josephus lets the servant who chooses to stay serve only until the Jubilee, the fiftieth year, when he leaves with his wife and children (compare Leviticus 25:40–41). He reads “eye for eye” as written, then adds that the injured man may take money instead, since the law makes the sufferer judge of the value. The rabbis go further.

The Talmud denies that “an eye for an eye” ever meant maiming. A teaching reads the verse with the law for killing an animal, where the penalty is payment (Leviticus 24:18–19), and concludes that injuring a person is paid in money too. Numbers 35:31 forbids taking ransom only for a murderer's life, which implies that payment is allowed for lesser injuries.

Rabban Yohanan ben Zakkai asks why the ear is the part that is bored. That ear heard God say at Sinai that Israel are his servants (Leviticus 25:55), yet its owner went and took a human master. Another sage explains the door and doorpost: they were witnesses in Egypt when God passed over the doorposts and brought Israel from slavery to freedom.

The great French commentator notes that the chapter begins “and these,” which ties the judgments to what came before: these too were given at Sinai. They follow the altar law of 20:24–26, he says, to teach that the high court should sit beside the sanctuary. “Set before them” means like a table fully laid, so Moses must explain the reasons and not only drill the words.

Jesus quotes v. 24 and answers it with turning the other cheek, giving up the cloak, and going the second mile. Later readers like Marcion and the Manichees took the passage as proof that the Old Testament law and its God were harsh. Tertullian and Augustine wrote to answer them (below), and 3 Nephi 12 gives the same sermon to the Nephites.

Against Marcion, Tertullian argues that the law of retaliation gave no license to injure. It was a check on violence for a hard people who could not yet wait for God's own vengeance; fear of suffering the same harm at once would stop the first blow. Allowing the return blow, he says, was in effect a ban on starting one.

Faustus the Manichee said Christ destroyed this law. Augustine answers that revenge tends to exceed the injury, and the law capped it, so the rule was “a covering to prevent the fire already kindled from spreading.” Christ's command not to retaliate at all fulfills the same aim; whoever forgives gives up what he could justly claim.

22.overview:
The laws turn from injury to property. A thief who kills or sells a stolen ox repays five oxen; a burglar killed in the dark brings no blood guilt; crops eaten by a neighbor's animals or burned by his fire are made good; goods and animals left in someone's keeping are settled by oath or evidence before the judges. A man who seduces an unbetrothed girl must marry her or pay the bride-price. Then the style changes to short commands: no witch may live, no one may lie with a beast or sacrifice to another god. The stranger, the widow, the orphan, and the poor borrower are protected, and the chapter closes with firstfruits, firstborn, and holiness.

Watch who enforces the law. Theft and damage go before the judges, but for the widow and the orphan God himself promises to hear their cry, and his sentence falls on the oppressors' own wives and children (v. 24).

22.hermeneutics:
Theft was punished hard in Mesopotamia. Hammurabi §8 makes a man who steals an animal repay thirty times over if it belonged to a god or the palace and ten times if it belonged to a commoner, and puts him to death if he cannot pay. §21 executes a man who breaks through a house wall and buries him in front of the hole. Exodus asks five oxen for an ox and four sheep for a sheep (v. 1), double when the animal is found alive (v. 4), and sells the thief who has nothing (v. 3). A burglar killed in the dark brings no blood guilt, but once the sun is up the householder may not kill him (vv. 2–3). No theft of goods costs a life here.

Old Babylonian law settled losses no one saw with an oath before the god. Hammurabi §266 has a herdsman whose animal is killed in the fold by a lion clear himself before god, and the owner bears the loss; §§120 and 126 use the same oath for stored goods. Exodus fills the same gap with the *elohim* (KJV “judges”) and “an oath of the LORD” (vv. 8–11), and lets a shepherd bring the torn carcass as evidence (v. 13). Amos 3:12 pictures the scene: a shepherd pulling two legs or a piece of an ear from a lion's mouth.

A potsherd letter from Mesad Hashavyahu, a small fort near Yavneh-Yam on the coast (late 7th century BC), records a field hand's appeal to an official. An overseer had taken his garment over a dispute about his quota of grain, and he asks to have it back. It is the kind of seizure vv. 26–27 limit: a cloak held in pledge goes back by sundown, because it is the poor man's only covering for the night.

structure.summary: No strong pattern; the chapter moves in sequence, from case law on property to direct commands.
notes: **Making good:** The Hebrew verb for “make restitution” or “make good” (*shalem*) comes 15 times in vv. 1–15, and “double” 3 times (vv. 4, 7, 9).
**A change of voice:** From v. 18 the “if” cases give way to commands, and in vv. 21–27 God speaks in the first person. Words for crying out and for hearing come 3 times each, in vv. 23 and 27.
**One Hebrew word:** Hebrew *elohim* stands behind “judges” in vv. 8–9 (three times), “god” in v. 20, and “gods” in v. 28.

The middle of the Book of the Covenant (20:22–23:33). The case laws on property end at v. 17; from v. 18 the commands mix worship with care for the weak, and that mix runs on through 23:19. The law protecting the stranger, grounded in Israel's own years in Egypt, appears here (v. 21) and again at 23:9.

**Later echoes:** Deuteronomy 24:10–13 restates the pledge law, adding that the lender may not enter the borrower's house to take it. Ezekiel 18:7–8 lists restoring the pledge and refusing interest among the marks of a righteous man.

traditions.text: The JST changes two verses. Verse 18 reads “Thou shalt not suffer a murderer to live” in place of “a witch,” and the footnote at v. 28 gives “against God” where the King James text has “the gods.” Both readings had ancient company: the Greek translators and Josephus took v. 18 as a law against deadly sorcery or poison (below).

Under the Nephite judges, robbing and stealing were punished like murder and adultery, but there was no law against a man's belief. Mormon gives this as the reason the unbeliever Korihor could not be punished for what he taught. The passage separates robbing from stealing, a distinction the Talmud also draws (Bava Kamma 79b, below).

The Greek translators rendered the “witch” of v. 18 as “sorcerers,” using a word related to drugs. Josephus goes further and makes it a ban on keeping deadly poison: whoever is caught with it dies and suffers what he meant for others. Both point to harm done to people, as the JST's “murderer” does.

Josephus sets the penalty for stolen cattle at fourfold, fivefold for an ox, and double for gold or silver. A thief who cannot pay becomes the servant of the man he wronged, and a householder who kills a thief is guiltless “although the man were only breaking in at the wall.” Josephus does not mention the night-and-day distinction of vv. 2–3.

Philo explains the five-and-four ratio of v. 1 by what each animal gives. A sheep yields four things a year: milk, cheese, fleece, and a lamb. An ox yields five, adding plowing and threshing, so the thief repays one animal for each kind of use he stole.

The Talmud gives two other reasons for the ratio. Rabbi Meir says the ox was taken from its work, and labor is precious. Rabban Yohanan ben Zakkai says the thief walked the ox away but had to carry the sheep on his shoulder, and that shame reduces his penalty. Yohanan also explains why a sneak thief pays double and a robber does not: the thief feared people more than God.

The Mishnah's tractate on damages opens by naming four primary causes of harm: the ox, the pit, the grazing animal (or, by another view, a person), and fire. All four come from Exodus 21:28–22:6. Each has its own rules, the Mishnah says, and none can be derived from another. The rest of the tractate works out how far each owner is liable, so the rabbinic law of damages grows out of these verses.

Both read “thou shalt not revile the gods” (v. 28) as respect for other peoples' gods. Josephus forbids blaspheming the gods other cities honor and robbing foreign temples. Philo says Israel must not insult what converts once worshiped, lest the converts answer by speaking against the true God.

Rabbi Eliezer the Great observes that the Torah warns against wronging the stranger in thirty-six places, some say forty-six. The Talmud counts “vex” and “oppress” in v. 21 as two separate wrongs, hurtful words and oppression, and adds the ban on acting as a creditor (v. 25) as a third.

When Jesus stays at his house, the tax collector Zacchaeus promises half his goods to the poor and to restore fourfold anything he has taken by false accusation. Fourfold is the rate v. 1 sets for a stolen sheep, the penalty for a convicted thief, which Zacchaeus takes on himself without being tried. Jesus answers that salvation has come to the house that day.

Struck on the high priest's order, Paul calls him a “whited wall.” Told whom he has insulted, he quotes the second half of v. 28, “Thou shalt not speak evil of the ruler of thy people,” and says he did not know the man was high priest.

This church order applies “thou shalt not speak evil of the gods” to the bishop, whom it calls the people's earthly god after God, citing Psalm 82:6, “Ye are gods.” Where Josephus and Philo took the gods of v. 28 to be foreign deities, this reading takes them to be human authorities.

Answering Greek critics of Moses, Clement collects the humane laws. The ban on interest covers any brother of the same faith, he says, and God takes as his own interest mildness and generosity. The rule that a firstborn animal stays seven days with its mother (v. 30) trains people in gentleness through the way they treat beasts.

23.overview:
The laws turn to honest courts and to Israel's sacred calendar. No false report, no siding with a crowd, no bribe; bring back an enemy's straying ox, and help his ass up from under its load. The land rests every seventh year so the poor can eat, and people and animals rest every seventh day. Three times a year every male is to appear before the Lord, at the feasts of unleavened bread, harvest, and ingathering. God then promises an angel to lead Israel, blessing on bread and water, and the gradual driving out of the land's peoples, and forbids any covenant with them or their gods.

The stranger law of 22:21 comes back at v. 9 with a new reason: “ye know the heart of a stranger.” Israel's own memory of Egypt is to shape how it treats outsiders, in court and on the Sabbath alike (v. 12).

23.hermeneutics:
A small limestone tablet from Gezer, usually dated to the 10th century BC, lists the farming year in Canaan by its work: months of ingathering, of sowing and late sowing, of barley harvest and general harvest, of pruning vines, and of summer fruit. It begins with ingathering, the same point Exodus calls “the end of the year” (v. 16). Israel's three feasts sit on that farmer's calendar: unleavened bread in Abib, as the barley ripened; the feast of harvest, when grain was cut; and ingathering in the autumn, when the fruit and vintage were in. Worship followed the work of the fields.

Hammurabi's laws are framed by a prologue and an epilogue. The epilogue promises that Shamash will lengthen the reign of any later king who keeps the laws, and calls down curses from the great gods, one by one, on any who changes them. The Book of the Covenant closes in the same way, with what follows obedience: an angel to lead, bread and water blessed, sickness taken away, no miscarriage or barrenness, enemies driven out (vv. 20–31). A first hearer would recognize a law collection that ends by naming its blessings.

Hammurabi's collection also opens with the courts. Its first laws put to death a man who brings a capital charge he cannot prove (§§1, 3), and a judge who reverses his own sealed verdict pays twelve times the claim and loses his seat for good (§5). Exodus 23:1–8 covers the same ground from the side of the witness and the judge: no false report, no going along with the majority to twist a verdict, no gift that “blindeth the wise.”

notes: **Sixes and sevens:** Six years of sowing and a seventh of rest, then six days of work and a seventh day of rest (vv. 10–12). The Book of the Covenant opened with the same count, the servant's six years (21:2).
**The stranger:** The Hebrew word *ger* comes three times in v. 9 and again in v. 12, where the stranger shares the Sabbath rest.
**God sends:** The verb “send” comes three times in God's mouth: an angel (v. 20), “my fear” (v. 27), and hornets (v. 28). “Drive out” follows 4 times in vv. 28–31.

The last part of the Book of the Covenant (20:22–23:33). The laws end with Israel's sacred calendar (vv. 10–19) and an epilogue of promise and warning (vv. 20–33). In the next chapter Moses reads the book aloud and the people agree to it (24:3–7).

**Repeated later:** The feast laws of vv. 15–19, the kid in its mother's milk included, return almost word for word when the covenant is renewed after the golden calf (34:18–26). Deuteronomy 16:16 restates the three yearly appearances and names them unleavened bread, weeks, and tabernacles.

traditions.text: Where the King James text says “neither shalt thou countenance a poor man in his cause,” the Joseph Smith Translation reads “a wicked man.” The Church's footnote also points to D&C 56:17–18, which rebukes poor men whose hearts are not broken and blesses the poor who are pure in heart. Leviticus 19:15 sets the general rule: judgment favors neither the poor nor the mighty.

As the Saints prepare to march to Missouri, the Lord promises to raise up a man to lead them “like as Moses led the children of Israel.” He contrasts them with their fathers, to whom he said that his angel would go before them but not his presence; this time angels and his presence both will go. The revelation joins the angel promised in vv. 20–23 to its later limit in 33:2–3.

This Greek book from Alexandria takes up the hornets of v. 28 and the slow conquest of vv. 29–30. God sent “wasps, forerunners of thine host,” and destroyed the Canaanites gradually though he could have done it in one stroke, to give them room to repent. Exodus gives a practical reason for the delay, the land going wild; Wisdom gives a moral one.

Philo reads the kid law of v. 19 as a lesson in compassion. It is monstrous, he says, for the milk that fed the living young to become the seasoning of its dead body. Yet he finds no fault in cooking meat with milk in general, since milk is plentiful; only the mother's own milk is barred. The rabbis drew the line far wider (below).

Josephus makes the three yearly appearances of v. 17 a journey from every corner of the land to the temple city, to thank God for past gifts and ask for future ones. He adds a social purpose: people of one stock and one law should meet and feast together, or they will become strangers to one another.

The kid law appears three times (here, 34:26, and Deuteronomy 14:21), and the school of Rabbi Ishmael takes each as a separate ban: on eating meat cooked in milk, on profiting from it, and on cooking it. The Mishnah extends the rule from a mother's milk to the meat and milk of any clean domestic animal. The Jewish separation of meat and dairy grows from this verse.

In the dispute over the oven of Akhnai, Rabbi Eliezer calls on a carob tree, a stream, and at last a voice from heaven to prove his ruling. Rabbi Yehoshua answers that the Torah “is not in heaven” (Deuteronomy 30:12), and Rabbi Yirmeya explains that Sinai already gave the rule to incline after the majority. The rabbis read v. 2, a warning against following a crowd to do evil, as the basis for deciding by majority vote.

In his Guide for the Perplexed, Maimonides calls meat boiled in milk heavy food, but suspects another reason: it was probably part of some pagan rite or festival. He notes that the ban comes twice right after the command to appear before God at the feasts, as if to say not to cook as the heathen did. He admits that the books of pagan rites he had read never mention the custom.

Mark opens his Gospel with “Behold, I send my messenger before thy face,” crediting “the prophets.” In Greek these words match the Septuagint of v. 20, where God sends his angel before Israel's face; the rest of the line comes from Malachi 3:1. John the Baptist now stands where the angel stood, preparing the way.

Justin argues to Trypho that the angel of v. 20, of whom God says “my name is in him,” bore the name Jesus. The man who actually led Israel into the land was Oshea, renamed Joshua, whose name in Greek is Jesus (Numbers 13:16). So the name placed in the angel, Justin says, was the name of the one who would bring the people in.

Clement counts the command to help an enemy's ass up from under its burden (v. 5) among the law's lessons in kindness. It teaches, he says, not to rejoice at a neighbor's troubles or gloat over enemies, and it prepares those trained by it to pray for their enemies, as Christ taught.

The Roman historian, in a hostile sketch of Jewish origins, says the Jews first rested on the seventh day because it ended their toils, and later, led on “by the charms of indolence,” gave the seventh year to idleness as well. He records both rest laws of vv. 10–12 from the outside, and reads them as laziness.

24.overview:
God calls Moses, Aaron, Nadab, Abihu, and seventy elders to come up and worship from a distance. Moses tells the people all the words and judgments, and they answer with one voice that they will do them. He writes the words down, builds an altar with twelve pillars for the tribes, and reads the book of the covenant aloud; the people promise again, and he sprinkles half the blood on the altar and half on them. The leaders then go up, see the God of Israel above a pavement like sapphire, and eat and drink. Moses climbs higher, enters the cloud, and stays forty days and nights.

The covenant is sealed twice: by blood shared between altar and people, and by a meal in God's presence. Later Moses is told that no man can see God's face and live (33:20). Here the leaders see him, and v. 11 stresses that he “laid not his hand” on them.

historicalContext.text: Not named in the text. Verse 4 says Moses “wrote all the words of the LORD,” and tradition credits him with the book.

historicalContext.label: Date written

historicalContext.label: Date of events
historicalContext.text: Soon after the law is given at Sinai, in or after the third month of the Exodus year (19:1); 1 Kings 6:1 places the Exodus about 1446 BC, many scholars in the 13th century BC.

historicalContext.label: Setting (events)
historicalContext.text: An altar “under the hill” at the foot of Sinai (v. 4), then the mountain itself, covered by cloud and glory.

historicalContext.label: Parallel accounts

24.hermeneutics:
Hittite treaties of the 14th–13th centuries BC were written on tablets, placed before the gods, and read aloud to the subject people at set times. The treaty of Suppiluliuma with Shattiwaza of Mitanni, for example, lays a copy before the storm god Teshub and orders it read before the king and his people. Exodus 24 has the same pieces: the words are written (v. 4), read to the people (v. 7), and accepted by a sworn answer (vv. 3, 7). Scholars such as George Mendenhall have compared the Sinai covenant to these treaties; the likeness is one of form, with God as the great king and Israel as the people bound to him.

Treaties were also sealed with slaughtered animals that stood for the fate of a traitor. An Aramaic treaty from Sefire (8th century BC) says that as a calf is cut in two, so may the vassal Mati'el and his nobles be cut, and Jeremiah 34:18 knows the same rite of cutting a calf and passing between the pieces. Exodus 24 divides the blood instead, half on the altar and half on the people (vv. 6, 8). The one blood marks both parties to the covenant.

Mesopotamian scholars pictured heaven in floors of precious stone. A text known as KAR 307 makes the middle heaven of a blue stone and seats the god Bel on a throne in a sanctuary of lapis lazuli. The “sapphire” of v. 10 is most likely lapis lazuli, the deep blue stone of royal and divine décor. When the elders look up and see under God's feet a pavement like it, “as it were the body of heaven in his clearness,” they are seeing the floor of heaven from below.

notes: **Promise, then blood, twice:** Each answer of the people (vv. 3, 7) is followed by blood, first on the altar (v. 6), then on the people (v. 8). “Blood” comes 4 times in vv. 6–8, and “words” 4 times in vv. 3–8.
**Going up:** The verb “go up” (*alah*) occurs 8 times, counting the burnt offerings “offered” in v. 5. Each ascent takes fewer people higher, until Moses alone enters the cloud (v. 18).
**Six days and the seventh:** The cloud covers the mountain six days, and God calls Moses on the seventh (v. 16), the rhythm of the creation week.

This chapter closes the Sinai covenant section (19:1–24:18). Verses 1–11 seal the covenant offered in ch. 19 and spelled out in 20:1–23:33; vv. 12–18 open the next stage, as Moses goes up to receive the tablets and, in chs. 25–31, the plans for the tabernacle. The tablets come only at the end of those plans (31:18).

**Looking ahead:** While Moses is on the mountain for these forty days, the people make the golden calf (32:1), breaking the covenant they have just sworn twice to keep. Nadab and Abihu, who see God here, later die offering “strange fire” (Leviticus 10:1–2).

traditions.text: The revelation on priesthood says Moses taught Israel plainly and sought to sanctify them “that they might behold the face of God.” They hardened their hearts and could not endure his presence, so the Lord took Moses and the holy priesthood from among them. In Exodus 24 only Moses and a few leaders go up and see God; D&C 84 gives the reason the rest did not.

King Benjamin's people answer him with one voice that they are willing to enter a covenant to do God's will and obey him in all things, much as Israel answers in vv. 3 and 7. Benjamin then records the names of all who entered the covenant, and not one soul old enough held back. Like Moses, he binds a whole people to God at a single assembly.

The Greek translators soften v. 10: the elders “saw the place where the God of Israel stood.” In v. 11 none of the chosen ones was missing, and they were seen in God's place and ate and drank. Seeing God becomes seeing the place where he stood, a caution the Aramaic Targum shares (next entry).

The Aramaic translation read in synagogues says the elders saw “the glory of the God of Israel,” and that his feet rest on the throne of his glory. Verse 11 becomes a statement about worship: they rejoiced over their offerings, which were accepted as if they had eaten and drunk.

Following the midrash, Rashi says the leaders stared too boldly and deserved death, but God would not spoil the joy of the giving of the Torah; Nadab and Abihu died later, at the tabernacle's dedication. The sapphire brickwork, he adds, had been before God through the years of slavery as a reminder of Israel's bricks. He also dates vv. 1–11 before the Ten Commandments, on the fourth and fifth of Sivan.
traditions.cite: Rashi on Exodus 24:1, 4, 10–11 (citing Tanchuma and Shabbat 88a)

traditions.text: The early midrash on Exodus asks what “the book of the covenant” (v. 7) held. Its answer: the Torah from Genesis up to the giving of the law at Sinai, together with the commands given at Marah (15:25). On that reading the people promise obedience after hearing their own history read back to them.

In Hebrew the people's answer in v. 7 runs “we will do, and we will hear.” Rabbi Simai teaches that because Israel put doing before hearing, 600,000 ministering angels came and tied two crowns on each Israelite, one for each word. When the people made the golden calf, angels of destruction came down and took the crowns away.

Jubilees opens with the scene of vv. 12–18 and dates it: the sixteenth day of the third month in the first year of the Exodus. God calls Moses up to receive the stone tablets, the glory rests on Sinai, the cloud covers it six days, and on the seventh God calls from the cloud. During the forty days God shows Moses the history before and after, which Jubilees presents as its own contents.

Josephus fills the forty days of v. 18 with the people's fear. Some said Moses had fallen among wild beasts, others that he had gone to God, and the camp did not move because he had told them to stay. When he came down he had eaten nothing, and he brought the plan for a tabernacle where God would come down among them.

Hebrews retells the rite with details Exodus lacks: the blood of calves and of goats, mixed with water, scarlet wool, and hyssop, sprinkled on the book as well as the people. It quotes v. 8 as “This is the blood of the testament” and concludes that without shedding of blood there is no remission, pointing to Christ's blood as the seal of a better covenant.

At the Last Supper Jesus gives the cup with words that echo v. 8: “my blood of the new testament” in Matthew and Mark, and the same phrase reversed in Luke and Paul. Moses sprinkled the blood on the people; Jesus has the disciples drink from the cup.

Barnabas says Moses fasted on Sinai forty days and forty nights to receive the covenant for the people, but they were not found worthy and lost it when they turned to idols. The covenant passed instead to Christians, sealed in their hearts through Jesus. D&C 84 also has Israel lose the higher blessing at Sinai, though it speaks of priesthood rather than a transfer to another people.

25.overview:
On the mountain God asks Moses to collect a freewill offering: gold, silver, and brass, dyed yarn and fine linen, goats' hair and skins, acacia wood, oil, spices, and precious stones. With it Israel is to make him a sanctuary “that I may dwell among them,” built after the pattern he will show Moses. The instructions begin with the ark, a gold-covered chest carried on poles that holds the testimony. Its lid, the mercy seat, is pure gold, with two gold cherubim facing each other above it. Then come the table for the shewbread and a golden lampstand with seven lamps.

The plans start from the inside. Before any tent, curtain, or court is described, God speaks of the ark in the holiest place and names it as the spot where he will meet Moses and speak with him, “from between the two cherubims” (v. 22).

25.hermeneutics:
Egyptians carried what was holy on poles. Tutankhamun's tomb (c. 1325 BC) held a gilded wooden chest topped by a figure of Anubis, mounted on a sledge with carrying poles, and temple reliefs show priests bearing a god's shrine on their shoulders in procession. The ark belongs to that world: a gold-covered box with rings and poles, made to be carried, and its poles are never to be removed (v. 15). Israel's God would travel with his people rather than stay in one temple.

Winged guardians flanked thrones across the Levant. The stone coffin of Ahiram, king of Byblos (c. 1000 BC), shows the king seated on a throne carved with winged sphinxes. Cherubim with outstretched wings over the ark (v. 20) would have read as a throne, with the ark beneath as its footstool. Later scripture says just that: God “dwelleth between the cherubims” (1 Samuel 4:4), and David calls the ark “the footstool of our God” (1 Chronicles 28:2). There is no image on the throne. The space between the cherubim is where God's voice will come from (v. 22).

Hittite treaties were deposited in temples, before the gods who witnessed them. The ark has the same job. It is first of all a container for “the testimony” (vv. 16, 21), the stone tablets of the covenant just sealed in ch. 24, kept at the feet of the God who made it. 1 Kings 8:9 reports that when the ark entered Solomon's temple it held nothing but the two tablets.

structure.summary: Inclusio: “pattern” at v. 9 and again at v. 40 frames the first three furnishings. Verses 1–8 introduce the offering and its purpose.

open.text: After the pattern … even so shall ye make it

close.text: Make them after their pattern, shewed thee in the mount

notes: **The frame:** The Hebrew *tabnit* (“pattern”) occurs 3 times, twice in v. 9 and once in v. 40, and nowhere between. Everything inside is made to match something Moses was shown.
**Sevens:** “Cherub” occurs 7 times (vv. 18–22), “mercy seat” 7 times (vv. 17–22), and “candlestick” 7 times (vv. 31–35), a lampstand that itself carries seven lamps (v. 37).
**Gold:** The word for gold comes 17 times, and “pure gold” 8 times. Every object inside the frame is gold or covered with it.

Chapters 25–31 give the plans for the tabernacle and its priests in seven speeches, each opening with the LORD speaking to Moses (25:1; 30:11, 17, 22, 34; 31:1, 12). The seventh is about the Sabbath, as the seventh day of creation was. Chapters 35–40 then report the building, often word for word, with the golden calf in between.

**Back and ahead:** In ch. 24 a few leaders saw God on the mountain; here he asks for a dwelling among the whole people (v. 8). When Solomon's temple is finished, the ark and its poles are carried into the holiest place under the cherubim's wings (1 Kings 8:6–8).

traditions.text: Commanding the Nauvoo Temple, the Lord says he had Moses build a tabernacle to carry in the wilderness, and a house in the land of promise, so that ordinances hidden from before the world was might be revealed. He then lists the ordinances of his house, from washings and anointings to baptisms for the dead. The portable tent becomes the first in a line of sacred buildings that runs to latter-day temples.

Like Moses, the Saints in Kirtland were told to build “according to the pattern which I have given unto you.” The plan of the House of the Lord was to be shown to three men the Church would appoint, and its inner court divided into a lower and a higher part. A house in Zion was likewise to follow the pattern given.

Verse 7 asks for stones to be set in the ephod and the breastplate, and Exodus 28:30 places the Urim and Thummim in the high priest's breastplate. Moroni told Joseph Smith of two stones in silver bows, fastened to a breastplate and deposited with the plates, which constituted the Urim and Thummim. The breastplate of Exodus reappears in the Restoration as part of the means of translation.

Solomon prays that God commanded him to build a temple on the holy mountain as a copy of “the holy tabernacle, which thou hast prepared” from the beginning. The pattern of vv. 9 and 40 becomes a heavenly tabernacle that existed before the earthly one. Hebrews develops the same idea (below).

On the mountain, Philo says, Moses contemplated “the incorporeal patterns” of what was to be made, and built copies the senses could perceive. Some read the cherubim as the two hemispheres of heaven; Philo prefers God's two highest powers, the creative and the kingly. The seven lamps of the lampstand stand for the seven planets, with the sun in the middle like the central shaft.

Josephus says the cherubim were flying creatures unlike any that men have seen, though Moses said he had seen such beings near God's throne. He reads the whole tabernacle as a model of the universe: two parts open to the priests like land and sea, the third reserved for God like heaven. The twelve loaves stand for the months, and the seven lamps for the planets.

Rabbi Yosei son of Rabbi Yehuda teaches that an ark of fire, a table of fire, and a lampstand of fire came down from heaven, and Moses made the vessels in their likeness, as v. 40 says. The school of Rabbi Ishmael lists the lampstand among three things too hard for Moses to grasp, until God pointed them out to him with his finger.

The ark is gold “within and without” (v. 11), and Rava draws the lesson: a scholar whose inside does not match his outside is no scholar. Rabbi Yohanan reads the gold crowns on the ark, the table, and the altar as the crowns of Torah, kingship, and priesthood. The priesthood went to Aaron and the kingship to David, but the crown of Torah still waits for anyone who will take it.

Hebrews quotes v. 40 and calls the earthly priests' service “the example and shadow of heavenly things.” It then lists the furniture: the lampstand, the table and shewbread, and the ark with the cherubim over the mercy seat. It adds that the ark held the pot of manna and Aaron's rod along with the tablets, details from elsewhere in the Torah.

In his defense before the council, Stephen recalls that the fathers had “the tabernacle of witness” in the wilderness, made after the fashion Moses had seen. He sets that portable tent against the later temple, and reminds his hearers that the Most High does not dwell in temples made with hands.

Against Gnostic teachers who built endless chains of higher worlds, Irenaeus says Israel received its offerings and sacrifices “in a figure, as was shown to Moses in the mount,” from the one God the church now worships. Earthly things can be types of heavenly ones, he argues, but there is no further world above heaven for which heaven itself is a type.

Clement follows Philo closely. The lampstand south of the altar of incense shows the seven planets, with the sun in the middle, and the cherubim may stand for the two hemispheres. He adds Christian readings: the golden lamp is a symbol of Christ, who gives light to believers, and the loaves on the table signify churches joined into one body.

26.overview:
God gives Moses the plans for the tent itself. Ten linen curtains, woven in blue, purple, and scarlet with cherubim, are joined into one inner covering. Over them go eleven curtains of goats' hair, then rams' skins dyed red and an outer layer of skins. Gold-covered frames of acacia wood stand in silver sockets to make the walls, locked together by bars. Inside, a veil hangs on four pillars, and an embroidered screen closes the door.

The veil is the new thing. Until v. 33 the dwelling is a single space; the veil makes it two, “the holy place and the most holy.” The ark goes behind it, alone. The table and lampstand stay outside it. From here on, everything in the tabernacle is ranked by how close it stands to that inner room.

26.hermeneutics:
Egypt built portable shrines the same way. The canopy of Queen Hetepheres I (about 2600 BC, found at Giza in 1925) is a wooden frame sheathed in gold, its posts fitted with tenons into sockets so it could be taken apart and set up again, with curtains hung from it. Tutankhamun's burial chamber (about 1325 BC) held gilded wooden shrines nested one inside another, with a linen pall stretched over a wooden frame. Exodus 26 uses that technology on a larger scale: gold-covered boards, two tenons each into silver sockets, bars, and layered curtains. A first hearer would picture a royal pavilion built to travel, not a house.

Winged guardians flanked thrones and doorways across the region. An ivory from Megiddo (about 1200 BC) shows a ruler seated on a throne whose sides are winged sphinxes, and the sarcophagus of Ahiram of Byblos shows the same kind of throne. Weaving cherubim into the inner curtains and the veil (vv. 1, 31) makes the inner room read as a guarded throne room, with the ark beneath the cherubim as its seat.

Blue and purple dyes came from murex sea snails along the Phoenician coast, and a great many snails yielded very little dye. That is why purple marked kings across the Mediterranean world. Scarlet came from a scale insect. The inner curtains, the veil, and the door screen all carry these colors (vv. 1, 31, 36). In a camp of people just out of brickmaking, God's dwelling wears royal cloth.
