structure.summary: No strong pattern; the chapter moves in sequence, from the innermost layer outward.
notes: **One dwelling:** the loops and clasps exist to make many pieces “one tabernacle” (v. 6) and a tent “that it may be one” (v. 11). The Hebrew word for curtain comes 24 times in vv. 1–13.

**Metals step down outward:** gold appears 8 times, on the inner clasps, frames, bars, and pillars. Silver (4 times) is used only for sockets. Bronze (KJV “brass,” 2 times) is kept for the clasps of the outer goats' hair tent (v. 11) and the sockets at the door (v. 37).
**Cloth follows the same order:** the cherub-woven linen is innermost and seen only from inside; plain goats' hair and skins face the weather.

Exodus 25:1–31:18 is one long speech given on Sinai, and 35:1–40:38 tells how each item was made, often in the same words; this chapter returns as 36:8–38. Between the plan and the building stands the golden calf (chs. 32–34). Ch. 25 described the furniture; ch. 26 builds the house around it.

**Cherubim at the threshold:** the cherubim woven into the veil echo the cherubim placed at the east of Eden “to keep the way of the tree of life” (Genesis 3:24). Solomon's temple carries them on into stone, carved on every wall (1 Kings 6:29).

traditions.text: Commanding a temple in Nauvoo, the Lord explains why Moses was told to build a tabernacle that Israel could carry in the wilderness, and later a house in the land of promise. It was so that ordinances “which had been hid from before the world was” might be revealed. The portable tent of ch. 26 thus stands at the head of a line of sacred houses that runs to latter-day temples.

Like Moses, Joseph Smith received a sacred building's plans by revelation. The Kirtland temple was to be built “after the manner which I shall show unto three of you,” with set dimensions and an inner court divided into a lower and a higher part. Verse 30 has the same idea: the builder follows a design already shown, not his own.

Solomon, praying for wisdom, calls the temple he was commanded to build “a resemblance of the holy tabernacle” which God had prepared from the beginning. The writer takes the pattern shown to Moses (v. 30) as a heavenly original older than the earthly tent, the reading Hebrews 8:5 also gives.

Josephus says the tabernacle imitates the universe: the two parts open to the priests stand for land and sea, and the inner room for heaven, which men cannot enter. The veil's four materials are the four elements, with linen for earth, purple (dyed from a sea creature) for water, blue for air, and scarlet for fire. Oddly, he describes the veil as embroidered with flowers “excepting the forms of animals,” though v. 31 calls for cherubim.

Philo gives the same four-element reading of the curtains and veil that Josephus gives: flax grows from the earth, purple comes from the water, blue is like the air, and scarlet is like fire. Moses chose exactly four materials, he says, because the world is made of four elements. Two Jewish writers of the same century arrive at one symbolic key for this chapter.

Rabbi Jacob son of Issi says the tabernacle is equal to the creation of the world and matches it day by day. On the first day God stretched out the heavens “like a curtain” (Psalm 104:2), and Moses makes curtains (v. 7). On the second day a firmament divides the waters, and here the veil “shall divide” (v. 33).

The rabbis could not identify the *tachash* whose skins make the top covering (v. 14; KJV “badgers”). Rabbi Nehemiah likens it to a many-colored animal, and Rav Yosef notes that the Aramaic translation's word for it means it delighted in its colors. Rabbi Meir says it was a creature of its own kind, with one horn on its forehead, that appeared for Moses while the tabernacle was built and was not seen again.

Rashi asks why v. 15 says “the boards,” with the article, as if they already existed. He answers from midrash: Jacob planted acacia trees in Egypt and told his sons to take them when they left, since God would one day command a sanctuary of acacia wood in the wilderness.

This Aramaic paraphrase gives the middle bar of v. 28 a history. It comes from the tree Abraham planted at Beersheba, which angels cut down and set floating on the sea for Israel to find after the crossing. Seventy cubits long, it wound around the frames like a serpent when the tent went up and straightened like a rod when it came down. Like Rashi's acacias, it ties the tent's wood to the patriarchs.

Hebrews describes the two rooms of this chapter, the first with the lampstand and table and the second behind the veil, entered by the high priest alone once a year. While that first room stood, it says, the way into the holiest was not yet open. Believers now enter “through the veil, that is to say, his flesh.”

At Jesus' death the veil of the temple, the successor of the veil in v. 31, is torn in two; Matthew and Mark add “from the top to the bottom.” Read alongside Hebrews 10:20 (above), Christian interpreters took the torn veil as the opening of the way into God's presence.

Clement repeats the four-element reading of the veil's colors found in Philo and Josephus. He takes the four pillars of the inner veil as a sign of the “sacred tetrad” and links them with God's four-letter name. The outer screen on its five pillars, he says, holds back those who trust only their five senses.

27.overview:
Three items complete the plan for the outside. First comes the altar for burnt offerings: a hollow acacia box five cubits square and three high, overlaid with bronze, with a horn at each corner, a bronze grate, and poles for carrying. Next is the courtyard, a fence of linen hangings on pillars set in bronze sockets, a hundred cubits long and fifty wide, with an embroidered gate on the east. Last, Israel is to bring pure olive oil so the lamp inside can burn through every night.

The gold is gone. Chs. 25–26 covered the ark, table, lampstand, and frames in gold, but here the Hebrew word for gold never appears, and the word for bronze (KJV “brass”) comes ten times. The court was where ordinary Israelites came with their animals, and its metal marks how far in they stand.

27.hermeneutics:
Horned altars have turned up across Israel. In the Judahite shrine at Tel Arad stood an altar of earth and unhewn stones about five cubits square and three high, the same size as v. 1. At Beersheba the stones of a large horned altar were found taken apart and reused in a later wall. The horns were the altar's most sacred point: blood was daubed on them (29:12), and a man in danger could grab them and claim protection, as Adonijah and Joab did (1 Kings 1:50; 2:28). The bronze box “hollow with boards” (v. 8) is a portable version of the same object. Many commentators suggest it was filled with earth or stones at each camp, in line with the altar of earth in 20:24.

Ramesses II carved his war camp at Kadesh (about 1274 BC) on temple walls at Abu Simbel, Luxor, and the Ramesseum. The reliefs show a walled rectangle twice as long as it is wide, entered at the middle of a short side, with the king's tent at the center: an outer room leading to a smaller square inner room. The tabernacle court is also twice as long as wide, 100 by 50 cubits, with its gate in the middle of the short east side (vv. 13–16), and the tent inside has an outer room and a cube-shaped inner one. Michael Homan argues from this that Israel pictured the tabernacle as the field camp of a divine king who marches with his people. On that reading, the court of ch. 27 is the edge of the royal enclosure.

structure.summary: No strong pattern; the chapter moves in sequence, ending the outward tour of the sanctuary at the court gate.
notes: **Inside out:** the instructions began with the ark behind the veil (25:10) and end here at the court gate. A worshiper walks it in reverse: through the east gate, to the altar, toward the tent.
**Built on fives:** the altar is 5 by 5 cubits, the court 100 by 50, its hangings 5 high, and the east side is 15 + 20 + 15 cubits, hangings on either side of the gate.
**A turn at the end:** vv. 20–21 move from objects to a standing duty. “Thou shalt make” gives way to “thou shalt command” Israel to bring oil, and Aaron, last seen at 24:14, returns with his sons.

The court closes the description of the sanctuary's structure that began in 25:10; altar and court are built in 38:1–20. The lamp law then hinges the unit toward the priests: “Aaron and his sons” (v. 21) leads straight into their garments (ch. 28) and consecration (ch. 29).
**Forward:** Leviticus 24:2–4 repeats the lamp law, and 1 Samuel 3:3 shows the lamp of God still burning at Shiloh in the night when the boy Samuel hears the Lord call.

traditions.text: Adam offers the firstlings of his flock long before any tabernacle altar. When an angel asks why, Adam answers that he does not know, only that the Lord commanded it, and the angel explains that the offering is “a similitude of the sacrifice of the Only Begotten of the Father.” In Restoration scripture the bronze altar of v. 1 continues a practice that began with Adam and pointed to Christ from the start.

Lehi's first act after leaving Jerusalem is to build an altar of stones and give thanks. Generations later the Nephites gather at the temple to offer burnt offerings “according to the law of Moses.” Far from any tabernacle court, they kept the altar worship this chapter sets up, and Amulek explains that the whole law pointed to a great and last sacrifice, the Son of God.

Josephus describes the court's pillars as bronze with silver tops, tied with cords to bronze pins driven into the ground so the wind could not shake them. He says the bronze plates of the altar shone “as bright as gold,” and that the altar had no bottom, so the ground beneath took the fire through the grate. He also places the laver just inside the gate.

Philo notes that the altar of sacrifice stood in the open air directly opposite the tent's entrance, with just enough space between for the priests' daily work. He says the altar's name points to what is really consumed, which is not the victim but the intention of the one who offers it. If the offerer is foolish and ignorant, he adds, his sacrifices are no sacrifices.

The Mishnah ranks nine grades of olive oil from three harvests a year. The finest comes from olives picked ripe at the top of the tree, crushed in a mortar, and left to drip through a basket before any beam presses them. That first-pressed oil, beaten rather than milled, is the oil of v. 20.

Tractate Middot shows how far the altar of v. 1 grew: the Second Temple altar was thirty-two cubits square at its base, rising in stages to horns a cubit wide, with a red line around its middle to divide blood put above from blood put below. Its stones were unhewn, because iron, made to shorten life, should not touch the altar, made to lengthen it. Avot adds that rain never put out the altar's fire and wind never bent its column of smoke.

Rashi explains “beaten” in v. 20 by the Mishnah's method: the olives are pounded in a mortar, not ground in a mill, so the first oil runs clear. Only that first oil goes to the lamp; oil from the later milling may be used for meal offerings. He reads “to burn always” as lighting each night until the flame rises on its own.

A teaching asks whether God needed the lamp's light, since Israel walked forty years by his pillar of fire. The answer is that the lamp is a testimony to the world that the Divine Presence rests among Israel. Rav finds the testimony in the westernmost lamp, which held the same oil as the others yet burned on through the day, so the priest lit the rest from it each evening.

Hebrews tells Christians they “have an altar” from which those who serve the tabernacle have no right to eat. The writer sets Christ's sacrifice beside the altar of this chapter and treats the bronze altar's service as a shadow that has given way to the one offering.

When the fifth seal opens, John sees “under the altar the souls of them that were slain” for God's word. The image fits the bronze altar, where sacrificial blood was poured out at the base (29:12) and where Leviticus 17:11 locates the life in the blood. The court's altar gains a counterpart in heaven.

In his Banquet, a dialogue on virginity, Methodius reads the tabernacle as a figure of the Church and its two altars as two groups within it. The bronze altar in the open court stands for the widows, a living altar to which offerings are brought. The golden altar inside, where no blood is offered, stands for the virgins.

28.overview:
God names Aaron and his four sons as priests and orders “holy garments” for Aaron “for glory and for beauty.” The high priest's dress is described piece by piece: the ephod, a woven garment with an onyx stone on each shoulder; the breastplate, a square pouch set with twelve gems in four rows; a blue robe with golden bells and pomegranates around the hem; and a gold plate on the turban engraved “HOLINESS TO THE LORD.” Plainer linen coats, sashes, caps, and undergarments are made for his sons.

Aaron carries Israel's names twice. The twelve tribes are engraved on the shoulder stones (v. 12) and again on the breastplate “upon his heart” (v. 29), each time as a “memorial” before the LORD. When he walks into the holy place, the whole people goes in with him.

28.hermeneutics:
Egypt's chief judge, says the Greek historian Diodorus (1st century BC), wore a small image made of precious stones on a golden chain around his neck. It was called Truth, and a hearing began when he put it on. Aaron's “breastplate of judgment” (v. 15) is also a jeweled piece worn on the chest and tied to judging; he bears Israel's judgment “upon his heart” (v. 30). The comparison explains why a verdict would be worn rather than written: the jewel marks its wearer as the one through whom judgment comes.

Across the Near East a seal was a person's signature. Cylinder seals rolled across clay closed contracts, and hundreds of small stamp seals from Israel and Judah carry their owners' names. Three times this chapter orders engraving “like the engravings of a signet”: the tribal names on the shoulder stones (v. 11), the names on the twelve gems (v. 21), and the words on the gold plate (v. 36). Aaron enters the sanctuary bearing Israel's names as seals, and wearing the LORD's own mark of ownership on his forehead.

In the Babylonian creation epic *Enuma Elish*, Tiamat fastens the Tablet of Destinies to her champion Kingu's breast; Marduk defeats him, seals the tablet, and lays it on his own breast. Worn on the chest, the tablet is the power to decide what will happen. Aaron's breastplate holds the Urim and Thummim (v. 30), by which Israel later asked God for decisions (Numbers 27:21). In Babylon gods fight to wear the tablet; Aaron only carries what God decides.

notes: **Memorial:** the Hebrew *zikkaron* comes three times, twice for the shoulder stones (v. 12) and once for the breastplate (v. 29). The names are carried so that the people are remembered before God.

**Continually:** *tamid* marks the three things Aaron wears at all times before the LORD: the names on his heart (v. 29), the judgment on his heart (v. 30), and the plate on his forehead (v. 38). “Upon his heart” itself occurs three times (vv. 29, 30 twice).
**Warnings at the edges:** the robe's sound is heard “that he die not” (v. 35), and the chapter ends with linen breeches so the priests “bear not iniquity, and die” (v. 43).

Chs. 28–29 turn from the building to the people who serve in it, and the lamp law at 27:20–21 is the hinge. The garments are made in 39:1–31 and put on Aaron in Leviticus 8:7–9, where Moses carries out this chapter step by step.

**Later echoes:** Zechariah foresees the words of Aaron's plate written even on the horses' bells (Zechariah 14:20), so that ordinary things become as holy as the high priest's forehead. Revelation 1:13 clothes the risen Christ in a robe to the feet with a golden girdle.

traditions.text: Moroni told Joseph Smith that two stones in silver bows, fastened to a breastplate, were deposited with the plates, that they were called the Urim and Thummim, and that God had prepared them for translating. D&C 17 promises the Three Witnesses a view of “the breastplate” and of the Urim and Thummim given to the brother of Jared. Latter-day Saint scripture thus links the instrument of the translation to the breastplate and Urim and Thummim of v. 30.

Abraham says he had the Urim and Thummim, given to him in Ur of the Chaldees, and learned about the stars through it. Ammon tells King Limhi of “interpreters” that only one commanded may look into, and that such a person is called a seer. In Restoration scripture these instruments are older than Aaron and are tied to seeing and translating, not only to answering questions.

Joseph Smith taught that the place where God resides is a great Urim and Thummim, that the earth in its sanctified state will become one for its inhabitants, and that the white stone of Revelation 2:17 will be a Urim and Thummim to each person who receives it. The instrument Aaron wore over his heart becomes a pattern for how the exalted will know things.

Ben Sira's praise of famous men lingers over Aaron's clothes: the long robe and ephod, the pomegranates and many golden bells sounding in the temple “for a memorial to the children of his people,” the engraved stones, the breastplate with Urim and Thummim, and the gold crown engraved with holiness. He adds that no stranger ever wore them, only Aaron's children and their descendants.

Retelling how Aaron stopped a plague with his censer (Numbers 16:46–48), the writer says that “in the long garment was the whole world.” The four rows of stones carried the glory of the fathers, and God's majesty rested on the diadem. It is the earliest statement that Aaron's clothing pictures the universe, a reading Philo and Josephus develop at length.

A Greek-speaking visitor describes watching the high priest Eleazar serve in Jerusalem. He notes golden bells on the robe “giving forth a peculiar kind of melody,” twelve stones in the oracle on his breast with the names of the tribal leaders, and God's name on a gold plate on his forehead. The sight, he says, made one feel in the presence of a man from another world.

Philo calls the breastplate the *logeum* and says it bore two virtues, manifestation and truth, which is how the Greek Bible renders Urim and Thummim. He reads the whole costume as the universe: flowers and pomegranates for earth and water, the bells for their harmony, the shoulder emeralds for sun and moon, the twelve stones for the circle of the zodiac.

Josephus gives a similar cosmic reading and adds a claim of his own. The right shoulder stone shone when God was present at the sacrifices, and the twelve breastplate stones flashed before a victory, so that Greeks called the breastplate the Oracle. Both stopped shining, he says, two hundred years before he wrote, because God was displeased with the breaking of his laws.

The rabbis explain *Urim* from “light,” because it made its words clear, and *Thummim* from “complete,” because its words came true. The tribal names on the breastplate supplied the letters of each answer: Rabbi Yohanan says the letters stood out, and Resh Lakish that they joined into words. Another passage says each garment atones for a sin, the robe with its bells for slander and the breastplate for perverted judgment.

Rashi says the Urim and Thummim was a writing of God's proper name placed between the folds of the breastplate. In the Second Temple the breastplate was still worn, but without the Name, so it no longer gave answers. Ezra 2:63 shows that gap: priests had to wait until one stood up “with Urim and with Thummim.”

Justin tells Trypho that the twelve bells hanging from the high priest's robe were a figure of the twelve apostles, whose voice has filled the earth. Exodus gives no number of bells. The rabbis of Zevachim 88b argued for seventy-two or thirty-six, and Clement (below) counts 360.

Clement reads the robe as the world of the senses. The shoulder emeralds are sun and moon, the twelve breast stones the zodiac through the four seasons, and the bells, which he numbers at 360, the days of a year, “the acceptable year of the Lord.” The gold plate bearing the Name stands for Christ's rule above every authority.

29.overview:
The ordination of Aaron and his sons is laid out as a seven-day rite. Moses washes them at the door of the tent, dresses them, and pours oil on Aaron's head. Three animals follow: a bull for a sin offering, a ram burned whole, and a second “ram of consecration,” whose blood is put on each priest's right ear, right thumb, and right big toe. The priests eat its meat with bread at the door of the tent. The chapter ends with the daily offering, a lamb every morning and every evening, for all generations.

The last verses say what all of it is for. God will meet Israel at the tent door and “dwell among the children of Israel” (v. 45). He brought them out of Egypt, v. 46 says, “that I may dwell among them.” The Exodus had a destination: God living in the middle of the camp.

29.hermeneutics:
Installing a priest took days and oil elsewhere too. At Emar in Syria (14th–12th century BC) a ritual text, Emar 369, sets out how the storm god's high priestess was installed. She was chosen by lot, fine oil from the palace and the temple was poured on her head on the first and second days, and the rite moved through shaving, enthronement, sacrifices, and feasts over about nine days, with a recurring seven-day phrase inside it. Exodus 29 has the same building blocks: oil on the head (v. 7), sacrifices, a meal eaten at the sanctuary (vv. 31–34), and seven days (v. 35). What differs is the scope. Exodus ordains a whole family line “for a perpetual statute” (v. 9), and the altar itself must be made holy over the same seven days (v. 37).

Temples across the Near East fed their gods on a schedule. A Seleucid-era tablet from the temple of Anu at Uruk sets out a main meal and a second meal each morning and each evening, with bread, beer, wine, and meat laid before the god's statue. Exodus 29:38–42 keeps the same rhythm: a lamb in the morning and a lamb at evening, with flour, oil, and wine. But no image sits in the tent to eat. The offering goes up in smoke as “a sweet savour,” and the morning and evening times become set hours of meeting, “where I will meet you” (v. 42). The schedule of a royal table becomes the schedule of an audience.

notes: **Who sanctifies:** Moses is told to hallow the priests (v. 1), but at the end God says he will sanctify tent, altar, and priests himself (v. 44). The Hebrew verb for serving as priest occurs in ch. 29 only in these two verses.
**Sevens:** “seven days” occurs three times: the son who succeeds Aaron wears the garments seven days (v. 30), the ordination lasts seven days (v. 35), and the altar is atoned for seven days (v. 37).

**The right side:** blood marks the right ear, right thumb, and right big toe (v. 20), and the right shoulder of the ram goes to the altar (v. 22). The same three marks are used again to cleanse a healed leper (Leviticus 14:14).

Vv. 45–46 answer 25:8, “that I may dwell among them.” The Hebrew verb for dwelling occurs in chs. 25–31 only in those three verses, so 25:1–29:46 is framed by God's wish to live with Israel. Ch. 30 then adds items not yet covered.

**Carried out:** Leviticus 8 performs this rite, and on the eighth day fire from the LORD consumes the offering (Leviticus 9:24). Nadab and Abihu, consecrated here, die soon after for offering “strange fire” (Leviticus 10:1–2).

traditions.text: The Lord “confirmed a priesthood also upon Aaron and his seed” throughout their generations, matching the “perpetual statute” of v. 9. D&C 84 calls it the lesser priesthood, holding the key of the ministering of angels and the preparatory gospel. It says this priesthood continued with the house of Aaron until John the Baptist.

John the Baptist conferred the Priesthood of Aaron on Joseph Smith and Oliver Cowdery, saying it would not be taken again until the sons of Levi offer an offering in righteousness. D&C 107 explains that it bears Aaron's name because it was conferred on Aaron and his seed, and that it administers outward ordinances. A firstborn literal descendant of Aaron has a legal right to its presiding office, the bishopric, when designated by the First Presidency.

Hebrews says no one takes the honor of priesthood to himself, “but he that is called of God, as was Aaron.” The fifth Article of Faith states the same principle: a man must be called of God by prophecy and by the laying on of hands by those in authority. Aaron's call here, given through Moses, is the pattern both texts invoke.

Ben Sira says Moses consecrated Aaron and anointed him with holy oil, and that this was an everlasting covenant for him and his seed “so long as the heavens should remain.” Their charge was to minister, serve as priests, and bless the people in the LORD's name. He reads the ordination of Exodus 29 as a covenant, not merely a ceremony.

Philo explains the blood on ear, hand, and foot: the perfect man must be pure in word, deed, and the whole path of his life, since the ear judges words, the hand acts, and the foot walks. All three are extremities on the right side, which he takes as a sign of skill and right aim. He also notes that blood mixed with oil was sprinkled on the priests and their garments, so they shared the purity of both the open court and the inner shrine.

Mar Ukva could not answer the question of what Moses wore while he served as priest during the seven days of ordination, before Aaron could serve. The study house's answer: neither his own clothes nor priestly garments, but a white cloak. Rav Kahana adds that it had no hem. The question arises from the text itself: until the seven days end, Aaron is not yet a priest, so every act of this chapter falls to Moses.

The Mishnah has the high priest removed from his home to a chamber in the temple seven days before the Day of Atonement. Rabbi Yohanan derives the custom from this ordination, when Aaron and his sons stayed at the tent door for seven days before serving on the eighth (Leviticus 8:33–35). The seven days of v. 35 became the pattern for every later preparation of a high priest.

The daily lamb of vv. 38–42 was meant to continue “throughout your generations.” The Mishnah lists its end among five disasters of the seventeenth of Tammuz, the day the tablets were broken: the daily offering ceased and was never offered again. The fast of that day still marks it.

Hebrews sets the daily offering of vv. 38–42 beside Christ's single offering. Every priest stands daily offering the same sacrifices, which cannot take away sins, while Christ offered one sacrifice and sat down. He did not need to offer daily, first for himself and then for the people, “for this he did once, when he offered up himself.”

The bull of the sin offering is burned outside the camp (v. 14), a rule repeated for later sin offerings. Hebrews draws on the practice: Jesus also “suffered without the gate,” so believers are to go out to him outside the camp and bear his reproach.

Teaching the newly baptized about the anointing that followed their baptism, Cyril points to this rite: Moses washed Aaron in water and then anointed him, and Aaron was called “Christ,” anointed, from the typical chrism. Solomon too was anointed after bathing in Gihon. What was a figure for them, he tells his hearers, is truth for those anointed with the Holy Ghost.

30.overview:
Five more items complete the plan. A small gold altar for incense stands just outside the veil, and Aaron burns incense on it every morning and evening. Every man counted in a census pays half a shekel as “a ransom for his soul,” and the silver goes to the tabernacle. A bronze basin stands between the tent and the altar so the priests can wash their hands and feet. Last come two recipes: a holy anointing oil of myrrh, cinnamon, calamus, cassia, and olive oil, and an incense of four spices, both forbidden for private use.

The census rule stands out. The rich may “not give more,” and the poor may “not give less” (v. 15). Every other gift for the tabernacle came from whoever was willing, in whatever amount (25:2). This one is the same small coin for every man over twenty, because each life counted is ransomed at the same price.

30.hermeneutics:
Small horned incense altars of stone are common finds at Iron Age sites in Israel, Megiddo among them. In the Judahite shrine at Tel Arad (8th century BC), two limestone altars stood on the steps leading up to the inner niche. A 2020 analysis of the residue on them found frankincense mixed with animal fat on the larger altar and cannabis on the smaller. Frankincense came by caravan from southern Arabia, so every burning was costly. The altar of vv. 1–10 is the same type, a cubit square and two cubits high with horns (v. 2), and it also stands at the threshold of the inner room (v. 6). The difference is control: one recipe only (vv. 34–35), no “strange incense” (v. 9), and no copies for private use (vv. 37–38).

A census was not a neutral act. In the Mari archives (18th century BC) the census is called *têbibtum*, a word from a verb meaning “to cleanse.” E. A. Speiser argued that counting people put them in ritual danger that had to be purified, which would explain why v. 12 ties numbering to the threat of a plague and requires a ransom. Other scholars point out that the Mari census was run by civil officials with no ritual attached, so the parallel may lie in the name only. Either way, Exodus treats being counted as being exposed, and the half shekel covers each man before God.

notes: **Seven speeches:** from 25:1 to 31:17 the LORD opens a new speech to Moses seven times (25:1; 30:11, 17, 22, 34; 31:1, 12), and four of them fall in ch. 30. The seventh is about the Sabbath. Some scholars, following P. J. Kearney, pair the seven speeches with the seven days of creation.
**Atonement:** the Hebrew root behind “atonement” and “ransom” occurs seven times: three times for the incense altar (v. 10) and four for the census (vv. 12, 15, 16 twice).

**Most holy, not to be copied:** “most holy” marks the incense altar (v. 10), the anointed furnishings (v. 29), and the incense (v. 36). Anyone who copies the oil or the incense is “cut off” (vv. 33, 38).

The instructions seemed to close at 29:46; ch. 30 adds what remains. The incense altar is the surprise. The table and lampstand that stand beside it were described in ch. 25, but this altar waits until after the priests who will burn incense on it have been ordained. The section ends at 31:18 with the tablets.
**Forward:** the census silver is cast into the sockets that hold up the tabernacle's frames (38:25–27; compare 26:19). David's census without ransom ends in a plague (2 Samuel 24:10–15).

traditions.text: Among the ordinances the Lord says belong to his holy house are “your anointings, and your washings.” In Exodus the washing at the laver (vv. 19–21) and the holy anointing oil (v. 30) prepared priests to serve before God. D&C 124 places washings and anointings among the ordinances the Saints were commanded to build a temple to receive.

Philo reads the half shekel as a unit, which can be neither added to nor taken from, the image of the one complete God. That, he says, is why the rich may not add and the poor may not subtract. The half offered as ransom stands for the part of the soul set free by God; the other half is left to the part that stays enslaved to the passions.

The four spices of the incense, mixed in equal weights (v. 34), are for Philo the four elements of the world: stacte (from drops) is water, onycha is earth, galbanum is air, and clear frankincense is fire. Burning the incense is the world giving thanks to its Maker. It matches the four-element reading he and Josephus give the veil's four colors.

Josephus says the half shekel was paid by free men above twenty years old “but under fifty,” an upper age the text does not give, and that a shekel equals four Athenian drachmas. He describes the anointing oil as boiled and blended by the perfumer's art, and the incense as offered twice a day, before sunrise and at sunset.

In the Second Temple period the half shekel of v. 13 became a yearly tax for the public offerings. On the first of Adar the court announced it; on the fifteenth money changers set up tables in the towns, and on the twenty-fifth in the temple, after which pledges were taken from those who had not paid. Gifts from gentiles and Samaritans were refused for this fund.

Resh Lakish links the half shekel to the book of Esther. God knew Haman would one day weigh out silver shekels to buy Israel's destruction (Esther 3:9), so he arranged for Israel's shekels to come first. The announcement on the first of Adar comes before Haman's date later in the same month.

On the opening words of v. 13 Rashi cites the midrash that God showed Moses a coin of fire weighing half a shekel and said, “Like this shall they give.” The image answers a practical question the text raises: Moses had to know exactly what coin was meant.

Rabbi Judah says the anointing oil Moses made was only twelve log, yet it anointed the tabernacle, its vessels, Aaron and his sons through the seven days, and later high priests and kings, and all of it remains for the future. He reads this from the words “throughout your generations” (v. 31). A related teaching says Josiah hid the flask of oil with the ark, the jar of manna, and Aaron's rod.

Exodus names four incense spices; a teaching quoted in the Talmud lists eleven used in the temple, among them myrrh, cassia, spikenard, saffron, and cinnamon, with set weights of each. Adding honey disqualified it, and whoever left out any one spice was liable to death at the hand of Heaven.

Collectors of the temple tax, the yearly half shekel, ask Peter whether his master pays it. Jesus asks whether kings take tribute from their own children or from strangers, and concludes “Then are the children free.” He pays anyway with a coin found in a fish's mouth, enough for himself and Peter, so as not to offend.

Zacharias is burning incense in the temple, while the people pray outside, when an angel appears “on the right side of the altar of incense.” In Revelation an angel offers incense with the prayers of all saints on the golden altar before God's throne. Both tie the altar of vv. 1–10 to prayer, as Psalm 141:2 had done.

Explaining the anointing that followed baptism, Tertullian traces it to the old practice of anointing men entering the priesthood “ever since Aaron was anointed by Moses.” From that chrism Aaron was called “Christ,” a name that passed in a spiritual sense to the Lord, anointed with the Spirit. Cyril of Jerusalem makes the same link a century and a half later.

31.overview:
The LORD finishes his instructions for the tabernacle by naming its builders. Bezaleel of the tribe of Judah is filled with the spirit of God for every kind of craft, and Aholiab of Dan is given to work with him, along with every skilled worker. Then comes a last charge: keep the Sabbath, a sign between God and Israel and a perpetual covenant, on pain of death. Moses receives the two tables of stone, written with the finger of God.

The last word before the golden calf is about rest. After six chapters of building plans, God insists that even work on his own sanctuary must stop on the seventh day, and he grounds the command in creation: in six days he made heaven and earth, and on the seventh he rested (v. 17). The holy place and the holy day are given together.

31.hermeneutics:
In Mesopotamia a cult statue was made by human craftsmen and then ritually taken away from them. In the mouth-washing ritual (*mīs pî*), the sculptors’ hands were bound and symbolically cut with a knife of tamarisk wood, and they declared that they had not made the image; Ea, god of the smiths, had made it. Exodus goes the other way. Bezaleel and Aholiab are named, with their fathers and tribes, and their skill is credited openly to God’s spirit (v. 3). Nothing they make is an image of God, so there is nothing to disown.

Babylonian scholars kept calendars of lucky and unlucky days. The 7th, 14th, 19th, 21st, and 28th of the month were marked as dangerous, days when the king or the physician should hold back, and the 15th, the full moon, was called *šapattu*. Israel’s Sabbath is tied neither to the moon nor to bad luck. It falls every seventh day without a break, and vv. 13 and 17 make it a sign of a relationship: Israel rests because God rested.

Hittite treaties were written on tablets and laid up before the gods who witnessed them. A copy of King Suppiluliuma’s treaty with Shattiwaza of Mittani was deposited before the storm-god Teshub at Kahat. The two tables of v. 18 are called tables of “testimony,” and the ark in the holy of holies was built to hold that testimony (25:16). Israel’s covenant document was to be kept the same way, in the presence of the God who gave it.

notes: **Seven speeches:** Each section of the instructions opens with “the LORD spake (or said) unto Moses.” The seventh and last concerns the seventh day. Some scholars (Kearney) match the seven speeches to the seven days of Genesis 1; others see only a list.

**Echoes of creation:** Bezaleel is filled with “the spirit of God” (v. 3), the same Hebrew phrase as Genesis 1:2, and v. 17 repeats the rest of Genesis 2:2–3. In the KJV, “filled him with the spirit of God” occurs only here and at 35:31.
**Repetition to watch:** “sabbath” comes 6 times in vv. 13–16, “keep” 3 times, and “sign” twice (vv. 13, 17), once at each end of the Sabbath speech.

Chapter 31 ends the instructions that began at 25:1, given while Moses spent forty days on the mountain (24:18). The tables of v. 18 are the hinge: Moses carries them straight into the golden calf story (32:15), and the next three chapters ask whether God will still dwell among Israel at all.

**Repeated after the calf:** When the building begins, Moses gives the Sabbath charge first (35:1–3) and Bezaleel’s call last (35:30–35), the reverse of this chapter’s order, so the two halves of the tabernacle story frame the calf.

traditions.text: The reason given in v. 17, that God rested on the seventh day after six days of making, appears in the Restoration creation account in God’s own voice: “I, God, blessed the seventh day, and sanctified it.” Abinadi recites the Sabbath command to the priests of king Noah with the same grounding in creation. He then asks whether they have taught the people to keep these commandments, and answers that they have not.

Given on a Sunday in Jackson County, Missouri, this revelation calls the Sabbath “my holy day” and “the Lord’s day.” It keeps the purpose Exodus gives, a day “to rest from your labors,” and adds going to the house of prayer, offering sacraments, and confessing sins. Like v. 13, it ties the day to holiness, here to keeping oneself unspotted from the world.

The Joseph Smith Translation says the tables Moses received in v. 18 held more than the second set would. When God orders new tables, he adds that “it shall not be according to the first,” because the priesthood, his holy order, and its ordinances would be taken from Israel’s midst. D&C 84 says the same: Moses sought to sanctify the people to see God’s face, and when they hardened their hearts the holy priesthood was taken.

Exodus says the tables were written “with the finger of God.” The Book of Mormon tells of the brother of Jared, who saw the Lord’s finger touch sixteen stones he had made and was told that he saw it because of his faith. In both accounts the Lord’s own finger touches stone.

This early rabbinic commentary on Exodus takes the “but” of v. 13 as a limit and asks how saving a life can override the Sabbath. Rabbis Ishmael, Eleazar ben Azariah, and Akiva each argue that it does, and Rabbi Shimon ben Menasya draws the rule from v. 14: the Sabbath is given to you, and you are not given to the Sabbath. Jesus makes a like point in Mark 2:27, “The sabbath was made for man.”

The rabbis read Bezaleel’s name as “in the shadow of God” (*betzel El*). When Moses told him to make the ark and vessels first, Bezaleel replied that a person builds a house before furnishing it, and Moses said he must have stood in God’s shadow to know the order God gave (v. 7). Rav adds that Bezaleel knew how to join the letters by which heaven and earth were made, since v. 3 gives him the wisdom, understanding, and knowledge by which God founded the world (Proverbs 3:19–20).

Philo also explains the name as “God in his shadow” and takes the shadow to be God’s Word, the instrument he used in making the world. Moses, he says, received the pattern from God himself, while Bezaleel learned from Moses, so Moses shaped the archetypes and Bezaleel made the copies. The Talmud plays on the same name (above) but lets Bezaleel correct Moses.

Lists ten things created at twilight on the eve of the first Sabbath, among them the letters, the writing, and the tablets. On this reading the tables of v. 18 were ready before the first Sabbath was ever kept, made in the last moments of creation week.

Rashi asks why the Sabbath command follows the building plans. Even if the people were eager to finish God’s house, he says, the “but” (*akh*) of v. 13 excepts the Sabbath, so the sanctuary work must stop on that day. On v. 18 he holds, following Midrash Tanchuma, that the golden calf came before the tabernacle command was given, and that the Torah does not always tell events in order.

In his retelling Moses comes down after forty days, tells the people that God wants a tabernacle they can carry with them, and shows them the two tables with “five upon each table,” written by the hand of God. He then moves straight to the building, with no golden calf in between (see ch. 32).

Irenaeus quotes v. 13 with Ezekiel 20:12 to argue that the Sabbath, like circumcision, was given as a sign. Signs given by a wise Artist were not empty, he says; they pointed ahead to what would be fulfilled in Christ. In the same chapter he holds that the Ten Commandments themselves were never cancelled.

Augustine joins the “finger of God” of v. 18 to Luke 11:20, where Jesus casts out devils by the finger of God, and identifies it as the Holy Spirit. He counts fifty days from the first Passover to the law written on stone, and fifty days from Christ’s resurrection to Pentecost, when the same finger of God gathered the believers. The Spirit that wrote on stone at Sinai, he argues, now writes love on the heart.
traditions.cite: On the Spirit and the Letter 28 (ch. 16)

32.overview:
While Moses is on the mountain, the people press Aaron to make them gods to go before them. He melts their gold earrings into a calf, builds an altar, and proclaims a feast to the LORD. God tells Moses to go down and threatens to consume the people and start over with him; Moses pleads, and God relents. Coming down, Moses sees the dancing, smashes the tables, grinds the calf to powder, and makes Israel drink it. The Levites rally to him and about three thousand fall. Moses goes back up to seek atonement, asking to be blotted out of God’s book if the people are not forgiven.

Moses talks God out of his anger on the mountain, then loses his own at the foot of it. The same verb, “wax hot,” is used of God’s wrath (vv. 10–11) and of Moses’ anger when he sees the calf (v. 19).

32.hermeneutics:
Bulls stood for divine strength across Canaan. Ugaritic texts call the high god “Bull El,” and in 1990 excavators at Ashkelon found a small silver-plated bronze calf from about 1600 BC inside a pottery shrine. Storm gods were often shown standing on a bull’s back. Many scholars think Aaron’s calf was meant as a pedestal or emblem of the LORD, since he proclaims “a feast to the LORD” (v. 5). Either way, the text treats it as a plain breach of the commands against images and gods of gold (20:4, 23).

In the Ugaritic Baal Cycle the goddess Anat destroys Mot, the god of death, in a fixed series: she splits him with a blade, winnows him, burns him with fire, grinds him with millstones, and scatters him in the field. Moses does nearly the same to the calf. He burns it, grinds it to powder, and scatters it on water (v. 20). Scholars (Loewenstamm) read the match as a stock way of describing the total destruction of a god. Here the god is a lump of metal, and the people drink what is left of it.

Centuries later Jeroboam set up two golden calves at Bethel and Dan for the northern kingdom and introduced them with Aaron’s words, “behold thy gods, O Israel” (1 Kings 12:28). Both calves were offered as images of the God who brought Israel out of Egypt, and that is exactly what the text condemns. A reader who knew the history of the kings would hear the northern kingdom’s sin already present at Sinai.

notes: **Who brought them up?** “Brought … out of the land of Egypt” comes 6 times (vv. 1, 4, 7, 8, 11, 23), and the credit keeps moving: the people give it to Moses, then to the calf; God, speaking to Moses, calls them “thy people, which thou broughtest”; Moses answers that they are God’s people, whom God brought forth.
**A great sin:** the phrase comes 3 times in Hebrew (vv. 21, 30, 31): Moses says it to Aaron, then to the people, then to God.
Each mountain scene ends with only a partial answer. God relents from destroying the people (v. 14), then puts off punishment to “the day when I visit” (v. 34).

Chapters 32–34 break into the tabernacle story: the instructions end at 31:18 and the building starts at 35:1. The calf breaks the covenant sealed in ch. 24, and these chapters ask whether God’s presence can still go with Israel. The answer comes in 34:10: “Behold, I make a covenant.”

**Echoes later:** Psalm 106:19–20 remembers that Israel “changed their glory” for the likeness of an ox, and Deuteronomy 9–10 has Moses recall the calf and the second tables before Israel enters the land.

traditions.text: In the KJV Moses asks God to repent, and the LORD “repented” (vv. 12, 14). The Joseph Smith Translation changes both verses: Moses says “Thy people will repent of this evil,” and the Lord answers that if they repent he will spare them, while Moses is to execute judgment on all who will not repent that day. The repentance becomes the people’s, and it prepares for the Levites’ work in vv. 26–28.

Explains what was lost at Sinai. Moses sought to sanctify his people so they could behold the face of God, but they hardened their hearts and could not endure his presence. The Lord swore in his wrath that they would not enter his rest, took Moses and the holy priesthood out of their midst, and left the lesser priesthood and “the law of carnal commandments” with the house of Aaron.

Abinadi explains why Israel received a very strict law: they were “a stiffnecked people,” the words God uses in v. 9, quick to do iniquity and slow to remember him. So they were given a law of performances and ordinances to keep them in remembrance of God, and all of it, he adds, pointed to things to come.

Reads the word for “delayed” in v. 1 as two words, “six has come.” Moses had promised to return after forty days at the sixth hour; Satan darkened the world with a storm, told the people Moses was dead, and showed them an image of his bier in the clouds. Rashi adds that the people counted the day of his ascent and so expected him a day early.

Hur, it says, rebuked the people and was killed, which is why Aaron built the altar in fear. The women refused to give up their earrings, so the men gave their own. When Moses saw the dancing, the writing flew off the tables and they grew too heavy to hold, so he let them fall; Targum Pseudo-Jonathan on v. 19 also has the holy writing fly away.
traditions.cite: Pirkei de-Rabbi Eliezer 45; Targum Pseudo-Jonathan on Exodus 32:19

traditions.text: Rabbi Abbahu notes that God says “let me alone” (v. 10) before Moses has said a word. He takes it to mean that Moses had seized hold of God like a man grabbing his friend by the garment and would not let go until the people were forgiven. Were the verse not written, he says, no one would dare to say it.

Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi says Israel made the calf only to give an opening to penitents. A people who had just heard God at Sinai should not have been capable of it, so the story shows that even a whole community’s worst sin can be repented of, as David’s showed for one man. The JST’s “if they will repent” (above) puts the same hope into the text.

In the synagogue the first account of the calf is read aloud and translated, but the second is read without translation. The Mishnah lists it with other passages handled the same way, such as Reuben’s sin with Bilhah, and later commentators identify the second account as Aaron’s report in vv. 21–24.

Philo says the people became “eager imitators of the Egyptian inventions” and made a golden calf after the animal held most sacred in that land. He does not name it, though Egypt’s best-known sacred bull was the Apis of Memphis. The Levites who answered Moses’ call proved their zeal, Philo says, and received the temple service as their reward, as Numbers 3:12 later sets them apart.

Josephus describes the people’s fear while Moses was gone forty days, some saying wild beasts had killed him and others that he had gone to God. Then Moses returns to general joy, with the tables in hand. The golden calf is missing; Josephus leaves it out entirely and never says why.

Stephen retells v. 1 almost word for word and says the fathers turned back to Egypt in their hearts and rejoiced in the works of their own hands. Paul quotes v. 6, the people sat down to eat and drink and “rose up to play,” as a warning to the Corinthians against idolatry.

Barnabas quotes v. 7 and says that when Moses cast the tables from his hands, “their covenant was broken.” In his reading Israel lost the covenant at the moment it was given, so that the covenant of Jesus could be sealed on Christian hearts. D&C 84 also says something was taken away at Sinai, though it speaks of the higher priesthood and leaves a lesser law in force.

Irenaeus holds that God first asked of Israel only the Ten Commandments. When they made the calf and turned back to Egypt in their minds, he says, they were placed under a further law suited to their wish, a yoke of bondage, and he cites Ezekiel 20:24 and Stephen’s speech. His picture of a law added because of the calf is close to D&C 84 and Mosiah 13 (above).

33.overview:
God tells Moses to lead the people on to Canaan, but he will send an angel and not go up among them himself, lest he consume a stiffnecked people. The people mourn and strip off their ornaments. Moses pitches a tent outside the camp, where the pillar of cloud comes down and the LORD speaks with him face to face, as a man speaks to his friend. Moses then pleads twice: that God’s presence go with them, which God grants, and that he may see God’s glory. God will make his goodness pass by and proclaim his name, but Moses will see only his back.

The chapter says both that the LORD spoke to Moses “face to face” (v. 11) and that “thou canst not see my face” (v. 20). The text leaves the two statements standing nine verses apart without explaining them.

33.hermeneutics:
When the god El in the Ugaritic Baal Cycle hears that Baal is dead, he comes down from his throne, sits on his footstool and then on the ground, pours dust on his head, and puts on a mourning cloth. Grief in Israel’s world meant stripping away the signs of ordinary life. The people do the same at the “evil tidings” of v. 4: they take off their ornaments at Horeb and do not put them on again (vv. 4–6). The gold for the calf had come from ornaments just like these (32:2–3).

Peoples of the ancient Near East took their gods with them into war and into great works. Assyrian palace reliefs show divine standards riding into battle on chariots, and Gudea of Lagash set the standards of the gods in front of the work gangs he raised to build a temple. At Sinai the people had asked for gods “which shall go before us” (32:1). This chapter answers the same need without an image: first an angel will go before them (v. 2), and then, at Moses’ plea, God’s own presence (v. 14).

In Akkadian letters, to “see the face” of the king meant to be admitted to his presence, and the same phrase was used of coming before a god in the temple where his statue stood. Israel’s God had no statue to look at. In v. 11 Moses has that kind of audience, face to face as with a friend. In vv. 18–23 he asks for more, to see God’s glory itself, and he is given God’s name and goodness instead (v. 19).

The tent outside the camp; face to face as a friend

The tent: God speaks with Moses face to face
Second plea: the glory, but not the face

notes: **Face:** the Hebrew *panim* occurs 10 times. The KJV renders it “face” (vv. 11, 16, 20, 23), “presence” (vv. 14, 15), and “before” (vv. 2, 19). God’s presence going with Israel and God’s face that cannot be seen are the same word.
**Grace and knowing:** “grace” comes 5 times in vv. 12–17, and the verb “know” 7 times in the chapter. God knows Moses “by name” (vv. 12, 17); Moses asks to know God’s way (v. 13).

Chapter 33 is the middle of the golden calf section (chs. 32–34). Chapter 32 breaks the covenant and ch. 34 renews it; here Moses argues with God over whether he will go with Israel at all. The request of vv. 18–23 is answered in 34:5–7, when the LORD passes by and proclaims his name.
**Later echo:** Elijah travels forty days to Horeb, stands at the mouth of a cave, and “the LORD passed by” (1 Kings 19:8–13): the same mountain, and nearly the same scene.

traditions.text: The Joseph Smith Translation adds a reason and a time limit. Moses cannot see God’s face at this time, lest God’s anger destroy him and his people, because the people are exceedingly sinful, and no sinful man has ever seen God’s face and lived. In v. 23 the face will not be seen “as at other times,” for God is angry with Israel, which brings v. 20 into line with v. 11.

Moses 1 opens with Moses seeing “God face to face” on a high mountain, with God’s glory upon him so that he could endure his presence. Afterward Moses explains that he saw with spiritual eyes rather than natural ones, because he was transfigured; otherwise he would have withered and died. The account holds both halves of Exodus 33 together: no one sees God’s face in the natural state, yet a transfigured Moses did.

D&C 84 says that without the ordinances and authority of the priesthood no man can see “the face of God, even the Father,” and live and that Moses sought to prepare Israel to behold it. D&C 67 adds that no one has seen God in the flesh except when quickened by the Spirit of God. D&C 93 promises that every soul who forsakes sins and keeps the commandments shall see his face.

Rabbi Yohanan says Moses asked three things here and received them all, beginning with the Divine Presence resting on Israel (v. 16). Another teacher says that because Moses hid his face at the bush (3:6), he was refused the sight now, yet earned a shining face later. What Moses saw of God’s back, says Rav Hana bar Bizna, was the knot of God’s phylacteries at the back of his head, a reading Rashi repeats on v. 23.

Philo has Moses ask first to see God himself and be told that no created being can grasp him. Moses then asks to see the glory around God, which Philo takes to be God’s powers; God answers that the powers are invisible too, known only by the impressions they leave, like a seal pressed into wax. Moses may know God by those marks in the world, never by his essence.

Rashi reads v. 7 as a habit that began after the calf: Moses moved his tent outside the camp, reasoning that one put under a ban by the Master should be put under a ban by the disciple too. Everyone who sought the LORD went out to it, and Rashi, following Midrash Tanchuma, takes this to mean that visiting a teacher of the law is like greeting the Divine Presence.

The standard Aramaic translation softens the bodily language of v. 23. God removes the guidance of his glory in place of his hand, and Moses sees what is behind God, while what is before him stays hidden. The rabbis of Berakhot 7a kept the bodily picture; the Targum steers around it.

John’s Gospel answers the chapter’s question directly: “No man hath seen God at any time; the only begotten Son” has declared him. Like v. 20, it denies that anyone has seen God, and it names the Son as the one who makes him known. Irenaeus and Tertullian (below) build on that answer.

Irenaeus says it was the Word who spoke with Moses as with a friend. Verses 20–22 teach him two things: no one can see God, and yet in the last times people would see him “in the depth of a rock,” that is, in his coming as a man. That is why, he says, the Lord spoke with Moses face to face on the mount of transfiguration, with Elijah present.

Tertullian uses vv. 11 and 20 against those who said the Father and the Son were one person. The God whom no one can see and live is the Father; the one whom Moses and the patriarchs saw was the Son, seen according to human capacity and not in the full glory of the Godhead. The tension between the two verses becomes for him evidence of two persons.

Augustine reads God’s “back parts” as Christ’s flesh, in which he was born, died, and rose again, called back parts because it came late in the world’s history. The face is the form of God, which no one can see and live. The place by God where Moses stands on the rock is, for him, the Church, where the back parts are seen by faith in the resurrection.

34.overview:
God tells Moses to cut two new tables of stone and climb Sinai alone. There the LORD descends in the cloud, passes by, and proclaims his name: merciful and gracious, longsuffering, forgiving iniquity, yet by no means clearing the guilty. Moses bows and asks God to go among a stiffnecked people, and God makes the covenant again, with warnings against the gods of Canaan and laws on feasts, firstborn, and the Sabbath. After forty days Moses comes down with the tables. His face shines so that the people fear to come near, and he veils it except when he speaks with the LORD.

What God proclaims in vv. 6–7 answers Moses’ request to see his glory (33:18): Moses is given God’s character in words. Later scripture returns to these lines again and again (Numbers 14:18; Nehemiah 9:17; Psalms 86:15; 103:8; Joel 2:13; Jonah 4:2).

historicalContext.text: A second forty days on Sinai after the golden calf (v. 28), in Israel’s first year out of Egypt. Rashi, following rabbinic tradition, dates Moses’ return with the second tables to the Day of Atonement.

34.hermeneutics:
Covenant documents could be replaced. The Hittite treaty between King Mursili II and Talmi-Sharruma of Aleppo survives in a copy issued by the next king, Muwatalli II, who explains that he wrote it out again because the original tablet had been stolen. The relationship outlived the lost document, and a new tablet restated it. Exodus 34 works the same way after the broken tables: new stones, the same words (v. 1), and a covenant stated afresh (vv. 10, 27).

The Gezer calendar, a small limestone tablet from about the 10th century BC, sets out the farmer’s year by its work: months of ingathering, sowing, late sowing, hoeing flax, the barley harvest, the harvest, pruning vines, and summer fruit. The three feasts of vv. 18–23 are pinned to that same year: unleavened bread in Abib, the month of green barley; weeks at the wheat harvest; and ingathering at the turn of the year. The renewed covenant binds Israel’s worship to its fields and claims the first of them for God (vv. 19, 26).

Mesopotamian texts describe gods, and kings who stand near them, wrapped in *melammu*, a terrifying radiance that overwhelms anyone who sees it, and gods in art wear horned crowns as a mark of divinity. Moses comes down from forty days with God with a face that shines, and Aaron and all the people are afraid to come near him (v. 30). The glory he was not allowed to see in full (33:20) now shows in his own skin, and he covers it with a veil for ordinary dealings (vv. 33–35).

notes: **Mercy first:** In 20:5–6 judgment on iniquity comes before mercy to thousands. In vv. 6–7 the order is turned around: a long run of mercy comes first, and the warning about iniquity last.

**Repetition to watch:** “covenant” comes 5 times. God’s covenant with Israel opens and closes the section (vv. 10, 27, 28); in between stands the covenant Israel must not make with the people of the land (vv. 12, 15).
“Shone” comes 3 times (vv. 29, 30, 35), and the veil 3 times (vv. 33, 34, 35).

Chapter 34 closes the golden calf section (chs. 32–34) by restoring what ch. 32 broke: new tables, a covenant restated, and Moses again going between God and the people. Chapter 35 then takes up the tabernacle plans of chs. 25–31 and begins to carry them out.
**Forward:** when Solomon’s temple is dedicated, nothing is in the ark “save the two tables of stone,” which Moses put there at Horeb (1 Kings 8:9).

traditions.text: Where the KJV says only that God will write the same words again, the Joseph Smith Translation says the second tables would not be like the first. God would take the priesthood, his holy order and its ordinances, out of Israel’s midst and give the law “after the law of a carnal commandment,” having sworn that they would not enter his presence, his rest, in their pilgrimage. D&C 84 tells the same story and adds that the lesser priesthood continued with the house of Aaron until John.

Two smaller changes concern God’s name and character. In v. 7 he will by no means clear the rebellious, and in v. 14 the LORD’s name is given as Jehovah, where the KJV reads “whose name is Jealous.” The Church’s note on the verse explains that Jehovah is one name by which the people of the Old Testament knew the Lord Jesus Christ.

When Abinadi has rebuked the priests of king Noah, they dare not lay hands on him, because the Spirit of the Lord is upon him and “his face shone with exceeding luster,” as Moses’ did on Sinai. He then recites to them the commandments Moses brought down from the mount.

Rabbi Yohanan says that in v. 6 God wrapped himself in a prayer shawl like a leader of public prayer and showed Moses the order of prayer: whenever Israel sins, let them recite these attributes of mercy and he will forgive. Rav Yehuda adds that a covenant was made with the thirteen attributes that they would never return empty, reading v. 10, “Behold, I make a covenant,” with them. The thirteen attributes are still recited in Jewish prayers of repentance.

Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi tells his sons to honor an elder who has forgotten his learning through no fault of his own, because both the whole tables and the broken tables were kept in the ark. The pieces of the first tables, smashed in ch. 32, stayed holy and traveled with the new set made here.

The command not to seethe a kid in its mother’s milk appears three times in the Torah: here, at 23:19, and at Deuteronomy 14:21. The school of Rabbi Ishmael took the three as three bans, on eating meat cooked in milk, on profiting from it, and on cooking it. Targum Onkelos already renders v. 26 as a ban on eating meat with milk, the basis of the Jewish separation of meat and dairy.

Rashi explains “hew thee” with a parable from Midrash Tanchuma: a king’s bride was disgraced by her maids, and the king’s friend tore up the marriage contract to save her; once the king was reconciled, he told the friend to buy new paper and he would write it himself. Moses broke the first covenant, so he cuts the new stones, and God writes. On v. 29 Rashi notes that the verb for “shone” is related to “horns,” since light projects like a horn, and says the rays began in the cleft where God’s hand covered Moses’ face (33:22).

Philo says Moses spent the forty days without bodily food, fed by contemplation, and came down far more beautiful in face than when he went up. Those who saw him were amazed and could not bear to look at him, since “his countenance shone like the light of the sun.” Abinadi’s shining face (above) is described the same way.

Paul compares the glory on Moses’ face, which Israel could not steadily look at, with the greater glory of the covenant written by the Spirit. He reads the veil of vv. 33–35 as hiding the end of what was passing away, says the same veil lies on hearts when Moses is read, and says it is taken away when one turns to the Lord. Then believers, with open face, are “changed into the same image” from glory to glory.

Jerome’s Latin translation says in v. 29 that Moses did not know his face was “horned” (*cornuta*), taking the Hebrew verb from its link to the word for horn. Medieval artists followed the Latin, which is why Michelangelo’s Moses in Rome has horns. Rashi (above) knew the same link but explained it as rays of light.

35.overview:
Moses gathers the whole congregation and gives them the LORD’s commands. First the Sabbath: six days of work, a seventh of rest, and no fire kindled in their homes. Then a call for an offering from everyone of a willing heart, of metals, yarns, skins, wood, oil, spices, and gems, and for every skilled worker to come and make the tabernacle and all its parts. The people go out and come back with their gifts. Men and women bring jewelry, the women spin yarn and goats’ hair, and the rulers bring the stones for the ephod and breastplate. Moses ends by naming Bezaleel and Aholiab as the craftsmen and teachers.

Almost every line repeats the instructions of chs. 25–31. What is new is the response. The word “heart” comes 9 times in the chapter, for the willing heart that gives and the wise heart that makes.

35.hermeneutics:
Mesopotamian kings boasted of their temple building. Gudea of Lagash, about 2100 BC, tells on two clay cylinders how the god Ningirsu showed him in a dream the house he wanted, how Gudea raised a levy from the clans of his city, and how timber, stone, and copper came to him from Elam, Susa, Magan, and Meluhha. In Exodus the plan also comes from God (25:9), but the materials are not levied or carried in by foreign peoples. They come from Israel’s own households, from “whosoever is of a willing heart” (v. 5), so freely that Moses later has to stop the giving (36:5–7).

In the Ugaritic Baal Cycle the craftsman god Kothar builds Baal a palace of cedar, silver, and gold. A fire burns inside it for six days, and on the seventh the silver and gold are found worked into plates and bricks. Building a god’s house could be told on a seven-day pattern. Exodus opens its building account with the seventh day as a day when no work is done and no fire is kindled (vv. 2–3), before a single gift is collected.

Spinning and weaving were largely women’s work in the ancient Near East, and valuable work. Letters from the Old Assyrian merchant colony at Kanesh in Anatolia (19th century BC) show wives in the city of Assur making woolen cloth that their husbands’ caravans sold abroad. Verses 25–26 count the women who spin blue, purple, scarlet, linen, and goats’ hair as givers in their own right, and call their skill being “wise hearted,” the same term used for the craftsmen.

**Ch. 31 reversed:** chapter 31 gave the craftsmen first and the Sabbath last. Here the Sabbath opens (vv. 1–3) and the craftsmen close (vv. 30–35), so the instructions and the building frame the golden calf story between them.

Chapter 35 begins the last section of Exodus (35:1–40:38): the making of everything commanded in chs. 25–31, told in nearly the same words. It opens with Moses gathering the congregation (v. 1), and the section ends when the work is finished and the glory of the LORD fills the tabernacle (40:33–35).
**Backward:** the willing offering answers the first command of the tabernacle instructions, to take an offering from “every man that giveth it willingly with his heart” (25:2).

traditions.text: Commanding the Saints at Nauvoo to build a temple, the Lord calls them to come “with all your gold, and your silver,” with precious stones, iron, copper, brass, and all their precious things, and build a house for the Most High to dwell in. He explains that he commanded Moses to build a tabernacle and carry it in the wilderness so that ordinances hidden from before the world was might be revealed.

Exodus asks for gifts only from the willing-hearted. D&C 64 says the Lord “requireth the heart and a willing mind,” and Moroni 7 warns that a gift given grudgingly by an evil man counts as if he had kept it. Both make the giver’s heart part of the gift, as vv. 5, 21, and 29 do.

Nephi, newly settled in the promised land, teaches his people to build and to work in wood, iron, copper, brass, steel, gold, silver, and precious ores, and then builds a temple after the manner of Solomon’s, though with fewer precious things, since they were not to be found in that land. As in Exodus, the craftsmen’s skills come first and a house for God follows.

The Mishnah lists thirty-nine kinds of work forbidden on the Sabbath, from sowing and plowing to spinning, weaving, writing two letters, and kindling a fire. Rabbi Hanina bar Hama explains the list: it matches the kinds of work done to build the tabernacle. Rashi notes that Moses gives the Sabbath warning before the building command in vv. 1–3 to show that the building does not set the Sabbath aside.
traditions.cite: Mishnah Shabbat 7:2; Shabbat 49b; Rashi on Exodus 35:2

traditions.text: The rabbis ask why v. 3 singles out kindling fire when all work is already banned. Rabbi Natan says it was singled out to show that each kind of work counts as a separate offense; Rabbi Yose says it was singled out as a lesser prohibition. Rabbi Natan also finds the thirty-nine labors in the opening words of v. 1, “These are the words,” by counting the plural, the article, and the letters of “these.”

Rabbi Yitzhak learns from v. 30 that a leader may be appointed only after consulting the community. God asks Moses whether Bezaleel suits him, Moses says that whatever suits God suits him, and God tells him to ask Israel anyway; the people give the same answer. Moses’ words “See, the LORD hath called by name Bezaleel” are read as that consultation.

Rashi reads v. 22 to say the men came “with the women,” following close behind them. The rulers came last, he says, following Numbers Rabbah, because they planned to supply whatever the people left lacking; when the people gave everything, only the stones for the ephod and breastplate remained. For that delay a letter is missing from their title in v. 27.

Josephus says everyone was eager to further the work even beyond their ability, and that the women too were ambitious to do their part on the priests’ garments. He makes Bezaleel “the grandson of Miriam,” Moses’ sister, and says the people would have chosen the same craftsmen had the choice been theirs. Pirkei de-Rabbi Eliezer likewise makes Hur, Bezaleel’s grandfather, the son of Miriam.

Answering critics who said Israel wrongly took goods from the Egyptians (12:35–36), Irenaeus points out that the tabernacle was built from those very spoils, an argument he credits to an elder he had heard. Christians do the same, he says, when they put wealth gained in their pagan past to the Lord’s use, and so build the tabernacle of God in themselves.

In a letter to his student Gregory, Origen guesses where the Egyptian gold went: the best into the ark, mercy seat, and cherubim, a lesser grade into the candlestick and table, and Egyptian cloth into the embroidered work. He makes it a picture of Greek learning put to the service of Christian teaching, the same image Irenaeus (above) applies to property.

Stephen recalls that the fathers had “the tabernacle of witness” made after the pattern Moses had seen. Hebrews walks through the furniture listed in vv. 11–19, from candlestick, table, and shewbread to veil, ark, mercy seat, and cherubim, and reads it all as a figure pointing to Christ, who entered the true holy place by his own blood.

36.overview:
Bezaleel, Aholiab, and the skilled workers receive the people's gifts from Moses and begin to build. The gifts keep arriving every morning until the craftsmen report that the people have brought far more than the work needs, and Moses has it proclaimed through the camp that no one should bring anything more. The rest of the chapter makes the dwelling's fabric and frame: ten linen curtains joined with gold clasps, a tent of goats' hair, two leather coverings, acacia frames standing in silver sockets, the bars that hold them, the veil woven with cherubim, and the hanging for the door.

From v. 8 on, the chapter repeats Exodus 26 almost word for word, with “he made” where ch. 26 had “thou shalt make.” What is new is vv. 1–7: a people who have to be told to stop giving, only a few chapters after they handed over their gold for a calf (32:2–4).

36.hermeneutics:
Wooden frames, sockets, and gold sheathing were a known way to build furniture that could travel. The canopy of Queen Hetepheres, mother of Khufu (c. 2600 BC), is a frame of wooden poles cased in gold and joined with tenons and sockets, made to be taken down and set up again and hung with curtains. In Tutankhamun's burial chamber a linen pall decorated with gilded rosettes hung over a gilded wooden frame. Against that background, vv. 20–34 describe real technology for royal and sacred shrines.

The vocabulary was familiar too. At Ugarit on the Syrian coast (13th century BC), gods live in dwellings called by the same two words Exodus uses, *ohel* (“tent”) and *mishkan* (“tabernacle”), and the Ugaritic word for a tent frame matches the Hebrew *qeresh*, the “boards” of v. 20. The Ugaritic Kirta epic closes a divine assembly with the gods going home to their tents and tabernacles, and 18th-century BC letters from Mari speak of setting up heavy tent frames with a related word. A God who lived in a tent among his people fit a category the first hearers already knew.

The builders are the difference. In Ugarit's Baal myth the craftsman god Kothar-wa-Khasis, a name meaning roughly “skilled and clever,” builds Baal's palace of silver and gold. Exodus gives the work to human artisans, credits their skill to the LORD (v. 1), and pays for it with gifts the people bring of their own accord, so many that Moses has to stop them.
