notes: The repetition is deliberate. Telling the plan twice, once as command and once as deed, shows that nothing was left out or changed. Ch. 26's instructions for where things go (26:33–35) and its reminder of the pattern shown on the mount (26:30) drop out, since they belong to the setting up in ch. 40.
**The order changes.** Chs. 25–26 begin with the ark and end with the tent. The builders here start with the tent, and the ark waits until 37:1.
**Work:** The Hebrew word for work (*melakhah*) appears 9 times in vv. 1–7, as the giving outruns the making.

Chapters 35–40 tell the building of the tabernacle and mirror the instructions of chs. 25–31. The golden calf and the renewed covenant (chs. 32–34) stand between the two halves, so the dwelling is built by a people who have already broken the covenant and been forgiven. Chapter 36 finishes the opening of the unit (35:4–36:7) and starts the work itself.
**Looking back and ahead:** The free gifts answer the call of 25:2 and 35:5. Every later sanctuary in Israel's story picks up the same curtains, cherubim, and veil (1 Kings 6:29–32; Hebrews 10:20).

traditions.text: The revelation calling the Saints to build the Nauvoo Temple begins much as Exodus 35–36 does, with a call for materials. Messengers are to invite people to come with their gold, silver, precious stones, iron, copper, and brass, and build a house “for the Most High to dwell therein.” Later in the same revelation the Lord points back to the tabernacle Moses was commanded to build and carry in the wilderness, as the earlier pattern for a house where hidden ordinances would be revealed (124:38).

The Greek translation tells chs. 35–40 in a shorter form and a different order. Right after the gifts of 36:1–7 it moves to the priestly garments, which the Hebrew puts in ch. 39, and only then makes the curtains and frames. Scholars still debate whether the translator abridged and rearranged or worked from a different Hebrew text.

His retelling makes Bezaleel the grandson of Miriam, Moses' sister, since Josephus elsewhere makes Hur her husband. He says the people gave with such eagerness, each trying to outdo the others, that Moses had to restrain them by proclamation once the craftsmen reported there was enough. He adds that the women competed to work on the priests' garments.

Philo reads the curtains' numbers as meaningful: ten curtains for the perfect number, 28 cubits long, a “perfect” number equal to the sum of its factors. The four materials of vv. 8 and 35 stand for the four elements: linen from earth, purple from water, blue for air, scarlet for fire. Josephus and Clement of Alexandria read the colors the same way.

Rabbi Shmuel bar Nahmani notices the order of this chapter. In the Talmud's telling, Moses gave Bezaleel the order of chs. 25–26, ark first, but Bezaleel objected that people build a house before they furnish it. Moses answered that he must have been “in the shadow of God,” a pun on his name (*Betzal-El*), because that was indeed God's order. Rashi repeats the story on 38:22.

Rabbi Yohanan finds the Sabbath law against carrying between domains in v. 6. Moses sat in the Levites' camp, a public area, and told the people not to carry their gifts out of their own tents into it. The Talmud links the proclamation to a Sabbath and treats Moses' order to stop giving as a halt to carrying as well as a report that there was enough.

Rashi, following a midrash, explains why the tribal princes gave last, bringing only the onyx and other stones (35:27). They had planned to let the people give first and make up whatever was missing. When v. 7 reported that there was already enough and to spare, little was left for them to bring, and Rashi notes that their title is spelled with a letter missing to mark their slowness.

Ramban reads vv. 3–7 as praise for everyone involved: the people for giving so freely, the craftsmen for honestly reporting the surplus, and Moses for stopping the gifts. Unlike other rulers, Moses showed he had no desire for the people's silver and gold, as he later says he took not one ass from them (Numbers 16:15). Ramban also counts five tellings of the tabernacle in Exodus, with this chapter beginning the fifth and most detailed.

Stephen's defense recalls that Israel's fathers had “the tabernacle of witness in the wilderness,” made by God's appointment after the fashion Moses had seen. He uses it to argue that God does not live in houses made with hands. Hebrews 8:5 cites the same pattern command to say the tabernacle copied heavenly things.

The veil of v. 35 kept everyone but the high priest out of the most holy place. Hebrews reads it as a figure of Christ's body: believers now enter “through the veil, that is to say, his flesh.” The Gospels report that the temple veil, the veil's successor, was torn at his death (Matthew 27:51).

Clement says the covering and veil were woven of blue, purple, scarlet, and linen to show that the elements of nature themselves reveal God. He takes the veil's four pillars as a sign of the four letters of the divine name. His reading of the colors follows Philo and Josephus closely.

37.overview:
Bezaleel makes the furniture of the sanctuary. He builds the ark of acacia wood overlaid with gold, with rings and poles for carrying it, and sets on it a mercy seat of pure gold with two cherubim hammered from the same piece, wings spread and faces turned toward the seat. Then he makes the table and its gold dishes, the seven-lamp lampstand beaten from a single talent of gold, and the incense altar with its horns. The chapter ends with the anointing oil and the incense.

Almost every line repeats the instructions of 25:10–39 and 30:1–5, 22–38, now in the past tense. What drops out is just as telling. In ch. 25 the LORD promised to meet Moses above the mercy seat (25:22). Here the seat is finished, but nobody speaks from it yet. That waits until the glory arrives in 40:34.

37.hermeneutics:
Winged guardians around a throne were royal furniture across the Levant. An ivory plaque from Megiddo (Late Bronze Age) shows a ruler seated on a throne whose sides are winged sphinxes, and the sarcophagus of King Ahiram of Byblos shows the same kind of throne. Israel's own phrase for its God was the one “which dwelleth between the cherubims” (1 Samuel 4:4), and David calls the ark “the footstool of our God” (1 Chronicles 28:2). Read with those thrones in mind, vv. 6–9 build a throne and its footstool. The seat itself is left empty: there is no statue, only the space above the wings.

Sacred chests carried on poles were familiar in Egypt. Priests carried the gods in boat-shaped shrines on poles during festivals, and Tutankhamun's tomb held a wooden shrine sheathed in gold, mounted on carrying poles, with a figure of the jackal god Anubis on its lid. The ark matches the form: wood, gold overlay, rings, and staves (vv. 3–5). It differs in what sits on top and inside. The cherubim face the mercy seat, and the box will hold the covenant tablets (40:20) where an Egyptian shrine held an image.

The lampstand is a gold tree. Its cups are shaped like almond blossoms (vv. 19–20), and the almond, the first tree to flower in the Israelite year, gave Jeremiah a wordplay on God's watchfulness (Jeremiah 1:11–12). Stylized trees of life were common in the art of the region, so a lamp in the form of a flowering tree, set before the veil, would have read as life and light in God's house.

**Gold:** The word for gold appears 20 times in 29 verses, in both the Hebrew (*zahav*) and the KJV, with “pure gold” 9 times. Every item in the chapter is gold or covered with it.
**Moved items:** The incense altar, held back in the instructions until ch. 30, now stands with the other holy-place furniture.

Chapters 35–40 carry out the instructions of chs. 25–31. Chapter 36 built the dwelling; ch. 37 furnishes the holy place and the most holy place, working from the inside out. Chapter 38 moves outside to the bronze altar, the laver, and the court.

**Looking ahead:** The furniture is put in place in 40:20–27. Solomon makes gold furnishings on the same plan for the temple (1 Kings 7:48–50), and Hebrews 9:2–5 lists this furniture to explain Christ's priesthood.

traditions.text: The Lord tells the Saints in Nauvoo that he commanded Moses to build a tabernacle that Israel could “bear it with them in the wilderness,” and later a house in the land of promise, so that ordinances hidden from before the world might be revealed. The rings and poles of this chapter are what made that possible. The revelation treats the portable sanctuary as the first step in a line of holy houses that leads to latter-day temples.

Rashi notices that v. 1 says “Bezaleel made the ark,” naming him alone, though many craftsmen worked on it. Following the midrash Tanhuma, he explains that Bezaleel gave himself to the work more than the others, so the ark is called by his name. Rashi links the same Bezaleel to the tradition that he knew God's intended order better than Moses' instructions (see 38:22).

Describes the cherubim as flying creatures unlike anything people have seen, though Moses said he had seen them near God's throne. He says the lampstand was cast gold weighing a talent, which the Hebrews called *kinchares*, with seventy ornaments in all. Its seven branches, he says, stood for the seven planets, counting the sun among them.

Philo reports that some read the two cherubim as the two hemispheres of the sky. His own view is that they stand for God's two highest powers: his creative power, named “God,” and his kingly power, named “Lord.” Like Josephus, he takes the lampstand's seven lamps as the seven planets, with the sun in the middle as the fourth.

A letter preserved at the start of 2 Maccabees says that before Babylon destroyed Jerusalem, Jeremiah carried the tabernacle, the ark, and the incense altar to the mountain where Moses saw the promised land. He sealed them in a cave and said the place would stay unknown until God gathered his people again. The legend accounts for the absence of the ark from the Second Temple.

Explains why the ark, made first in the instructions of ch. 25, is made only after the dwelling here. Bezaleel argued that a man builds a house before he brings in the furniture, and Moses agreed that he must have stood “in God's shadow,” a play on his name. Chapter 37 is the furniture going into the house already made.

The rabbis count the lampstand's ornaments from the description in vv. 17–22: twenty-two almond cups, eleven knobs, and nine flowers. They compare the cups to long, narrow Alexandrian goblets. Josephus, counting differently, had reached seventy ornaments.

Gives a different answer than 2 Maccabees to where the ark went. King Josiah, knowing that exile was coming, buried it so it would not be carried off. A baraita adds that the jar of manna, the anointing oil of v. 29, and Aaron's budding rod were hidden with it, and Hebrews 9:4 also puts the manna and the rod with the ark.

Hebrews walks through this chapter's furniture: the lampstand and the table in the first room, then the ark with “the cherubims of glory shadowing the mercyseat.” It adds things Exodus 37 does not mention, putting the golden censer, the pot of manna, and Aaron's rod with the ark. The writer declines to explain further and turns to Christ as the high priest who enters the true holy place.

The Greek Bible calls the mercy seat of v. 6 the *hilasterion*, “place of atonement.” Paul uses the same word when he says God set forth Christ as a “propitiation” through faith in his blood. Many interpreters read this as making Christ the new mercy seat, where atoning blood was sprinkled on the Day of Atonement (Leviticus 16:14).

John's visions reuse this chapter's furniture in heaven. The risen Christ stands among seven golden lampstands, which are the seven churches. Later the heavenly temple opens and “the ark of his testament” is seen in it, the ark that 2 Maccabees said was hidden.

Clement reports readings of the golden cherubim as the two bears of the night sky or the two hemispheres, and glosses the word cherubim as “much knowledge.” He takes the ark itself as a sign of the hidden world of thought. His hemisphere reading and his gloss both match Philo, whom he knew well.

38.overview:
Bezaleel moves outside the tent. He makes the altar of burnt offering of acacia wood covered in bronze, with its grate, rings, poles, and tools, and the bronze laver and its stand. Then he hangs the court: linen screens a hundred cubits by fifty on bronze-footed pillars with silver hooks, and an embroidered gate on the east. The chapter closes with an audit kept by Ithamar at Moses' command: about 29 talents of gold, 100 talents of silver from a half-shekel paid by 603,550 men, and 70 talents of bronze, with what each was used for.

Only the laver gets a new detail. Exodus 30:18 simply ordered a bronze basin. Verse 8 adds that it was made from the mirrors of the women who served at the door of the tent of meeting, a group otherwise mentioned only in 1 Samuel 2:22.

38.hermeneutics:
Egyptian mirrors were polished discs of copper alloy fixed to a handle, often a papyrus stem or the face of Hathor, goddess of love and beauty. The Egyptian word for mirror sounded like the word for life, and some mirrors were given to Hathor as offerings. Verse 8 takes such costly, personal objects and melts them into a washbasin. A mirror once used to make the self beautiful becomes the place where priests wash before they serve (30:19–21).

The court of vv. 9–20 is a rectangle twice as long as it is wide, a hundred cubits by fifty, with its gate in the middle of the east side. Michael Homan has compared it to the camp of Ramesses II at the battle of Kadesh (c. 1274 BC), carved at Abu Simbel, Luxor, and the Ramesseum. There too a 2:1 enclosure faces east with the entrance in the short wall, and a long reception tent leads back to a square throne room. The comparison is Homan's argument, not a consensus, but if it holds, the court is laid out like a king's war camp, with the throne room at the back.

The weights in vv. 24–29 used real units. Stone weights inscribed *beka*, the half-shekel of v. 26, have been found in Judah, one of them near the Temple Mount in 2018. The totals also show the system: 603,550 half-shekels make 301,775 shekels, which the text gives as 100 talents and 1,775 shekels, so a talent here is 3,000 shekels. At roughly 11.4 grams to the shekel, that is about a ton of gold and three and a half tons of silver.

notes: **Bronze:** The word for bronze or brass (*nechoshet*) appears 15 times, in both the Hebrew and the KJV. Gold dominated the furniture inside the tent in ch. 37; outside, almost everything is bronze, with silver for hooks and bands.
**Inside to outside:** The inventory lists gold, then silver, then bronze, which is also the order from the most holy place outward. The more precious the metal, the closer it stands to the ark.
**A new heading:** “This is the sum of the tabernacle” (v. 21) opens a separate account. The weekly Torah reading named for it, *Pekudei* (“sums”), runs from here to the end of Exodus.

Chapters 35–40 carry out the instructions of chs. 25–31. Having built the tent (ch. 36) and its furniture (ch. 37), the builders now finish the court outside it. The account of metals (vv. 21–31) looks back over the whole project before the priests' clothing is made in ch. 39.

**Looking back and ahead:** The silver comes from the half-shekel ordered in 30:11–16. The same census figure reappears in Numbers 1:46, and Solomon's temple replaces the laver with a great bronze “sea” (1 Kings 7:23).

traditions.text: The laver was for washing before priests entered the tent or approached the altar (30:19–21). In the revelation on the Nauvoo Temple the Lord asks how the Saints' washings can be acceptable unless they are performed in a house built to his name. He then ties those washings, with anointings and other ordinances, to the reason he commanded Moses to build a tabernacle.

Rashi tells, from the midrash Tanhuma, that Moses wanted to refuse the women's mirrors as tools of vanity. God told him to accept them as dearer than all the other gifts. In Egypt the women had used them to win back their exhausted husbands, and so the hosts of Israel were born, which is why the women are called by a word related to “hosts.” Rashi adds that the laver later supplied the water for the test of a suspected wife (Numbers 5), making peace between husband and wife.

Ibn Ezra notes that women everywhere look in brass or glass mirrors each morning to arrange their head coverings. The women of v. 8 had turned away from worldly pleasures and no longer needed them, so they gave them up. They came every day to the door of the tent of meeting to pray and to hear the commandments. He also observes that, unlike Solomon's lavers, this one is given no measurements: its size was whatever the mirrors made.

The Aramaic translations make the women worshipers: they “came to pray” at the door of the tent. Pseudo-Jonathan adds that they brought offerings of thanks and confession after childbirth and went home to their husbands as mothers of righteous children. Both readings answer the question of what women were doing at a tent that, in Exodus' order, had only just been built.
traditions.cite: Targum Onkelos and Pseudo-Jonathan on Exodus 38:8

traditions.text: Philo says no one asked the women for their mirrors; they gave them freely, in a contest of piety with the men. Bezaleel made nothing but the laver from them, so that a priest washing there would remember what it was made of. He should look into his own mind as into a mirror and wash away whatever he finds deformed there.

Moses gives a public account of the metals because scoffers had whispered that he was growing rich. While reckoning, he forgot what had become of 1,775 shekels and worried that Israel would accuse him of taking them. Then God opened his eyes and he saw them made into the hooks of the pillars (v. 28), and all Israel was satisfied.

Rashi notices that v. 21 says “tabernacle” twice. Following the midrash, he hears in the Hebrew *mishkan* an echo of *mashkon*, “pledge”: the sanctuary would twice be taken as a pledge, destroyed for Israel's sins. He also explains “tabernacle of testimony” as testimony that God had forgiven the golden calf, since he let his presence dwell among them.

Retells the census tax with his own details. He values the shekel at four Athenian drachmae, gives the number of givers as 605,550, and says the payers were free men over twenty but under fifty. Exodus and Numbers give 603,550 and set no upper age. In his description of the court he places the laver just inside the gate, where the priests washed their hands and sprinkled their feet.

The half-shekel of v. 26 became a yearly gift for the temple's public offerings. The Mishnah has the court announce the collection on the first of Adar, a month before Nisan, the month the tabernacle was raised (40:17). A whole tractate, Shekalim, governs how the money was collected, stored, and spent.

Collectors of the temple tax, the two-drachma coin that stood for the half-shekel, ask Peter whether Jesus pays it. Jesus says the king's children are free, but to avoid offense he sends Peter to find a coin in a fish's mouth, enough for both of them. The yearly tax of the Mishnah, which Jesus pays here, grew from the half-shekel recorded in v. 26.

The priests had to wash at the laver before entering the tent. Hebrews invites every believer to draw near to God with “bodies washed with pure water,” language many readers connect with baptism. The washing once limited to priests becomes the way in for all.

39.overview:
The workers make the priests' clothing. The high priest's ephod is woven with gold thread beaten and cut from sheet gold, and two onyx stones on its shoulders carry the names of Israel. The breastplate holds twelve stones in four rows, one for each tribe, chained and laced to the ephod. Then come the blue robe with pomegranates and gold bells on its hem, linen coats, mitre, breeches, and sash, and a gold plate engraved HOLINESS TO THE LORD. The work is finished, the people bring every piece to Moses, he sees that they have done it as the LORD commanded, and he blesses them.

Listen for the refrain. “As the LORD commanded Moses” closes seven sections of the garments, then returns three more times as the work is handed over. The closing verses also borrow the words of Genesis 1–2: the work is finished, Moses looks and “behold,” and he blesses.

39.hermeneutics:
Three times the chapter says the engraving was done “like the engravings of a signet” (vv. 6, 14, 30). Seals in Israel and its neighbors were small engraved stones pressed into clay to mark ownership, and the typical Hebrew seal reads simply “belonging to” a named person. The gold plate on the high priest's forehead reads *qodesh la-YHWH*, “holy, belonging to the LORD” (v. 30), in the same form. A listener who handled seals would hear it as an owner's mark: the man who wears it, and the people whose sins he bears (28:38), belong to the LORD.

A stone emblem worn on the chest also had a known meaning in judgment. The Greek historian Diodorus (1st century BC) reports that Egypt's chief justice wore, on a gold chain around his neck, a small image of precious stones called Truth, and that hearings began when he put it on. The instructions call this piece the “breastplate of judgment” (28:15), and the Greek translators rendered the Thummim placed in it as “truth.” Chapter 39 makes the breastplate but never mentions the Urim and Thummim. They are not crafted; Moses simply puts them in when he dresses Aaron (Leviticus 8:8).

Verse 3 gives the only description of a craft technique in the whole account: gold beaten into thin sheets and cut into threads to weave with the dyed wool and linen. The result was cloth that combined the tent's own colors with gold, so the high priest dressed in the materials of the sanctuary itself.

notes: **Seven refrains:** “As the LORD commanded Moses” ends vv. 1, 5, 7, 21, 26, 29, and 31. Verses 32, 42, and 43 repeat the wording as the work is handed over, ten uses in all. Chapter 40 has its own run of seven.

**Creation words:** “Finished” in v. 32 is the verb of Genesis 2:1–2, and v. 43 pairs “saw” with “behold” as in Genesis 1:31. The finished sanctuary is presented as a small world made by God's design.
**What is missing:** The Urim and Thummim of 28:30 are not made here; they appear again only when Aaron is dressed (Leviticus 8:8).

Chapters 35–40 carry out the instructions of chs. 25–31. Chapter 39 completes the making: the priestly garments, then the hand-over of every finished piece in vv. 32–43, which closes the building account. Chapter 40 turns from making to setting up.
**Looking back and ahead:** The garments follow ch. 28 point by point. Aaron wears them for the first time in Leviticus 8, when Moses ordains him and his sons.

traditions.text: The angel Moroni tells Joseph Smith of two stones in silver bows, “fastened to a breastplate,” deposited with the gold plates. These, he says, are what is called the Urim and Thummim, used by seers in ancient times and prepared for translating the book. The pairing of breastplate and seer stones recalls Exodus 28:30, where the Urim and Thummim go in Aaron's breastplate.

The Three Witnesses are promised a view of the plates, the breastplate, the sword of Laban, and the Urim and Thummim. The revelation says these interpreters were given to the brother of Jared on the mount, so the Restoration's Urim and Thummim has its own history apart from Aaron's. The shared name ties both to revelation received through a priestly or prophetic instrument.

In his praise of Aaron, Ben Sira lists the garments of this chapter as signs of God's favor. The golden bells are there “that as he went there might be a sound” heard in the temple, the engraved stones are a memorial for the tribes, and the crown on the mitre is engraved “Holiness.” He later describes the high priest Simon of his own day putting on his robe of honour at the altar, the same garments still in use.

Retelling how Aaron stood between the living and the dead to end the plague in the wilderness (Numbers 16:46–48), Wisdom says his garments carried the universe. On his long robe was “the whole world,” on the four rows of stones the glory of the fathers, and on his diadem God's majesty. The high priest went out dressed as a figure of creation.

A Greek visitor describes the high priest Eleazar at the Jerusalem temple wearing these garments. He hears the golden bells on the robe give out a peculiar melody, sees the twelve stones of the breastplate, which he calls “the oracle of God,” flashing each its own color, and notes the gold plate with God's name in sacred letters. The sight, he says, made one feel in the presence of a man from another world.

For Philo the whole vestment is a copy of the world. The blue robe is the air, reaching from the moon to the earth as the robe reaches to the feet; its flowers stand for earth, its pomegranates for water, and its bells for the harmony between them. Wisdom of Solomon and Josephus read the garments as a cosmos in the same way.

Josephus matches the two shoulder stones to the sun and moon and the twelve breastplate stones to the months or the signs of the zodiac. He adds that the right shoulder stone shone when God was present at the sacrifices, and the breastplate blazed before a victory, so that Greeks called it the Oracle. Both stopped shining, he says, two hundred years before he wrote, because God was displeased with the breaking of his laws.

Quoting vv. 22–26, the rabbis debate how many bells hung on the robe, seventy-two or thirty-six. They also teach that each garment atoned for a sin: the robe, which makes a sound, for evil speech in public, and the plate on the forehead for brazenness, the “whore's forehead” of Jeremiah 3:3.

Rashi asks why the people brought the finished tabernacle to Moses (v. 33) instead of setting it up themselves. Following the midrash, he says its boards were too heavy for anyone to raise, and since Moses had done none of the work, God left the raising to him; Moses made the motion and it rose by itself. On v. 43 he gives Moses' blessing as a prayer that the divine presence would rest on the work of their hands (Psalm 90:17).

John sees the risen Christ in a robe reaching to the feet with a golden sash across his chest, dressed much like the high priest of this chapter. The New Jerusalem's gates carry the names of the twelve tribes, and its twelve foundations are precious stones, several of them the breastplate's (jasper, sapphire, emerald, sardius, beryl, topaz, amethyst). The tribes and the stones that Aaron wore together on his heart reappear in the walls of the holy city.

Clement takes the robe as the world of sense and the twelve stones in four rows as the zodiac turning through the four seasons, as Josephus had. He counts 360 bells on the hem, one for each day, and calls them the “acceptable year of the Lord” announcing the Savior. The gold plate on the mitre, he says, shows the royal power of Christ, the head of the church.

40.overview:
The LORD tells Moses to set up the tabernacle on the first day of the first month, put each piece in its place, and anoint the tent, its furniture, and Aaron and his sons. On that day of the second year out of Egypt, Moses does it: frames and tent, the testimony in the ark, the veil, table and bread, lampstand, incense altar, door hanging, the altar with its first offering, the laver, and the court. “So Moses finished the work.” Then the cloud covers the tent and the glory of the LORD fills it, so that Moses cannot go in. From then on the cloud by day and fire by night lead Israel's journeys.

The book ends where its story has been heading. Israel began Exodus building store cities for Pharaoh (1:11). It ends having built a dwelling for the LORD, and he moves in: the glory that rested on Sinai (24:16) now travels with the camp.

40.hermeneutics:
Temple-building stories in the ancient Near East follow a pattern: a god commands, materials are gathered, the house is built, and the god moves in. The fullest example is the cylinders of Gudea, ruler of Lagash (c. 2100 BC), on the temple Eninnu. When the work is done, the text says, a year ended and a new year began, and in its first days the god Ningirsu entered his house like a storm, followed by days of feasting. Exodus 25–40 follows the same outline, down to the new-year date (vv. 2, 17). The difference is what enters. Mesopotamian gods lived in their temples through cult statues; Exodus brings in no image at all, only a cloud and a glory too strong for Moses to approach (v. 35).

The first thing Moses puts in the ark is “the testimony” (v. 20), the tablets of the covenant (31:18). Hittite treaties of the 14th and 13th centuries BC were stored the same way. The treaty between the Hittite king Suppiluliuma and Shattiwaza of Mitanni says a copy was deposited before the storm god Teshub, and it was to be read aloud at set times. Placing the covenant document in the most holy place, under the mercy seat, put the agreement before the divine king who would hold Israel to it. Deuteronomy 31:9–13, 26 later adds the public reading.

notes: **Seven refrains:** “As the LORD commanded Moses” ends seven steps of the setting up (vv. 19, 21, 23, 25, 27, 29, 32), after a summary in v. 16. The pattern matches the seven refrains of the garments in ch. 39.
**A command held over:** The anointing of vv. 9–15 has no matching panel. It is carried out in Leviticus 8, when Aaron and his sons are ordained.
**Finished:** “So Moses finished the work” (v. 33) uses the verb and noun of Genesis 2:2, “God ended his work.” The glory then fills the tent, as the seventh day followed the finished creation.

Chapter 40 closes the unit begun in ch. 35 and the book. Chapters 35–39 made the pieces; here they are assembled, and the LORD takes up residence, fulfilling “that I may dwell among them” (25:8; 29:45).

**Looking ahead:** Leviticus opens with the LORD calling to Moses from this tent (Leviticus 1:1), and Numbers 9:15–23 expands vv. 36–38. When Solomon's temple is dedicated, the cloud fills the house and the priests cannot stand to minister, as Moses could not enter here (1 Kings 8:10–11).

traditions.text: The revelation on priesthood begins by promising a house built to the Lord in that generation, on which “a cloud shall rest,” a cloud that is the glory of the Lord filling the house. It also says the Lord confirmed a priesthood on Aaron and his seed throughout all their generations, the language of v. 15. The scene of this chapter becomes a promise for a latter-day temple.

The Lord promises that if his people build him a house and let nothing unclean enter it, his glory will rest on it and his presence will be there. If it is defiled, he will not come. The glory of v. 34 is offered again, but on a condition the tabernacle story leaves implicit.

At the dedication of the Kirtland Temple, Joseph Smith prayed that the Lord's glory would rest on the house and fill it “as with a rushing mighty wind.” A week later the Lord appeared in the temple and declared that he had accepted the house and would manifest himself there. Latter-day Saints read the occasion as a modern counterpart to the glory filling the tabernacle.

Josephus says the building took seven months and the tabernacle was consecrated at the new moon of Nisan, which the Macedonians call Xanthicus. He then softens the cloud of v. 34: under a clear sky a mist settled over the tabernacle alone, not so thick as a winter cloud nor so thin that one could see through it, and from it fell a sweet dew. The presence of God, he says, was evident to those who desired and believed it.

A teaching on v. 17 says that day “took ten crowns.” It was the first day of the week and of the month, the first day of the priesthood and of the service, the day fire first came down on the altar, the Shekhinah first rested on Israel, and the priests first blessed the people. From then on, offerings on private altars were forbidden.

Rashi sets v. 35 beside Numbers 7:89, where Moses does enter the tent to hear God speak. Following an old rule of interpretation, he lets the end of v. 35 resolve the conflict: Moses could not enter while the cloud rested on the tent, but could once it lifted. On v. 29 he adds that during the seven days of ordination Moses set the tabernacle up and took it down again, serving as priest himself.

This Aramaic paraphrase gives each anointing in vv. 9–11 a future meaning. The tabernacle is anointed for the crown of the house of Judah and the King Messiah who will redeem Israel at the end of days; the altar for Aaron's priesthood and Elijah, the great priest to be sent at the end of exile; the laver for Joshua and the Messiah son of Ephraim. The setting up of the sanctuary becomes a pledge of final redemption.

Ramban explains why Exodus ends with the tabernacle and not with the crossing of the sea or Sinai. Israel left Egypt but was still in exile, wandering in a land not its own. Only when the Divine Presence came to dwell among them again, as it had rested on the tents of the patriarchs, were they restored and the redemption complete.

After telling how Jeremiah hid the tabernacle and the ark, the letter promises that when God gathers his people, “the glory of the Lord shall appear, and the cloud also,” as it was shown under Moses and at Solomon's dedication. The cloud of this chapter becomes the sign of a future restoration.

John says the Word became flesh and “dwelt among us,” using a Greek verb built on the word for tent, and adds “we beheld his glory.” Tent and glory are the two terms of vv. 34–35. For John the presence that filled the tabernacle now lives in a human body.

The Greek Exodus says the cloud “overshadowed” the tent in v. 35. Luke uses the same verb when the angel tells Mary the power of the Highest will overshadow her, and again when a cloud overshadows the disciples at the transfiguration.

Hebrews remembers the dedication differently: Moses sprinkled the tabernacle and all its vessels with blood. Exodus 40 speaks only of anointing with oil, while blood appears at the covenant ceremony (24:6–8) and the priests' ordination (Leviticus 8:15, 30). The writer draws them together to argue that almost everything under the law was cleansed with blood.

John sees “the temple of the tabernacle of the testimony” opened in heaven and filled with smoke from God's glory, so that no one could enter until the plagues were finished, an echo of Moses shut out in v. 35. At the end of the book a voice announces that the tabernacle of God is with men and he will dwell with them.
